identification.summary: 1937CN is a Chinese hacking group that has been active since at least 2013. The group is known for targeting Vietnamese organizations, including government agencies, businesses, and media outlets. 1937CN has been linked to a number of high-profile cyberattacks, including the hacking of Vietnam Airlines in 2016 and the defacement of Vietnamese government websites in 2015.

Ababil of Minab is an emerging pro-Iranian hacktivist group with a limited public profile and little verifiable prior activity in threat intelligence reporting. The group claims responsibility for a cyberattack and allegedly possesses administrative access to targeted systems. Their pro-Iran messaging and targeting of a major US public transit authority align with known patterns of Iranian-aligned actors targeting US critical infrastructure. The use of escalatory language suggests potential for further activity.

admin@338 is a China-based cyber espionage group. FireEye says it has used newsworthy events as lures and has mostly targeted organizations involved in financial, economic and trade policy, usually with publicly available RATs such as Poison Ivy plus some non-public backdoors [S1][S6]. The name comes from a password the operators used with Poison Ivy [S3]. In March 2014 the group sent spear-phishing lures themed on Malaysian Airlines MH370 to an Asia-Pacific government and a US-based think tank [S4][S5]. In August 2015 FireEye linked it, with hedging, to spear phishing against Hong Kong media using the Dropbox-abusing LOWBALL backdoor [S1].
identification.firstObserved: Coverage of FireEye's 2013 Poison Ivy report says the group used Poison Ivy from about January 2008 [S3]. FireEye's 2015 post says FireEye had tracked the group since 2013 [S1][S7].
identification.notes: FireEye treated admin@338 as an uncategorized APT group with no APT number, saying it lacked enough information to assign one [S1]. MITRE tracks the group as admin@338 (G0018) [S6]. MISP-derived aliases TEMPER PANDA (CrowdStrike), Team338 and MAGNESIUM are already on the record. None of the sources opened for this profile give a current Microsoft Typhoon name for MAGNESIUM. Some low-quality secondary blogs equate admin@338 with APT18, Dynamite Panda, TigerMilk or Poseidon Group. Those are separately tracked clusters, and no primary source reviewed supports the merge, so they are not added.

attribution.sponsor: Not formally attributed by any government in the sources reviewed. FireEye describes the group as China-based [S1][S4].
attribution.confidence: FireEye said only that admin@338 'may have conducted' the 2015 Hong Kong media activity. It explicitly declined to attribute a second, related Dropbox-based operation to the group [S1]. The China-based assessment comes from FireEye, not from a government [S1].
attribution.basis: FireEye malware and infrastructure analysis. A BUBBLEWRAP sample in the 2015 campaign connected to a domain that resolved to an IP address the group had used before [S1]. Poison Ivy connection passwords linked the 2014 MH370 lures to the group [S4][S5]. FireEye also judged that the targets matched Beijing's likely intelligence interests [S1].

actors.objectives: Espionage. Earlier collection focused on financial, economic and trade-policy information [S1][S2]. FireEye assessed that the 2015 targeting of Hong Kong media was probably a response to political and economic challenges in Hong Kong and China. It said that access could give the government advance warning of protests, information on pro-democracy leaders, and insight needed to disrupt activity on the Internet [S1].

sectors: Financial services and financial, economic and trade-policy organizations [S1][S2]
ISP/telecommunications, government and defense (secondary per FireEye 2013) [S3]
targeting.notes: FireEye noted that the August 2015 campaign was the first it had seen from this group aimed at readers of traditional Chinese script. Earlier lures were in English and aimed at Western audiences [S1]. The campaign coincided with criminal charges against democracy activists and followed the late-2014 Umbrella Movement protests [S1].

capabilities.summary: Spear phishing with topical, news-cycle lure documents [S1][S4]. These included Word documents exploiting the old Office vulnerability CVE-2012-0158 [S1] and an executable disguised as a Flash video by binding a Flash icon to it [S4]. Malware includes the Poison Ivy RAT [S2][S4], WinHTTPHelper [S5], and the first-stage LOWBALL backdoor. LOWBALL uses the Dropbox API with a hard-coded bearer token over HTTPS port 443 for command and control, and runs operator-supplied batch files to gather directory, network, user/group, service and netstat information [S1]. The second-stage BUBBLEWRAP backdoor (Backdoor.APT.FakeWinHTTPHelper) persists at boot, communicates over HTTP, HTTPS or SOCKS, and supports plugins [S1]. Dropbox revoked the access token LOWBALL used after FireEye notified it [S1][S7].

attack.name: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location

campaigns.name: Poison Ivy espionage against finance and policy targets
campaigns.summary: In its 2013 Poison Ivy report, FireEye identified admin@338 as one of three groups (with th3bug and menuPass) using Poison Ivy in targeted attacks. It said admin@338 mainly targeted financial services, with significant activity against the ISP/telecom, government and defense sectors [S2][S3].

campaigns.name: MH370-themed spear phishing
campaigns.summary: On 10 March 2014, two days after the flight disappeared, the group sent a 'Malaysian Airlines MH370.doc' lure that dropped Poison Ivy to a government in the Asia-Pacific region. On 14 March it sent MH370-themed lures to a US-based think tank [S4][S5].

campaigns.name: Hong Kong media spear phishing (LOWBALL / Dropbox C2)
campaigns.summary: Traditional-Chinese lures about an Umbrella Movement anniversary and a Hong Kong University referendum carried CVE-2012-0158 Word exploits. They targeted Hong Kong newspapers, radio and TV, delivering LOWBALL with Dropbox command and control and the BUBBLEWRAP second stage. FireEye said admin@338 'may have' conducted the activity. It also found a possibly related second operation with up to 50 targets that it did not attribute [S1][S7].

diamond.adversary: China-based espionage group that FireEye tracks as an uncategorized APT. No government attribution has been made [S1].
diamond.capability: Topical spear-phishing lures, CVE-2012-0158 Office exploits, Poison Ivy, WinHTTPHelper, LOWBALL and BUBBLEWRAP [S1][S4][S5].
diamond.infrastructure: Legitimate cloud storage (a Dropbox account and API token) used as command and control. Dynamic-DNS-style domains such as accounts.serveftp[.]com resolving to IPs the group had used before [S1].
diamond.victim: Financial, economic and trade-policy organizations; Asia-Pacific government officials; a US think tank; Hong Kong media [S1][S2][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection aligned with Beijing's interest in economic policy and, per FireEye, in monitoring Hong Kong's pro-democracy movement and the press that covers it [S1].
diamond.technology: Unpatched Microsoft Office (CVE-2012-0158), user trust in news-related attachments, and trusted cloud services that mix C2 traffic into normal HTTPS [S1][S4].

gaps: No admin@338 activity after 2015 was found in the sources reviewed. Whether the group is still active, has been renamed or has been merged into another vendor cluster is unknown.
Microsoft's current name for MAGNESIUM, if any, was not confirmed. No Microsoft source was found.

The primary FireEye 2013 reports ('Poison Ivy: Assessing Damage and Extracting Intelligence' and 'Know Your Enemy: Tracking a Rapidly Evolving APT Actor') could not be opened. Their content here relies on press coverage [S2][S3].
The FireEye MH370 blog was seen only through a mirror and coverage. The MITRE ATT&CK, CFR Cyber Operations Tracker, Security Affairs and Dark Reading pages could not be fetched (DNS failures).
FireEye's attribution of the 2015 campaign is hedged ('may have'). The second Dropbox operation (up to 50 targets) is explicitly unattributed [S1].
Secondary blogs claim links to APT18, Dynamite Panda, TigerMilk, Poseidon Group and the MSS. None of these is supported by a primary source reviewed, so they are excluded.
Claims of a separate 2014 theft of classified MH370 investigation documents were not tied to admin@338 by any source reviewed.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): User email clients and Office document handling are key terrain, as are outbound HTTPS channels to sanctioned cloud storage, which this actor used for command and control [S1]. STEP 2 (effects): News-cycle lures (MH370, protests, political events) reach targets within days of an event, so lure risk rises during any high-profile crisis involving US or allied forces [S1][S4]. STEP 3 (adversary model): Topical spear phish, then an Office exploit or disguised executable, then a first-stage backdoor running discovery commands (directory, ipconfig, net user/group, services, netstat), then a second-stage persistent backdoor [S1]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is email-borne collection against policy, finance and think-tank-adjacent staff using topical lures and cloud-storage C2. MDCOA is persistent, low-visibility access to planning or liaison networks through trusted-cloud C2 that blends with normal traffic. Candidate indicators: Office documents exploiting CVE-2012-0158; executables with Flash icons; Dropbox API calls from non-browser processes with bearer tokens; files named [COMPUTER_NAME]_upload.bat or _download; connections to accounts.serveftp[.]com [S1][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: Track news-event lure activity and cloud-service API use from unusual processes. FireEye's case shows that defender-provider coordination (Dropbox revoking the token) can sever C2 [S1]. Authorities: Disrupting actor use of a commercial cloud account depends on the provider and on law-enforcement or industry channels, not DoD action. Mission assurance: Patch legacy Office vulnerabilities and restrict executable attachments, because the documented access vectors are old exploits and disguised executables [S1][S4]. Coordination: Share indicators with cloud providers, and with partners whose staff (think tanks, policy and finance liaisons) were historically targeted [S1][S4].

provenance.importedSummary: China-based cyber threat group. It has previously used newsworthy events as lures to deliver malware and has primarily targeted organizations involved in financial, economic, and trade policy, typically using publicly available RATs such as PoisonIvy, as well as some non-public backdoors. This threat actor targets prodemocratic activists and organizations in Hong Kong, European and international financial institutions, and a U.S.-based think tank.

identification.summary: Iran-based group that MITRE says has been active since at least 2010 and moved from website defacement to malware-based cyber espionage by 2014, targeting the US defense industrial base and Iranian users of anti-censorship tools [S1]. FireEye's Operation Saffron Rose report described the group using fake conference lures, spoofed login pages and 'Stealer' malware that exfiltrated data over FTP [S4]. CrowdStrike tracks the same activity as FLYING KITTEN [S3]. MITRE also associates the Rocket Kitten / Operation Woolen-Goldfish reporting with this group as a potential relationship [S1].
identification.firstObserved: MITRE: active since at least 2010 (defacement era) [S1]. CrowdStrike: tracking as FLYING KITTEN since mid-January 2014 [S3]. Rocket Kitten reporting: operating since at least mid-2014 [S8].
identification.notes: No Microsoft threat-actor name was found for this cluster in the sources gathered. MITRE G0130 groups Ajax Security Team, Flying Kitten, Operation Saffron Rose, AjaxTM, Operation Woolen-Goldfish and Rocket Kitten, but describes the Rocket Kitten link only as a 'potential relationship' based on infrastructure, tools and modes of operation [S1]. Ajax/Saffron Rose/Flying Kitten reporting comes from FireEye and CrowdStrike (2014) [S3]; Rocket Kitten, Woolen-Goldfish and Thamar Reservoir reporting comes from Trend Micro, ClearSky and Check Point (2015) [S5][S6][S8][S9]. Facts are kept attributed to the reporting vendor.

attribution.sponsor: Iran (suspected). FireEye assessed the Ajax Security Team was likely backed by the Iranian government but could not say whether it operated alone or within a larger coordinated effort [S4]. Press coverage of Check Point's Rocket Kitten report linked the group to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, though Check Point's own wording was more cautious [S9].
attribution.confidence: Vendor assessments only. FireEye: suspected Iranian-government backing; press coverage is inconsistent, with some quoting the report as calling the government relationship inconclusive [S4]. Trend Micro: Woolen-Goldfish 'possibly state-sponsored' [S5]. ClearSky: evidence points to Iranian hackers [S6]. Check Point: suggested an official body may have recruited local hackers; press coverage linked the group to the IRGC [S9]. No government attribution was found in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Persian-language and Iran time-zone settings on most victim machines found on one C2 server [S4]; Iranian forum origins and defacement history [S1][S4]; Persian-language references in code (Rocket Kitten, per researchers Anderson and Guarnieri) [S10]; operational-security failures exposing a developer persona 'Wool3n.H4T' [S9].

actors.objectives: Espionage supporting Iranian state interests: collecting information from US defense contractors and monitoring Iranian dissidents and users of anti-censorship tools [S4]. Trend Micro and ClearSky judged Rocket Kitten was not after monetary gain but was keeping tabs on individuals affiliated with foreign-policy and defense actors [S8]. ClearSky assessed Thamar Reservoir access was sought for espionage or other nation-state interests [S6].

sectors: Diplomacy, defense and security, journalism, human rights [S6]
targeting.notes: FireEye identified 77 victims on one C2 server, most with Persian-language and Iran time-zone settings [S4]. ClearSky counted about 550 targets, mostly in the Middle East, in the Thamar Reservoir / Rocket Kitten activity [S6][S8]. Citizen Lab's 2015 diaspora 2FA-phishing report shares infrastructure and tactics with earlier Iranian campaigns but does not name this group [S7].

capabilities.summary: Low-to-moderate sophistication social engineering and credential theft. Spearphishing with fake conference (IEEE) lures and spoofed credential pages such as Outlook Web Access, followed by prompts to install a fake 'browser patch' [S3][S4]. Custom 'Stealer' malware exfiltrating data over FTP [S4]. Trojanized anti-censorship software [S4]. Rocket Kitten used GHOLE malware, a modified version of a Core Security penetration-testing tool, and later OneDrive links to files posing as PowerPoint presentations [S5]. Thamar Reservoir activity combined compromised trusted websites hosting fake pages, multi-stage malware, phone calls and social-media messages [S6]. Real-time phishing designed to defeat Gmail two-factor authentication was documented against Iranian diaspora targets (not attributed by name) [S7]. Telegram account takeover via intercepted SMS codes and abuse of Telegram's API to enumerate 15 million Iranian phone numbers was attributed to Rocket Kitten by outside researchers [S10]. ClearSky judged the operators technically unsophisticated and prone to mistakes [S6].

campaigns.name: Website defacements
campaigns.summary: MITRE says the group has been active since at least 2010, initially defacing websites before moving to espionage by 2014.

campaigns.name: FLYING KITTEN tracking begins
campaigns.summary: CrowdStrike begins tracking FLYING KITTEN, observing targeting of multiple US defense contractors and political dissidents using spoofed login pages and 'Browser Patch' stealer downloads.

campaigns.name: Operation Saffron Rose
campaigns.summary: FireEye reports Ajax Security Team espionage against the US defense industrial base and Iranian anti-censorship tool users, with Stealer malware and 77 victims on one C2 server.

campaigns.name: Operation Woolen-Goldfish / GHOLE
campaigns.summary: Trend Micro reports Rocket Kitten spearphishing of Israeli and European organizations using GHOLE malware and OneDrive-hosted lures.

campaigns.name: Thamar Reservoir
campaigns.summary: ClearSky details an Iranian campaign against about 550 Middle East targets in diplomacy, defense, journalism and human rights, named after targeted Israeli researcher Thamar E. Gindin.

campaigns.name: Two-factor authentication phishing of Iranian diaspora
campaigns.summary: Citizen Lab documents phone-call-initiated real-time phishing to bypass Gmail 2FA; shares infrastructure with earlier Iranian campaigns but is not attributed by name.

campaigns.name: Rocket Kitten 2 (The Spy Kittens Are Back)
campaigns.summary: Trend Micro and ClearSky report continued Rocket Kitten targeting of Israelis, Iranian exiles and opponents of Iran, focused on personal accounts.

campaigns.name: Rocket Kitten: A Campaign With 9 Lives
campaigns.summary: Check Point exposes main developer persona 'Wool3n.H4T' after gaining access to a misconfigured group phishing server and a C2 server.

campaigns.name: Telegram account compromises
campaigns.summary: Researchers attribute compromise of more than a dozen Telegram accounts and enumeration of 15 million Iranian phone numbers to Rocket Kitten (reporting Reuters).

diamond.adversary: Iran-based operators who emerged from Iranian hacker forums and defacement activity; developer persona 'Wool3n.H4T' exposed by Check Point [S1][S4][S9].
diamond.capability: Spearphishing, spoofed login pages, Stealer malware, GHOLE malware, trojanized anti-censorship tools, real-time 2FA phishing, SMS-code interception [S3][S4][S5][S10].
diamond.infrastructure: Typosquat domains spoofing target organizations, FTP exfiltration servers, compromised trusted websites hosting fake pages, OneDrive-hosted lures [S3][S5][S6].
diamond.victim: US defense contractors; Iranian dissidents, activists and anti-censorship users; Israeli and European researchers, diplomats, journalists and defense personnel [S3][S5][S6][S10].
diamond.socioPolitical: Monitoring of regime opponents and collection on foreign-policy and defense communities of interest to Iran [S4][S8].
diamond.technology: Webmail and OWA credential flows, SMS-based authentication, consumer messaging apps (Telegram) and personal accounts that bridge into corporate networks [S3][S8][S10].

gaps: Cluster boundary: MITRE treats Rocket Kitten as only a potential relationship to Ajax Security Team; FireEye/CrowdStrike (Ajax/Flying Kitten) and Trend Micro/ClearSky/Check Point (Rocket Kitten) reporting may describe distinct but related clusters [S1].
No Microsoft threat-actor name, and no US government attribution or indictment, was found for this cluster.

Primary documents not opened directly: FireEye Saffron Rose PDF, Check Point 'Campaign With 9 Lives' report, Trend Micro white papers, ClearSky Thamar Reservoir PDF and the MITRE G0130 page (WebFetch failed); details rely on search-result summaries and press coverage.
The FireEye PDF is labeled 2013 while coverage dates publication to May 2014; exact publication date unverified.
Citizen Lab's 2015 2FA phishing report does not attribute the activity to a named group; inclusion here reflects shared Iranian infrastructure only [S7].
Imported aliases Group 26, Sayad, Timberworm, TEMP.Beanie and Thamar Reservoir were not confirmed by a source gathered in this pass.
No reporting on activity after 2016 was found; current status (dissolved, renamed or absorbed into other Iranian clusters) is unknown.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): key terrain is identity rather than networks: personal webmail, OWA portals, SMS-based 2FA and messaging accounts of defense staff, analysts and dissident contacts [S3][S7][S10]. STEP 2 (effects): personal-account compromise lets the actor bridge from weakly defended home networks into corporate accounts [S8]. STEP 3 (threat evaluation): template is spoofed domain or lure (fake conference, OneDrive document), credential capture, then a stealer or GHOLE implant with FTP exfiltration [S4][S5]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is persistent credential phishing of defense-industry and policy personnel and their personal accounts for espionage [S3][S8]. MDCOA is real-time 2FA bypass or SMS interception against personnel with access to mission systems, enabling account takeover and contact-network mapping [S7][S10]. Candidate indicators: lookalike domains of the unit or contractor, unsolicited conference invitations, 'browser patch' download prompts after login, unexpected 2FA codes or calls from foreign numbers, outbound FTP from user endpoints [S3][S4][S7].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: fuse phishing reports from personal and official accounts, since this actor targets both [S8]. Authorities: personal and diaspora-contact accounts fall outside DODIN defensive authority; coordinate with counterintelligence and law enforcement. Mission assurance: phishing-resistant MFA instead of SMS codes and awareness training for staff targeted via conference and Iran-studies lures [S4][S7][S10]. Coordination: share lookalike-domain and C2 indicators with DIB partners, who were primary 2014 victims [S3].

identification.summary: Amaranth-Dragon is a previously untracked threat actor assessed to be closely linked to the China-affiliated APT 41 ecosystem, exhibiting similar tooling and operational patterns. The group demonstrated technical maturity by rapidly operationalizing CVE-2025-8088, a vulnerability in WinRAR, shortly after its public disclosure. Check Point Research has identified multiple campaigns targeting Cambodia, Thailand, Laos, Indonesia, Singapore, and the Philippines, with operations typically focused on one or two countries at a time. The overlaps in technical and operational indicators strongly suggest that Amaranth-Dragon is either affiliated with or part of the broader APT-41 ecosystem.

identification.summary: Angry Likho is an APT group that has been active since 2023, primarily targeting large organizations and government agencies in Russia and Belarus. Their attacks typically involve spear-phishing emails with malicious attachments, such as RAR archives, and utilize a known payload, the Lumma stealer, for data exfiltration. The group employs a compact infrastructure and has been linked to espionage activities, particularly in sectors like aviation and pharmaceuticals. Their operations have shown a focus on collecting sensitive information, including cryptowallet files and user credentials.

Antique Typhoon (formerly tracked as Storm-0558) is a China-based threat actor that Microsoft says has espionage objectives and mainly seeks unauthorized access to employee email accounts at targeted organizations [S1][S8]. In 2023 it used an acquired Microsoft account (MSA) consumer signing key to forge authentication tokens and read Exchange Online and Outlook.com email at about 25 organizations, including government agencies [S1]. The US Cyber Safety Review Board (CSRB) later found the intrusion was preventable and resulted from 'a cascade of security failures at Microsoft' [S6][S7].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft: interest in OAuth applications, token theft and token replay since at least August 2021 [S1]. Forged-token email access began 2023-05-15 [S1]. CSRB Acting Deputy Chair Dmitri Alperovitch said industry has tracked the actor for over two decades (reporting) [S6].
identification.notes: Microsoft renamed Storm-0558 to Antique Typhoon in an August 2024 update to its July 2023 analysis [S1]; Microsoft's naming map lists Storm-0558 as the other name [S8]. Microsoft reports minor overlaps with Violet Typhoon (ZIRCONIUM, APT31) but holds high confidence that this is a distinct group [S1]. No MITRE ATT&CK group ID was found.

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China (assessed). Microsoft calls the actor China-based with espionage objectives [S1]. Press coverage of the CSRB report describes the group as affiliated with the PRC; China has denied involvement [S5][S6].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft assesses with moderate confidence that the actor is China-based, and with high confidence that it is distinct from Violet Typhoon [S1]. The CSRB report characterizes the actor as PRC-affiliated (per press coverage; the report text was not opened) [S6]. No indictment or sanctions naming this actor were found.
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and incident response, including activity hours matching China Standard Time, Monday to Friday [S1]; CSRB review of the 2023 intrusion (via press coverage) [S6][S7].

actors.objectives: Espionage through collection of email from government, diplomatic, economic and legislative targets, with particular focus on US and European bodies and on individuals tied to Taiwan and Uyghur geopolitical interests [S1]. In the 2023 campaign, nine of ten compromised State Department accounts reportedly belonged to people working on East Asia and the Pacific [S5].

sectors: Individuals tied to Taiwan and Uyghur interests [S1]
targeting.notes: The 2023 campaign hit about 25 organizations per Microsoft [S1]; CSRB coverage cites 22 organizations and over 500 individuals, including Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo, US Ambassador to China R. Nicholas Burns and Congressman Don Bacon [S7]. About 60,000 unclassified emails were taken from 10 State Department accounts, along with a list of the department's email accounts (reporting a Senate briefing and State Department confirmation) [S5].

capabilities.summary: Cloud identity abuse is the signature capability. The actor forged Azure AD and MSA tokens with an acquired MSA consumer signing key, which Microsoft code accepted for enterprise tokens because of a validation error, and abused a flaw in the GetAccessTokenForResource API to mint new tokens from issued ones [S1]. It ran a custom web panel for token replay, used dedicated SoftEther proxy infrastructure, and used PowerShell and Python scripts with hardcoded bearer tokens to call the OWA Exchange Store REST service, optionally over Tor or SOCKS5 [S1]. Wiz assessed the key could have signed OpenID v2.0 tokens for other Azure AD applications such as SharePoint, Teams and OneDrive, though no exploitation of those services was confirmed [S3][S9]. Historically Microsoft has seen phishing, credential harvesting, exploitation of public-facing applications leading to China Chopper web shells, the Cigril malware launched via DLL search-order hijacking, and credential theft from LSASS memory and the SAM hive [S1]. Microsoft's September 2023 account of key theft (crash dump moved to a corporate debugging environment, then a compromised engineer account) was later revised: in March 2024 Microsoft said it had not found a crash dump containing the key [S2].

campaigns.name: Early OAuth and token-theft interest
campaigns.summary: Microsoft says the actor has shown interest in OAuth applications, token theft and token replay since at least August 2021 [S1].

campaigns.name: Exchange Online / Outlook.com forged-token intrusion
campaigns.summary: Using forged tokens signed with an acquired MSA consumer key, the actor accessed email at about 25 organizations, including government agencies [S1]. A federal agency detected anomalous MailItemsAccessed events and reported them; Microsoft began its investigation on 2023-06-16 and blocked the key [S1][S4]. About 60,000 State Department emails were stolen [S5].

campaigns.name: CISA/FBI advisory AA23-193A
campaigns.summary: CISA and the FBI released advisory AA23-193A on detecting the activity through enhanced logging, including MailItemsAccessed [S4].

campaigns.name: Microsoft key-acquisition findings
campaigns.summary: Microsoft published its most probable explanation of how the key was obtained, then revised it on 2024-03-12 after finding no crash dump containing the key [S2].

campaigns.name: CSRB review published
campaigns.summary: The CSRB concluded the intrusion was preventable and faulted Microsoft's security culture; it recommended security reforms by Microsoft and other cloud providers (reporting) [S6][S7].

campaigns.name: Rename to Antique Typhoon
campaigns.summary: Microsoft updated its analysis to track Storm-0558 as Antique Typhoon [S1].

diamond.adversary: China-based espionage actor (Microsoft, moderate confidence), active on China Standard Time working hours [S1]; described as PRC-affiliated in CSRB coverage [S6].
diamond.capability: Forged MSA/Azure AD tokens, token replay panel, PowerShell and Python OWA scripts, China Chopper web shells, Cigril malware, credential dumping [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: Dedicated token-replay servers with a web panel at /#/login, SoftEther proxy hosts fingerprinted by JARM, Tor and SOCKS5 routing [S1].
diamond.victim: About 25 organizations incl. US government agencies and associated consumer accounts [S1]; State Department, Commerce Secretary and other officials [S5][S7].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection on US and European diplomacy and East Asia policy, plus Taiwan- and Uyghur-related individuals [S1][S5].
diamond.technology: Microsoft cloud identity: MSA consumer signing keys, Azure AD token validation, Exchange Online/OWA, Outlook.com [S1][S3].

gaps: How the actor actually obtained the MSA signing key is unresolved; Microsoft withdrew its crash-dump explanation in March 2024 [S2].
CSRB report (cisa.gov PDF) and CISA advisory AA23-193A could not be opened; details are from press coverage and search summaries [S4][S6][S7].
Victim count differs: Microsoft about 25 organizations vs CSRB coverage 22 organizations and over 500 individuals [S1][S7].

The reported link to Operation Aurora (2009) and RSA SecurID (2011) comes from a CSRB official's quoted remark in press coverage, not a verified primary attribution; vendor cluster boundaries for those older intrusions are not established here [S6].
Microsoft's July 11, 2023 blog and MSRC posts on blogs.microsoft.com and msrc.microsoft.com, and Wiz's original post, could not be fetched.
No public reporting on Antique Typhoon activity after 2023 was found; current operations are unknown.
Whether the key was used against Azure AD applications beyond Exchange Online (Wiz scenario) is unconfirmed [S3][S9].
No MITRE ATT&CK group entry was found.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: The operational environment includes commercial cloud identity providers and hosted email (Exchange Online/M365). Key terrain sits in the provider's token-signing infrastructure, outside DoD control [S1][S3]. STEP 2: A provider-side key compromise lets the actor bypass tenant authentication and MFA entirely, so tenant hardening alone does not close the gap. Detection depends on audit logs such as MailItemsAccessed [S1][S4]. STEP 3: Doctrinal template: acquire signing material or credentials, forge or replay tokens through dedicated proxy infrastructure, then run scripted bulk mailbox collection of selected officials, with no on-host malware in the victim tenant [S1]. STEP 4: MLCOA is quiet, targeted email collection against officials working East Asia and Pacific policy, especially around diplomatic events [S1][S5]. MDCOA is undetected forged-token access to DoD or coalition M365 tenants during a Taiwan crisis, exposing planning traffic and enabling follow-on targeting [S1][S3]. Candidate indicators: MailItemsAccessed from unusual AppIDs, tokens with unexpected issuers or key IDs, mailbox access from SoftEther/JARM-fingerprinted or Tor egress, and REST calls to OWA from unknown clients [S1][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: the intrusion was found by a customer agency's logs, not the provider, so JCC2 views must ingest cloud audit telemetry (premium logging) from mission-relevant tenants [S1][S4][S7]. (2) Authorities: response to a cloud-provider-side compromise relies on the provider and on CISA/FBI channels; define in advance who requests provider forensics and log access [S4][S7]. (3) Mission assurance: treat unclassified commercial email as exposed to collection for East Asia operations and keep sensitive planning on DoD-controlled systems [S5]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with CISA, the FBI and cloud providers quickly, as AA23-193A did; plan for vendor root-cause findings to change over time [S2][S4].

Aoqin Dragon is a China-linked cyberespionage cluster that SentinelLabs disclosed in June 2022. SentinelLabs says it has been active since at least 2013 and mainly targets organizations in Southeast Asia and Australia [S1][S5]. Its main focus is espionage against targets in Australia, Cambodia, Hong Kong, Singapore and Vietnam [S1]. Targeted sectors are government, education and telecommunications [S3][S7]. The group uses document lures, some on regional political affairs and some pornographic, and relies heavily on USB shortcut techniques and fake removable devices. Intrusions usually drop one of two backdoors: Mongall or a modified version of the open-source Heyoka project [S1][S3][S7].
identification.firstObserved: SentinelLabs: active since at least 2013 [S1]. Coverage of the report describes exploit-document campaigns running from 2012 to 2015 [S8][S9].
identification.notes: There is no Microsoft name for this cluster in the sources gathered. MITRE ATT&CK tracks it as Aoqin Dragon (G1007) [S2]. SentinelLabs assesses with moderate confidence a possible link to the cluster Mandiant tracks as UNC94 [S1][S4], and reports some tactical association with Naikon [S8]. These are possible overlaps, not merges.

attribution.sponsor: No government or vendor source gathered names a sponsoring state organization. SentinelLabs describes the actor as a small Chinese-speaking team whose targeting closely aligns with the Chinese government's political interests [S1][S7].
attribution.confidence: SentinelLabs assesses with moderate confidence that Aoqin Dragon is a small Chinese-speaking team with possible ties to Naikon and UNC94 [S1][S4][S8]. No government attribution was found.
attribution.basis: The assessment rests on SentinelLabs' malware, infrastructure and victimology analysis [S1], on Chinese-government-aligned targeting [S7], and on tooling and tactical overlaps with UNC94 and Naikon [S4][S8]. Vietnam's Authority of Information Security (AIS/NCSC) named Aoqin Dragon among APT groups expanding command-and-control infrastructure in the first half of 2022, but did not attribute it to a state [S6].

actors.objectives: Long-term espionage against government, education and telecommunications organizations in the Asia-Pacific region [S1][S3]. SentinelLabs says the targeting closely aligns with Chinese government political interests [S7]. Decoy content mostly targets readers interested in APAC political affairs [S7].

targeting.notes: Country list per SentinelLabs [S1]. Vietnam's AIS/NCSC told agencies to monitor for and block connections to listed Aoqin Dragon infrastructure in mid-2022 [S6].

capabilities.summary: Initial access, per SentinelLabs reporting: (1) weaponized documents exploiting the old, already-patched Office flaws CVE-2012-0158 and CVE-2010-3333, mainly in 2012-2015 [S8][S9]; (2) fake antivirus executables; and (3) forged removable-device folders, used since at least 2018, that trick users into opening the wrong folder and running the malware [S4][S7][S9]. The malware copies itself to real removable devices attached to the host, which spreads it through USB shortcut techniques [S3][S10]. For defense evasion it uses DLL hijacking, Themida-packed files and DNS tunneling [S8][S2]. Mongall, in use since about 2013, is a simple implant that provides a remote shell and file upload and download [S9]. The modified Heyoka is more capable: it can kill processes, manipulate files and collect process information [S9]. The original Heyoka project exfiltrates data over spoofed DNS requests, and the actor loads its version through DLL injection [S3].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): Key terrain is government, education and telecom networks in Australia and Southeast Asia, including partner-nation networks that coalition operations depend on. Removable-media transfer paths across air gaps or between enclaves are a relevant avenue [S1][S3]. STEP 2 (effects): The actor's reliance on old Office exploits and USB propagation means poorly patched systems and ones with weak media control are the most exposed. DNS tunneling can carry C2 through networks that only lightly inspect DNS [S3][S8][S9]. STEP 3 (adversary model): The template is a political or pornographic decoy document, fake antivirus or fake removable-device folder, followed by DLL-hijacked or Themida-packed Mongall or Heyoka, DNS-based C2, and spread to attached USB devices [S7][S8][S9][S10]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is quiet, long-duration espionage against regional government and telecom targets aligned with PRC political interests [S1][S7]. MDCOA is USB-borne spread into partner or coalition mission networks that share removable media with targeted regional agencies, enabling persistent collection on combined planning; this is an extrapolation, not reported activity. Candidate indicators: Office processes exploiting CVE-2012-0158 or CVE-2010-3333; executables masquerading as antivirus tools or as removable-drive folders; DLL side-loading from removable media; Themida-packed binaries; anomalous high-volume or encoded DNS queries; and hits on the Vietnamese AIS IOC list [S2][S6][S8].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: fuse the Vietnamese AIS IOC list and SentinelLabs indicators into DNS and endpoint monitoring for Indo-Pacific mission partner networks [S1][S6]. Authorities: activity is espionage against foreign partner-nation and civilian networks. Response on partner networks depends on partner consent and information-sharing agreements, and any action beyond DoDIN defense needs separate authorities. Mission assurance: enforce removable-media controls, patch legacy Office and inspect DNS for tunneling on systems exchanging data with regional partners, because the actor relies on USB propagation and DNS C2 [S3][S8][S10]. Coordination: share detections with partner CERTs (for example Vietnam's AIS/NCSC, which already tracks the cluster [S6]) and with vendor reporting on the UNC94 and Naikon overlaps, keeping vendor confidence levels distinct from government attribution [S1].

provenance.importedSummary: SentinelLabs has uncovered a cluster of activity beginning at least as far back as 2013 and continuing to the present day, primarily targeting organizations in Southeast Asia and Australia. They assess that the threat actor's primary focus is espionage and relates to targets in Australia, Cambodia, Hong Kong, Singapore, and Vietnam. We track this activity as 'Aoqin Dragon'. The threat actor has a history of using document lures with pornographic themes to infect users and makes heavy use of USB shortcut techniques to spread the malware and infect additional targets. Attacks attributable to Aoqin Dragon typically drop one of two backdoors, Mongall and a modified version of the open source Heyoka project.

identification.summary: AppMilad is an Iranian hacking group that has been identified as the source of a spyware campaign called RatMilad. This spyware is designed to silently infiltrate victims' devices and gather personal and corporate information, including private communications and photos. The group has been distributing the spyware through fake apps and targeting primarily Middle Eastern enterprises.

APT1 is the China-based cyber-espionage group that Mandiant exposed in February 2013 and tied to PLA Unit 61398, the 2nd Bureau of the PLA General Staff Department's 3rd Department, based in Pudong, Shanghai [S1][S2][S8]. Mandiant reported that APT1 stole hundreds of terabytes of data from at least 141 organizations across 20 major industries since 2006. It said 87% of those victims were headquartered in English-speaking countries [S1][S2]. In May 2014 the US Justice Department charged five Unit 61398 officers with economic espionage against US nuclear, solar, steel and metals companies and a labor union [S4].
identification.firstObserved: Mandiant: tracked since 2006 [S1][S2]. The 2014 US indictment describes intrusions from 2006 into 2014 [S4].
identification.notes: Also tracked as Comment Crew, Comment Panda, GIF89a and Byzantine Candor [S8]. Microsoft's public naming map has no Typhoon name for APT1, Comment Crew, Comment Panda or Unit 61398 (checked 2026-10-14) [S10]. Later activity reusing APT1 tooling (Siesta in 2014, Oceansalt in 2018) was not firmly attributed to APT1 by the reporting vendors; see campaigns and gaps [S5][S6].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China, People's Liberation Army: Unit 61398, 3rd Department of the General Staff Department (per Mandiant and the 2014 US indictment) [S1][S4].
attribution.confidence: Mandiant stated that the scale and duration of the attacks from a single group based in China 'leaves little doubt about the organization behind APT1' [S2]. The US government formally charged five named Unit 61398 officers in May 2014, which Attorney General Eric Holder called the first charges of their kind against a state actor [S4]. China's Defense Ministry denied the accusations and called the report 'unprofessional' [S9]. Some independent commentators, such as Jeffrey Carr, argued that Mandiant did not prove APT1 is Unit 61398 [S8].
attribution.basis: Mandiant traced APT1 activity to four large networks in Shanghai and linked it to Unit 61398 using infrastructure and persona analysis [S1][S2]. DOJ indictment allegations, which name Wang Dong, Sun Kailiang and Wen Xinyu as hackers and Huang Zhenyu and Gu Chunhui as managers of supporting infrastructure [S4].

actors.objectives: Long-term, large-scale theft of intellectual property and confidential business information from foreign organizations, chiefly in English-speaking countries [S1][S2]. The 2014 indictment alleges the stolen information benefited Chinese state-owned competitors. Several victims had filed trade complaints against Chinese rivals [S4].

sectors: Steel and specialty metals (U.S. Steel, Allegheny Technologies) [S4]
regions: United States (115 of the victims Mandiant counted, per press coverage) [S11]
15 countries in total, per press coverage of the Mandiant report [S11]
targeting.notes: Mandiant counted 141 victim organizations across 20 major industries [S1][S2] and said its visibility was probably only a small fraction of APT1's total activity [S2]. Sectors from the possibly related Siesta (energy, defense, telecom) [S5] and Shady RAT [S7] campaigns are left out of this list because attribution to APT1 is unconfirmed.

capabilities.summary: Mandiant described a mature, high-volume operation. Average dwell time in victim networks was 356 days and the longest was 1,764 days [S2][S3]. In one case APT1 took 6.5 TB of compressed data from a single organization over ten months [S2]. Its infrastructure included at least 937 command-and-control servers on 849 IP addresses in 13 countries, mostly registered in China (709) and the US (109) [S2]. The 2014 indictment separates hands-on-keyboard intrusion operators from personnel who managed domain accounts and other infrastructure [S4]. Its custom malware (for example Seasalt, circa 2010) was later partly reused in Oceansalt [S6]. The tool and technique list comes from MITRE ATT&CK G0006 separately.

diamond.capability: Spear-phishing-led intrusions, custom backdoors such as Seasalt, and long-dwell data theft at terabyte scale [S2][S5][S6].

gaps: The original Mandiant APT1 PDF was not fetched directly (fetches to mandiant/fireeye/lawfare hosts failed). Figures come from a course-site mirror listing and Lawfare and press reproductions [S1][S2][S3].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): For DoD, key terrain is the defense industrial base and industrial-supply-chain enterprise networks (aerospace, metals, energy engineering), which hold technical IP and negotiation data [S4][S11]. STEP 2 (effects): Average dwell times of nearly a year and terabyte-scale exfiltration mean an undetected intrusion can compromise whole program data holdings [S2]. STEP 3 (threat model): The template is spear-phishing, a custom backdoor beaconing to China-registered C2, long-term persistence, then bulk archive-and-exfiltrate. Separate personnel manage infrastructure [S2][S4][S5]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is sustained economic and technical espionage against firms tied to PRC industrial or trade interests [S4]. MDCOA is a successor PLA unit or a tool-reusing actor using APT1-style long-dwell access against DIB partners supporting Air Force programs. Old APT1 code may be reused under false-flag ambiguity [S6]. Candidate indicators: long-lived low-volume beacons to China-registered IPs, large compressed archives leaving the network, and spear-phishing lures tied to current business or infrastructure projects [S2][S6].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: APT1 shows that dwell time is measured in months to years [S2]. Treat historical log retention and retrospective hunting as mission requirements. (2) Authorities: The 2014 indictment shows how law enforcement responds to state-military intrusions against private firms [S4]. Coordinate DIB-victim intrusions with DOJ/FBI and DC3 rather than handling them as purely military events. (3) Mission assurance: Theft of contractor IP and program data erodes technological advantage without degrading operations, so include contractor networks in mission-relevant terrain analysis [S4]. (4) Coordination: Code reuse across actors complicates attribution [S5][S6]. Pair technical indicators with multi-source intelligence before naming an actor in operational reporting.

identification.summary: PLA Navy Anchor Panda is an adversary that CrowdStrike has tracked extensively over the last year targeting both civilian and military maritime operations in the green/brown water regions primarily in the area of operations of the South Sea Fleet of the PLA Navy. In addition to maritime operations in this region, Anchor Panda also heavily targeted western companies in the US, Germany, Sweden, the UK, and Australia, and other countries involved in maritime satellite systems, aerospace companies, and defense contractors. Not surprisingly, embassies and diplomatic missions in the region, foreign intelligence services, and foreign governments with space programs were also targeted.

Between November 26, 2015, and December 1, 2015, known and suspected China-based APT groups launched several spear-phishing attacks targeting Japanese and Taiwanese organizations in the high-tech, government services, media and financial services industries. Each campaign delivered a malicious Microsoft Word document exploiting the aforementioned EPS dict copy use-after-free vulnerability, and the local Windows privilege escalation vulnerability CVE-2015-1701. The successful exploitation of both vulnerabilities led to the delivery of either a downloader that we refer to as IRONHALO, or a backdoor that we refer to as ELMER.

We’ve uncovered some new data and likely attribution regarding a series of APT watering hole attacks this past summer. Watering hole attacks are an increasingly popular component of APT campaigns, as many people are more aware of spear phishing and are less likely to open documents or click on links in unsolicited emails. Watering hole attacks offer a much better chance of success because they involve compromising legitimate websites and installing malware intended to compromise website visitors. These are often popular websites frequented by people who work in specific industries or have political sympathies to which the actors want to gain access. In contrast to many other APT campaigns, which tend to rely heavily on spear phishing to gain victims, “th3bug” is known for compromising legitimate websites their intended visitors are likely to frequent. Over the summer they compromised several sites, including a well-known Uyghur website written in that native language.

APT37 has likely been active since at least 2012 and focuses on targeting the public and private sectors primarily in South Korea. In 2017, APT37 expanded its targeting beyond the Korean peninsula to include Japan, Vietnam and the Middle East, and to a wider range of industry verticals, including chemicals, electronics, manufacturing, aerospace, automotive and healthcare entities

identification.summary: APT9 engages in cyber operations where the goal is data theft, usually focusing on the data and projects that make a particular organization competitive within its field. APT9 was historically very active in the pharmaceuticals and biotechnology industry. We have observed this actor use spearphishing, valid accounts, as well as remote services for Initial Access. On at least one occasion, Mandiant observed APT9 at two companies in the biotechnology industry and suspect that APT9 actors may have gained initial access to one of the companies by using a trusted relationship between the two companies. APT9 use a wide range of backdoors, including publicly available backdoors, as well as backdoors that are believed to be custom, but are used by multiple APT groups.

APTIran has claimed responsibility for a large-scale campaign targeting Israeli critical infrastructure, asserting infiltration of government ministries, hospitals, universities, and financial institutions as retaliation for Israeli military operations. The group has leaked over 350,000 Israeli government login credentials and approximately 300 internal databases, while also threatening to create a 'zombie' network from infected devices. They have reportedly deployed ransomware strains such as ALPHV and LockBit as part of their offensive toolkit. Additionally, APTIran has made unverified claims of compromising Israeli water control systems and the state-owned food security agency Jordan Silos and Supply General Co.

Aqua Blizzard (formerly ACTINIUM, earlier DEV-0157) is what Microsoft calls the Russia-based actor that other vendors track as Gamaredon [S1][S2]. Microsoft describes it as an espionage and data-theft actor that mainly targets Ukrainian government, military, judiciary, law enforcement and non-profit organizations [S1][S2]. Its hallmarks are high-volume spearphishing, heavily obfuscated VBScript and PowerShell, self-extracting archives and LNK files, and fast-changing infrastructure [S1][S2]. Unit 42 named the group in 2017 and reported a shift from off-the-shelf tools to custom malware [S10]. ESET reports that the group was still very active in 2024 and 2025, running many spearphishing waves against Ukrainian government and military institutions [S8][S9].
identification.firstObserved: Active since at least mid-2013, per LookingGlass 'Operation Armageddon' [S11] and Unit 42 [S10]. Microsoft said in February 2022 that the group had been operating for 'almost a decade' [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Aqua Blizzard. It was ACTINIUM until April 2023 and DEV-0157 before that [S1]. Microsoft's profile lists Primitive Bear, ACTINIUM, SectorC08, Shuckworm, Gamaredon, UNC530 and Armageddon as other names [S2]. Unit 42 uses Trident Ursa [S5], and Symantec uses Shuckworm [S6]. The name 'Gamaredon' is an anagram of 'Armageddon', taken from LookingGlass's 2015 report [S10][S11]. Microsoft notes that Aqua Blizzard is distinct from DEV-0586 (Cadet Blizzard) [S1]. MITRE tracks the group as Gamaredon Group (G0047) [S12].

attribution.sponsor: Russian Federation, Federal Security Service (FSB). The Security Service of Ukraine (SSU) says the group consists of officers of the FSB in Crimea, operates from Sevastopol and takes orders from the FSB Center for Information Security (Center 18) in Moscow [S3][S9].
attribution.confidence: The attribution to the FSB is a Ukrainian government attribution (SSU, November 2021) [S3]. Microsoft repeats the Ukrainian attribution and says it observed ACTINIUM 'operating out of Crimea'; it does not give its own confidence level [S1][S2]. ESET says it believes with high confidence that Gamaredon collaborates with Turla [S7]. LookingGlass said in 2015 that it was 'highly confident' that the SBU's claims of FSB involvement were accurate [S11].
attribution.basis: The SSU named five individuals and cited intercepted communications, including published recordings of phone calls between members [S3]. Microsoft's telemetry places operations in Crimea [S1]. Vendor technical reporting from Unit 42, Symantec and ESET describes consistent tooling and targeting [S5][S6][S8][S9]. In 2025 ESET found technical links to Turla, another FSB-linked actor, with Gamaredon tools used to restart or deploy Turla's Kazuar backdoor [S7].

actors.objectives: Microsoft describes the objectives as espionage: exfiltrating sensitive information, maintaining access, and moving laterally into related organizations [S1][S2]. Since October 2021 Microsoft has seen a focus on organizations critical to emergency response, territorial security, and the coordination of international and humanitarian aid to Ukraine [S1]. Secondary coverage of Symantec's 2023 reporting says the material stolen from Ukrainian security, military and government bodies included casualty, engagement, air-strike, arsenal-inventory and training reports [S6]. ESET says the group probably gives Turla initial access to selected high-value machines [S7].

sectors: Emergency response, territorial security and humanitarian-aid coordination organizations [S1]
Energy: an attempted intrusion at a petroleum refining company in a NATO member state [S5]
Western government entity operating in Ukraine [S4]
regions: Ukraine, the primary and in 2024-2025 almost exclusive target [S1][S2][S8][S9]

targeting.notes: ESET reports that in 2024 the group refocused exclusively on Ukrainian government institutions [S8], and that throughout 2025 it targeted only Ukrainian governmental and military institutions [S9]. Targeting outside Ukraine appears opportunistic or tied to Ukraine support, but this is inferred from limited cases [S4][S5].

capabilities.summary: The tradecraft is high-volume rather than sophisticated. Initial access comes through spearphishing with macro documents that use remote template injection, web bugs that track email opens, and lures impersonating legitimate bodies such as the WHO [S1]. Later waves used archives and XHTML files with HTML smuggling to deliver HTA downloaders [S9]. From late September 2025 the group exploited the WinRAR flaw CVE-2025-8088 to plant downloaders in the Startup folder [S9]. Execution relies on multi-stage, heavily obfuscated VBScript and PowerShell, self-extracting archives and LNK files, with scheduled tasks for persistence [S1][S2]. Malware includes the Pterodo family, QuietSieve, PowerPunch, DinoTrain, DesertDown, DilongTrash, ObfuBerry and ObfuMerry, plus UltraVNC for interactive access [S1][S2]. ESET documented an expanding set of Ptero-series PowerShell tools, including PteroSand, PteroPaste, PteroOdd, PteroGraphin and PteroSetup, with six new tools in 2025 [S7][S9]. The group spreads through USB and removable drives, which can reach air-gapped machines [S6][S7]. Its infrastructure churns quickly: Microsoft saw more than 25 new domains and more than 80 IPs in a 30-day window, with DNS records changing about daily and mostly hosted on REG.RU [S1]. Unit 42 counted more than 500 new domains over 10 months [S5]. The group has used Telegram and Telegraph dead drops to find C2 addresses [S6]. It has hidden almost all of its C2 behind Cloudflare tunnels (2024) and Cloudflare Workers (from May 2025), and has also used devtunnels.ms, Loophole, No-IP, Clever Cloud, Supabase, Dropbox and S3-compatible storage for exfiltration [S8][S9].

gaps: Primary vendor reports could not be fetched (Unit 42, ESET WeLiveSecurity and ESET white papers, Symantec, The Record). Details for S4-S9 rely on search-result and press coverage of those reports.
The SSU's original 2021 announcement and its claims (names, more than 5,000 attacks, Center 18 tasking) were not opened directly and are not independently verified [S3].
Microsoft has not published its own confidence level for the FSB attribution; it repeats the Ukrainian government attribution [S1][S2].
The exact date of ESET's 2022-2023 toolset white paper (reported as September 2024) and its NATO-country targeting details were not verified from the primary document [S13].
The full scope and the victims of Gamaredon's non-Ukrainian targeting are unclear. The public cases are few and unnamed [S4][S5].
The division of labour between Gamaredon and Turla is not public beyond ESET's technical observations (for example, whether Gamaredon brokers access as tasked or opportunistically) [S7].
No public reporting was found on Aqua Blizzard targeting US DoD networks directly.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): The key terrain is Ukrainian government and military networks, and the networks of partners who coordinate aid to Ukraine [S1]. Western government and NATO-state entities operating in or supporting Ukraine are secondary terrain [S4][S5]. Removable media can bridge to air-gapped segments [S6]. STEP 2 (effects): Constant domain churn and abuse of trusted cloud and tunnel services such as Cloudflare, Telegram and Dropbox weaken static blocklists and reputation-based filtering [S1][S8][S9]. STEP 3 (adversary template): The chain runs from a spearphish (remote template, HTML smuggling, archive or WinRAR exploit) to an HTA, VBS or PowerShell downloader, then a Ptero-series implant with scheduled-task persistence, then USB spread and document theft. Selected hosts may be handed off to Turla's Kazuar [S1][S6][S7][S9]. STEP 4: The MLCOA is continued mass spearphishing for intelligence on Ukrainian military and government operations [S8][S9]. The MDCOA is access to a coalition or NATO-partner network supporting Ukraine, brokered to a more capable FSB actor (Turla) for long-term espionage [S5][S7]. Candidate indicators: mshta, wscript or PowerShell spawned from Office or WinRAR; new scheduled tasks with wordlist-style names; LNK files appearing on USB drives; and outbound traffic to trycloudflare, workers.dev, devtunnels.ms, Telegraph or Telegram from non-browser processes [S1][S6][S9].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: the actor's tempo (35 campaigns in 2025) and infrastructure churn mean behaviour-based detections must feed JCC2 common operating picture tools, not just IOC feeds [S1][S9]. (2) Authorities: the attribution to the FSB comes from the Ukrainian government and vendors. Microsoft has not given a confidence level, so planners should not present it as a US government attribution without a separate basis [S1][S3]. (3) Mission assurance: units and contractors supporting aid or security cooperation with Ukraine should enforce controls on removable media and Office and WinRAR patching, given the USB propagation and CVE-2025-8088 exploitation [S6][S9]. (4) Coordination: because Gamaredon may hand access to Turla, any Gamaredon detection on partner or coalition networks should trigger a hunt for Kazuar-class follow-on implants and be shared with coalition CERTs [S7].

provenance.importedSummary: Unit 42 threat researchers have recently observed a threat group distributing new, custom developed malware. We have labelled this threat group the Gamaredon Group and our research shows that the Gamaredon Group has been active since at least 2013. In the past, the Gamaredon Group has relied heavily on off-the-shelf tools. Our new research shows the Gamaredon Group have made a shift to custom-developed malware. We believe this shift indicates the Gamaredon Group have improved their technical capabilities.

identification.summary: Microsoft threat actor profile. Origin or category: Iran.

BLACKGEAR is an espionage campaign which has targeted users in Taiwan for many years. Multiple papers and talks have been released covering this campaign, which used the ELIRKS backdoor when it was first discovered in 2012. It is known for using blogs and microblogging services to hide the location of its actual command-and-control (C&C) servers. This allows an attacker to change the C&C server used quickly by changing the information in these posts. Like most campaigns, BLACKGEAR has evolved over time. Our research indicates that it has started targeting Japanese users. Two things led us to this conclusion: first, the fake documents that are used as part of its infection routines are now in Japanese. Secondly, it is now using blogging sites and microblogging services based in Japan for its C&C activity.

Blackwood is a China-aligned APT group that has been active since at least 2018. They primarily engage in cyberespionage operations targeting individuals and companies in China, Japan, and the United Kingdom. Blackwood utilizes sophisticated techniques such as adversary-in-the-middle attacks to deliver their custom implant, NSPX30, through updates of legitimate software. They also have the capability to hide the location of their command and control servers by intercepting traffic generated by the implant.

BladedFeline is an Iran-aligned APT group that has been active since at least 2017, targeting Iraqi and Kurdish government officials for cyberespionage. The group employs a variety of tools, including the Shahmaran backdoor, Whisper, and PrimeCache, which is a malicious IIS module. BladedFeline utilizes techniques such as spearphishing (T1566), exploiting public-facing applications (T1190), and timestomping to maintain access and exfiltrate data. The group is assessed with medium confidence to be a subgroup of OilRig, focusing on strategic access to high-ranking officials in the region.
Blue Termite is a group of suspected Chinese origin active in Japan.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Include state and local government systems and commercial software suppliers in the OE. They support National Guard, emergency management and DoD-adjacent functions and are soft entry points. STEP 2: Abuse of legitimate cloud services for C2 blends with normal business traffic. STEP 3: The template is web-application exploitation or spear-phishing, then web shells and custom backdoors, then credential theft and lateral movement, plus theft of code-signing material for later supply-chain use. Re-compromise after eviction is likely. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued espionage against government and technology targets mixed with profit-driven theft. MDCOA is a supply-chain operation using stolen signing certificates to reach DoD or DIB networks during a crisis. Candidate indicators: .NET deserialization exploit attempts, newly signed binaries with unexpected certificates, and calendar or cloud-API traffic from servers [S1][S2][S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Expect re-entry after eviction: JCC2 tracking should keep cases open with heightened monitoring after remediation. (2) Coordinate with state partners (National Guard cyber units, state CISOs, CISA) because state networks are in the target set. (3) Monitor code-signing certificate revocations and abuse reports as part of supply-chain situational awareness. (4) Cloud-service C2 requires provider cooperation (e.g. Google, Microsoft) for disruption, which should be built into response playbooks.

provenance.importedSummary: APT41 is a threat group that researchers have assessed as Chinese state-sponsored espionage group that also conducts financially-motivated operations. Active since at least 2012, APT41 has been observed targeting various industries, including but not limited to healthcare, telecom, technology, finance, education, retail and video game industries in 14 countries. Notable behaviors include using a wide range of malware and tools to complete mission objectives. APT41 overlaps at least partially with public reporting on groups including BARIUM and Winnti Group.

identification.summary: BrazenBamboo is a Chinese state-affiliated threat actor known for developing the LIGHTSPY, DEEPDATA, and DEEPPOST malware families. Their infrastructure includes capabilities for zero-day exploitation, specifically targeting vulnerabilities like FortiClient, and employs a command-and-control architecture that supports multi-platform operations. Volexity's analysis indicates that BrazenBamboo is a well-resourced entity with a focus on domestic targets, utilizing custom analyst software to manage data collected from their malware. The ongoing development of their malware families is evidenced by the timestamps associated with their latest payloads.

China-based cyberespionage group that Microsoft tracks as Brocade Typhoon (formerly BORON) and that other vendors call APT3, Gothic Panda, UPS, Buckeye and TG-0110 [S1][S4]. FireEye/Mandiant tied it to browser and Flash zero-day campaigns in 2014-2015 (Operation Clandestine Fox, Operation Clandestine Wolf) [S2][S9]. Symantec reported a targeting shift from the US to Hong Kong political entities starting in June 2015 [S4]. Security researchers linked the group to the Guangzhou firm Boyusec, three of whose personnel were indicted by the US in November 2017 [S6][S7]. Symantec reported that known Buckeye tool activity ceased in mid-2017 [S5].
identification.firstObserved: Symantec (2016) assessed the group had been operating for 'well over half a decade' [S4]; the 2017 US indictment alleges intrusions from 2011 to May 2017 (reporting DOJ indictment) [S7]. Earliest named public campaign: Operation Clandestine Fox, April 2014 [S9].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Brocade Typhoon. Microsoft's public mapping lists BORON, GOTHIC PANDA, UPS, APT3, OLDCARP, TG-0110, Red Sylvan and CYBRAN as other names [S1]. Symantec calls it Buckeye and equates it with APT3, Gothic Panda, UPS Team and TG-0110 [S4]. Palo Alto Unit 42 tracks the same activity as UPS and associates it with the Pirpi backdoor [S10]. MITRE ATT&CK tracks the group as APT3 (G0022) [S11]. Boyusec is a company the researchers link to the group; whether Boyusec is all of APT3 or only one component was unresolved in 2017 reporting [S8].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China, Ministry of State Security (MSS), per Recorded Future's assessment that Boyusec worked on behalf of the MSS [S6]. The US indictment does not name the Chinese government [S7][S8].
attribution.confidence: Recorded Future assessed with high confidence (May 2017) that APT3 is attributable to the MSS through the contractor Boyusec [S6]. FireEye's Ben Read said FireEye believed the indicted individuals and Boyusec are linked to APT3 [S7]. The November 2017 US indictment charged three Boyusec personnel (Wu Yingzhuo, Dong Hao, Xia Lei) but, per press reporting, made no reference to Chinese state links [S7][S8]. Microsoft's mapping lists the origin as China [S1].
attribution.basis: Domain-registration analysis by the anonymous 'intrusiontruth' blog tied Pirpi C2 domains to Boyusec shareholders, which Recorded Future corroborated and linked to Guangdong ITSEC, which it describes as subordinate to the MSS-run CNITSEC [S6][S8]. Charges against Boyusec personnel cited use of 'UPS'/'exeproxy' malware (reporting DOJ indictment) [S7]. Vendor malware and campaign reporting from FireEye/Mandiant, Symantec and Unit 42 [S2][S3][S4][S5][S10].

actors.objectives: Espionage and theft of commercial and technical intellectual property: the indictment alleges theft of Siemens energy, technology and transportation business data, Trimble satellite-navigation (GNSS) development data and Moody's Analytics economist email (reporting DOJ indictment) [S7]. From 2015 it also collected against political entities in Hong Kong [S4].

regions: Vietnam and the Philippines (later use of the Bemstour/DoublePulsar package; Symantec did not tie that later use to Buckeye's known tools) [S12]

The Vietnam and Philippines intrusions used the Bemstour exploit tool with different malware after Buckeye's known tools went quiet in mid-2017, so they may not belong to this cluster [S5][S12].

capabilities.summary: Early access to browser and plugin zero-days: Internet Explorer CVE-2014-1776 (Clandestine Fox, April 2014) [S9] and Adobe Flash CVE-2015-3113 delivered by phishing links to compromised servers, followed by the SHOTPUT backdoor (Clandestine Wolf, June 2015) [S2]. Rapid use of newly disclosed exploits such as CVE-2014-6332 and CVE-2014-4113 within days of disclosure (Operation Double Tap, November 2014), with PlugX/Kaba C2 noted [S3]. Custom backdoors including Pirpi/UPS [S10] and 'exeproxy' [S7]. From March 2016 the group used a DoublePulsar variant, newer than the Shadow Brokers version, delivered by the custom Bemstour exploit tool, which chained Windows vulnerabilities including the zero-day CVE-2019-0703 for remote kernel code execution; this was over a year before the Shadow Brokers leak [S5]. Spearphishing with malicious attachments or links is alleged in the indictment [S7]. MITRE lists software including PlugX, SHOTPUT, OSInfo, RemoteCMD and LaZagne [S11].

Activity after mid-2017 is not publicly attributed to this cluster. Bemstour/DoublePulsar use into late 2018 (Vietnam, Philippines) was with different malware, and Symantec did not attribute it to Buckeye [S5][S12].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Key terrain is user endpoints running browsers and plugins, enterprise mail servers and Windows SMB-exposed hosts at defense, aerospace, industrial and navigation-technology firms, including DIB contractors whose engineering data has value (Siemens, Trimble precedent) [S2][S5][S7]. STEP 2 (effects): Zero-day and fast n-day use (exploits within about a week of disclosure) shortens the defender's patch window; stealthy mail-forwarding rules allow long-term, low-noise collection [S3][S7]. STEP 3 (adversary template): phishing link or attachment, then browser/Flash exploit, then SHOTPUT/Pirpi/PlugX backdoor, then credential theft and lateral movement, possibly with a kernel-level implant such as DoublePulsar, then data staging and exfiltration [S2][S3][S5][S7]. STEP 4: MLCOA is quiet theft of engineering and program data (for example GNSS and energy technology) from DIB and partner networks. MDCOA is use of an unpublished exploit chain that gives kernel-level implants across many hosts. Candidate indicators: unexpected mailbox forwarding rules to external accounts, anomalous SMB traffic consistent with DoublePulsar, browser processes spawning shells, and connections to newly registered domains [S5][S7]. Note: no public activity has been attributed since mid-2017 [S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track emergency browser, plugin and Windows patches alongside exposure of mission-relevant enclaves, since this actor used exploits within days of disclosure [S3]. (2) Authorities: activity against contractors such as Siemens and Trimble falls under law enforcement and DIB channels; the US addressed it by indictment, not military response [S7]. (3) Mission assurance: PNT-related development data (Trimble GNSS) was a target, so protect PNT program and supplier data as mission-critical [S7]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with DC3/DIB CS partners and commercial vendors, since public attribution came from vendor and researcher reporting (Recorded Future, Symantec, FireEye) [S5][S6][S7].
