provenance.importedSummary: Symantec described UPS in 2016 report as: 'Buckeye (also known as APT3, Gothic Panda, UPS Team, and TG-0110) is a cyberespionage group that is believed to have been operating for well over half a decade. Traditionally, the group attacked organizations in the US as well as other targets. However, Buckeyes focus appears to have changed as of June 2015, when the group began compromising political entities in Hong Kong.'

identification.summary: In early 2021 CTU researchers observed BRONZE EDGEWOOD exploiting the Microsoft Exchange Server of an organization in Southeast Asia. The threat group deployed a China Chopper webshell and ran the Nishang Invoke-PowerShellTcp.ps1 script to connect back to C2 infrastructure. The threat group is publicly linked to malware families Chinoxy, PCShare and FunnyDream. CTU researchers have discovered that BRONZE EDGEWOOD also leverages Cobalt Strike in its intrusion activity. BRONZE EDGEWOOD has been active since at least 2018 and targets government and private enterprises across Southeast Asia. CTU researchers assess with moderate confidence that BRONZE EDGEWOOD operates on behalf the Chinese government and has a remit that covers political espionage.

In December 2020, the IT management software provider SolarWinds announced that an unidentified threat actor had exploited a vulnerability in their Orion Platform software to deploy a web shell dubbed SUPERNOVA. CTU researchers track the operators of the SUPERNOVA web shell as BRONZE SPIRAL and assess with low confidence that the group is of Chinese origin. SUPERNOVA was likely deployed through exploitation of CVE-2020-10148, and CTU researchers observed post-exploitation reconnaissance commands roughly 30 minutes before the web shell was deployed. This may have been indicative of the threat actor conducting scan-and-exploit activity and then triaging for victims of particular interest, before deploying SUPERNOVA and attempting to dump credentials and move laterally. BRONZE SPIRAL has been associated with previous intrusions involving the targeting of ManageEngine servers, maintenance of long-term access to periodically harvest credentials and exfiltrate data, and espionage or theft of intellectual property. The threat group makes extensive use of native system tools and 'living off the land' techniques.

BRONZE SPRING is a threat group that CTU researchers assess with high confidence operates on behalf of China in the theft of intellectual property from defense, engineering, pharmaceutical and technology companies. The threat group typically uses scan-and-exploit for initial access, deploys the China Chopper webshell for remote execution and persistence, and creates RAR archives with a '.jpg' file extension for data exfiltration. In July 2020 the U.S. Department of Justice indicted two Chinese hackers CTU researchers assess are members of the BRONZE SPRING threat group. The Department of Justice allege these hackers were responsible for compromising networks of hundreds of organisations and individuals in the U.S. and abroad since 2009, and that exfiltrated data would be passed to the Chinese Ministry of State Security or sold for financial gain.

BRONZE VAPOR is a targeted threat group assessed with moderate confidence to be of Chinese origin. Artefacts from tools associated with this group and open source reporting on related incidents indicate that BRONZE VAPOR have operated since at least 2017. The group conducts espionage against multiple industries including semiconductors, aviation and telecommunications. CTU researchers assess BRONZE VAPOR's intent to be information theft, with operations focused on intellectual property (semiconductors) and personally identifiable information such as traveller records (aviation). Compromise of telecommunications companies can yield personally identifiable information and meta data on client communications such as Call Data Records (CDR). Prior to 2019 their operational focus, with some exceptions, revolved around targets in East Asia particularity Taiwan with it's thriving semiconductor industry. In 2021 details emerged in open source of attacks on at least one European semiconductor company believed to date back to 2017. In 2019 BRONZE VAPOR attacked one of more entities in the European airlines sector. The group gains initial access via VPN services, may use spearphishing with 'Letter of Appointment' themed lures, and deploys Cobalt Strike along with custom data exfiltration tools to target organizations. Post-intrusion activity involves living-of-the-land using legitimate tools and commands available within victim environment as well as using AceHash for credential harvesting, WATERCYCLE for data exfiltration and STOCKPIPE for proxying information through Microsoft Exchange servers over email. BRONZE VAPOR uses a set of tactics that, although not individually unique, when viewed in aggregate create a relatively distinct playbook. Intrusions begin with credential based attacks against an existing remote access solution (Citrix, VPN etc.) or B2B network access. Cobalt Strike is deployed into the environment and further access is then conducted via Cobalt Strike Beacon and other features of the platform. Sharphound is deployed to map out the victim's Active Directory infrastructure and and collect critical information about the domain including important account names. Command and control infrastructure is hosted on subdomains of Azure and Appspot services to blend in with legitimate traffic. The threat actor also registers their own domains for command and control, often with a "sync" or "update" related theme. WinRAR is commonly used for compressing data prior to exfiltration. Filenames for these archives often involve a string of numbers and variations of the word "update". Data is exfiltrated using WATERCYCLE to cloud based platforms such as OneDrive and GoogleDrive.

Based on the evidence we have presented Symantec attributed the activity involving theDripion malware to the Budminer advanced threat group. While we have not seen newcampaigns using Taidoor malware since 2014, we believe the Budminer group has changedtactics to avoid detection after being outed publicly in security white papers and blogs over thepast few years.

Buhtrap has been active since 2014, however their first attacks against financial institutions were only detected in August 2015. Earlier, the group had only focused on targeting banking clients. At the moment, the group is known to target Russian and Ukrainian banks. From August 2015 to February 2016 Buhtrap managed to conduct 13 successful attacks against Russian banks for a total amount of 1.8 billion rubles ($25.7 mln). The number of successful attacks against Ukrainian banks has not been identified. Buhtrap is the first hacker group using a network worm to infect the overall bank infrastructure that significantly increases the difficulty of removing all malicious functions from the network. As a result, banks have to shut down the whole infrastructure which provokes delay in servicing customers and additional losses. Malicious programs intentionally scan for machines with an automated Bank-Customer system of the Central Bank of Russia (further referred to as BCS CBR). We have not identified incidents of attacks involving online money transfer systems, ATM machines or payment gates which are known to be of interest for other criminal groups.

Iran-based cyber espionage actor that Microsoft tracks as Burgundy Sandstorm and maps to REMIX KITTEN, Cadelle and Chafer [S1]. Mandiant defined APT39 to consolidate this activity and says it largely aligns with 'Chafer', though vendors report it differently [S2]. The group concentrates on collecting personal information and tracking individuals of interest. It has prioritized telecommunications, travel and the IT firms that support travel [S2]. In September 2020 the US government named Rana Intelligence Computing Company as an MOIS front company for APT39 [S3][S9].
identification.firstObserved: Symantec observed Cadelle/Chafer activity from at least July 2014, with C2 registration data hinting at activity possibly as early as 2011 [S4]. Mandiant has tracked APT39 activity since November 2014 [S2]. US government reporting describes APT39 activity since 2014 [S3].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Burgundy Sandstorm. Microsoft maps REMIX KITTEN, Cadelle and Chafer to it [S1]. MITRE tracks the group as APT39 (G0087) [S10]. Symantec originally described Cadelle and Chafer as two separate teams using different backdoors (Cadelspy and Remexi) [S4]. Microsoft and MITRE fold both into one actor, but that merge rests on vendor judgment [S1][S10]. Unit 42 noted code overlap with OilRig but tracks Chafer and OilRig separately [S6]. Mandiant judges APT39 distinct from APT34 while noting the groups may share resources [S2].

attribution.sponsor: Iran, Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS). The US Treasury and FBI stated in September 2020 that APT39 and its front company Rana Intelligence Computing Company are owned and controlled by MOIS [S3][S9].
attribution.confidence: US government: Treasury sanctioned APT39, 45 associated individuals and Rana under E.O. 13553, and the FBI issued a FLASH alert based on a long-term FBI Boston investigation (as reported by press) [S3][S9]. Mandiant states 'moderate confidence' that APT39 operations support Iranian national interests [S2]. Symantec assessed that Cadelle and Chafer victims are most likely of interest to an Iranian entity [S4]. Kaspersky did not directly attribute its 2018 Remexi activity to a specific Iranian group or individual [S7].
attribution.basis: Mandiant cited regional targeting, infrastructure, timing and similarities to APT34 [S2]. The US government action identified Rana personnel by role (managers, programmers, hacking experts) [S3][S9]. Microsoft's naming feed lists Iran as origin [S1].

actors.objectives: Mandiant assesses the main mission is to track or monitor targets of interest and to collect personal information, including travel itineraries and telecom customer data. A possible secondary goal is geopolitical data for government decision-making [S2]. The FBI and Treasury describe monitoring of Iranian citizens, dissidents and journalists as well as neighboring governments' networks [S3][S9]. Symantec assessed that compromising airlines and telecoms was possibly meant to monitor targets' movements and communications [S4].

sectors: Travel, airlines, aircraft services and air transportation [S2][S4][S5][S8]
IT and software firms supporting air and sea transport [S2][S5]
regions: Global scope, concentrated in the Middle East [S2]
Israel, Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and UAE (2017 activity) [S5]
Kuwait and Saudi Arabia (2018-2020 activity reported by Bitdefender) [S8]
targeting.notes: Targeting combines domestic surveillance of Iranians with access to regional telecom, travel and government data stores. Those holdings let the group track individuals at scale [S2][S4][S9].

capabilities.summary: Initial access through spearphishing with malicious attachments or links (typically POWBAT), lookalike domains impersonating services relevant to targets, web-server exploitation to plant web shells (ANTAK, ASPXSPY), and stolen credentials against exposed Outlook Web Access [S2]. Custom backdoors include SEAWEED, CACHEMONEY and a POWBAT variant [S2]. Other tooling includes Remexi, which captures keystrokes, screenshots, credentials and browser data and uses Windows BITS for C2 and exfiltration [S4][S7], and Cadelspy [S4]. MechaFlounder is a PyInstaller-compiled Python backdoor seen in 2018 [S6]. Post-exploitation relies on Mimikatz (including repacked builds), Windows Credential Editor, ProcDump, Ncrack, the BLUETORCH port scanner, the REDTRIP/PINKTRIP/BLUETRIP SOCKS5 proxies, RDP, SSH, PsExec, RemCom and xCmdSvc. Data is staged with WinRAR or 7-Zip [S2]. Bitdefender reported living-off-the-land techniques and Metasploit-related PowerShell in 2018-2020 Gulf intrusions [S8]. The FBI FLASH described eight malware sets, including VBS, AutoIt, BITS-based executables, a Python script and a malicious Android APK [S3][S9].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Key terrain is the regional telecom and travel providers that hold subscriber records and itineraries, plus Middle East government networks [S2][S5]. Host-nation and commercial providers supporting deployed forces in the Gulf fall within this terrain [S5][S8]. STEP 2 (effects): Compromise of telecom or airline data could expose personnel movements and communications patterns without touching DoD networks [S2][S4]. STEP 3 (adversary template): Spearphish or web-server exploit, then web shell or POWBAT/Remexi foothold, then Mimikatz credential theft and SOCKS proxy or RDP lateral movement, then archive and exfiltrate [S2][S7]. STEP 4: MLCOA is persistent collection of personal and travel data from regional telecom, aviation and government victims [S2][S8]. MDCOA is using that data to track specific individuals of interest, including personnel in the region [S2][S9]. Candidate indicators: lookalike domains spoofing services relevant to targets, ASPX web shells on public servers, bitsadmin-driven transfers, PyInstaller binaries named lsass.exe, and newly created local accounts [S2][S6][S7][S8].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: Exposure through third-party telecom and travel providers is outside DoDIN visibility, so JCC2 pictures should flag partner and commercial dependencies in the Gulf [S2][S8]. (2) Authorities: Activity against host-nation and commercial networks needs coordination with partner nations and interagency rather than unilateral DCO [S3][S9]. (3) Mission assurance: Treat personnel travel data and OWA credentials as protected assets. Mandiant documents OWA credential abuse [S2]. (4) Coordination: Use the FBI FLASH malware sets and MITRE G0087 for hunt content, and share with partner CERTs in states named as targets [S9][S10].

provenance.importedSummary: APT39 was created to bring together previous activities and methods used by this actor, and its activities largely align with a group publicly referred to as "Chafer." However, there are differences in what has been publicly reported due to the variances in how organizations track activity. APT39 primarily leverages the SEAWEED and CACHEMONEY backdoors along with a specific variant of the POWBAT backdoor. While APT39's targeting scope is global, its activities are concentrated in the Middle East. APT39 has prioritized the telecommunications sector, with additional targeting of the travel industry and IT firms that support it and the high-tech industry.

identification.summary: Cadet Blizzard is a Russian state actor that Microsoft associates with the GRU. Microsoft began tracking it as DEV-0586 in January 2022, after the WhisperGate destructive malware and defacements of Ukrainian government websites [S1][S2]. Microsoft says its goals are disruption, destruction, information collection and possibly intimidation. Its main targets are Ukrainian government organizations and IT service providers, with further targets in Europe, Central Asia and Latin America [S1]. US government agencies attribute WhisperGate and later operations against NATO members to GRU Unit 29155 [S3][S4].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft assesses the group has been operational in some capacity since at least 2020, with historical compromises of Eastern European entities as early as April 2021 [S1]. WhisperGate first appeared on victim systems on 2022-01-13 [S2]. The US joint advisory says Unit 29155 has conducted offensive cyber operations since at least 2020 [S3].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Cadet Blizzard (formerly DEV-0586; renamed in April 2023) [S1][S2]. Microsoft describes it as distinct from the other GRU-affiliated groups Forest Blizzard (STRONTIUM) and Seashell Blizzard (IRIDIUM) [S1]. MITRE tracks it as Ember Bear (G1003) with aliases UNC2589, Bleeding Bear, DEV-0586, Cadet Blizzard, Frozenvista and UAC-0056 [S7]. The joint advisory maps Cadet Blizzard, Ember Bear, Frozenvista, UNC2589 and UAC-0056 to Unit 29155 activity, and cautions that these may not exactly match US government attribution [S3]. CLUSTER BOUNDARY: MITRE tracks Saint Bear (G1031; Storm-0587, TA471, UAC-0056, Lorec53) separately. It is the Saint Bot/OutSteel phishing cluster, and MITRE says it is distinct from Ember Bear despite past confusion [S7][S8]. Microsoft reports that Cadet Blizzard has intersected with Storm-0587, a phishing and document-stealer cluster active since April 2021, but tracks it separately [S1]. This profile therefore does not merge Saint Bot or OutSteel campaign facts into Cadet Blizzard.

attribution.sponsor: Russian Federation: the GRU (Main Directorate of the General Staff). Microsoft assesses the actor is associated with the GRU [S1]. The FBI, NSA and CISA attribute the corresponding cyber activity to GRU Unit 29155 [S3], and a US indictment names a Unit 29155 cyber commander and officers [S4].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft says it has 'gained high confidence in our analysis and knowledge of the actor's tooling, victimology, and motivation' and assesses that Cadet Blizzard is associated with the GRU [S1]. The September 2024 joint advisory makes a US and allied government attribution to GRU Unit 29155. It also notes that vendor alias mappings may not exactly match US government attribution [S3]. US federal indictments (June 2024 and September 2024) charge a civilian and five GRU officers over WhisperGate. These charges are allegations, not convictions [S4][S5].
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and incident response [S1][S2]; FBI/NSA/CISA joint advisory AA24-249A [S3]; DOJ indictments of Amin Stigal (June 2024) and of Col. Yuriy Denisov and four Unit 29155 lieutenants (September 2024) [S4][S5]. Microsoft also assesses that at least one Russian private-sector organization materially supported the WhisperGate operation [S1]. The FBI assesses that the cyber operators are junior active-duty GRU officers working under experienced unit leadership, and that they rely in part on non-GRU cybercriminals [S3].

actors.objectives: Microsoft lists disruption, destruction, information collection and possibly intimidation, and notes that some operations appear designed as public signals [S1]. The US advisory says Unit 29155 conducts computer network operations against global targets for espionage, sabotage and reputational harm [S3][S4]. It exposes stolen data through hack-and-leak fronts such as 'Free Civilian' [S1].

regions: Europe and NATO member states, especially those providing military aid to Ukraine [S1][S3]
targeting.notes: Microsoft describes a 'compromise one, compromise many' approach through IT providers [S1]. The FBI observed more than 14,000 instances of domain scanning across 26 NATO members and several other EU countries (reported via secondary coverage of the advisory) [S3]. The Stigal indictment says later targets included systems in countries supporting Ukraine, including the United States [S5].

capabilities.summary: Destructive capability: WhisperGate is a two-stage wiper disguised as ransomware. It overwrites the Master Boot Record with a fake ransom note, then downloads a file corrupter from Discord that overwrites targeted files, and it has no recovery mechanism [S2]. Initial access comes mainly through exploitation of internet-facing web servers and of known Confluence and Exchange vulnerabilities, including CVE-2021-26084, CVE-2022-41040 and ProxyShell [S1]. Post-exploitation relies on web shells, renamed open-source and living-off-the-land tools (Impacket, netcat, GOST, procdump), and anonymization through commercial VPNs and Tor. Microsoft also reports anti-forensics and disabling of Microsoft Defender [S1][S2]. Operations are paired with website defacement and hack-and-leak information operations [S1]. Microsoft judges the group less prolific than Seashell Blizzard and its operational security weaker than that of Forest Blizzard or Seashell Blizzard [S1].

MITRE's Saint Bot software entry associates the tool with Ember Bear, while its Saint Bear group entry calls the two clusters distinct [S7][S8]. Unit 42 attributes Saint Bot and OutSteel phishing (for example against a Ukrainian energy organization on 2022-02-01) to UAC-0056, which other vendors call TA471, SaintBear and Lorec53 [S6]. The imported record's aliases (Saint Bear, SaintBear, Lorec53, TA471, Nodaria, Storm-0587, DEV-0587) may belong to the Saint Bear/Storm-0587 phishing cluster rather than to Cadet Blizzard and should be reviewed.
The imported record's software list includes Saint Bot, which may belong to Saint Bear/Storm-0587 rather than Cadet Blizzard [S8].
No public Microsoft reporting on Cadet Blizzard after 2023 was found in this research pass, so current activity levels are unverified.
The identity of the Russian private-sector organization that Microsoft says supported WhisperGate is not public in the sources reviewed [S1].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Key cyber terrain is internet-facing web servers and Confluence and Exchange instances on perimeters and in DMZs, plus IT service providers whose access reaches many government customers [S1]. The operating environment covers Ukraine and the NATO states that support it, including US systems [S1][S3][S5]. STEP 2 (effects): Destructive wipers can make government and NGO endpoints inoperable without recovery [S2]. Hack-and-leak and defacement add information effects aimed at intimidation and reputational harm [S1][S3]. STEP 3 (adversary template): exploit a public-facing service, then plant a web shell, dump credentials (LSASS, registry hives), move laterally with Impacket, and either exfiltrate data and leak it or deploy a wiper; anonymization runs through VPNs and Tor [S1][S2]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued espionage and hack-and-leak against Ukrainian and allied government and IT-provider networks, preceded by broad scanning of NATO domains [S1][S3]. MDCOA is coordinated destructive wiper deployment through compromised IT providers against allied government or critical-infrastructure networks during a crisis [S1][S2][S3]. Candidate indicators: scanning spikes against exposed Confluence and Exchange servers; new web shells on DMZ servers; renamed procdump, netcat or GOST binaries; reg save of SAM or SYSTEM hives; Impacket remote execution over ADMIN$; payloads retrieved from Discord; disabled Defender; new Free Civilian-style leak channels [S1][S2].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: track Cadet Blizzard, Ember Bear and Unit 29155 reporting together, but keep the Saint Bear/Storm-0587 phishing cluster separate to avoid mis-cueing defenders [S1][S3][S7][S8]. Authorities: US attribution rests on the joint advisory and indictments. Vendor alias mappings are flagged as inexact, so planners should cite the government attribution for actions and vendor reporting for TTPs [S3][S4]. Mission assurance: give priority to patching and monitoring internet-facing collaboration and mail servers, and to backups and MBR protection for mission systems that depend on IT service providers, given the 'compromise one, compromise many' approach and the destructive intent [S1][S2]. Coordination: because targeting includes allies that support Ukraine and the US, coordinate with CISA, FBI and allied CERTs (for example CERT-UA) on indicators and on hack-and-leak responses [S1][S3][S5].

capabilities.summary: Custom, regularly retooled malware: PLEAD backdoor and DRIGO exfiltration tool, KIVARS and Waterbear (secondary backdoor installed after privilege is gained) [S2]; Consock, Waship, Dalwit and Nomri backdoors plus dual-use and living-off-the-land tools in 2019-2020 [S5]; Flagpro downloader, SelfMake Loader and Spider RAT from 2020-2021 [S6]; BendyBear and FakeDead cited in the 2023 advisory [S7]; and Deuterbear, a Waterbear successor first seen in October 2022 with anti-memory-scanning, shellcode plugins and HTTPS C2 [S9][S10]. Waterbear is described by Trend Micro as having more than ten versions since 2009 with extensive anti-debug and anti-sandbox features [S9]. Code signing with stolen certificates from D-Link and Changing Information Technology to sign PLEAD and a password stealer (2018) [S3]. Probable router-level man-in-the-middle abuse of the ASUS WebStorage update process to deliver PLEAD (2019) [S4]. Spear-phishing with password-protected archives containing macro documents impersonating business partners [S6]. Network-device tradecraft: after gaining admin access (typically stolen credentials), modifying Cisco router firmware with an SSH backdoor that hides connections from logs, disabling logging, and exploiting router domain-trust relationships to move from subsidiaries to headquarters; the agencies note the technique is not limited to Cisco [S7][S8]. PLEAD operators were also reported to scan for vulnerable routers and enable their VPN feature to stage C2 or delivery servers [S2].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Key cyber terrain includes edge and branch routers connecting East Asian subsidiaries, partner sites and contractors to US and Japanese headquarters networks, since BlackTech pivots along those trust paths [S7]. Defense-supporting organizations in Japan and Taiwan sit inside this environment [S7]. STEP 2 (effects): Firmware-level router persistence with log suppression degrades defenders' visibility and survives host-level remediation; stolen code-signing certificates and hijacked update channels undermine software-trust assumptions [S3][S4][S7]. STEP 3 (adversary template): spear-phishing or stolen credentials, then first-stage downloader (Flagpro/PLEAD), then secondary backdoor (Waterbear/Deuterbear), then document theft; in parallel, admin access to routers, firmware replacement, and lateral movement from subsidiary to headquarters [S2][S6][S7][S9]. STEP 4: MLCOA is persistent technology and document theft from government, technology and defense-supporting entities in Taiwan, Japan and the US [S2][S5][S7]. MDCOA is covert firmware-level control of routers on paths serving US and Japanese military-support networks, positioning the actor to collect or disrupt traffic during a Taiwan Strait crisis (analyst extrapolation; no disruptive activity reported). Candidate indicators: router firmware image hash mismatches, unexpected reboots or image changes, SSH sessions not reflected in logs, outbound VTY connections, logging disabled on network devices, and executables signed with revoked Taiwanese vendor certificates [S3][S7][S8].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: network-device integrity (firmware hashes, configuration drift, logging status) should be a reported data feed, because host EDR alone will not see this actor's router persistence [S7]. (2) Authorities: many affected routers belong to coalition partners, contractors or overseas subsidiaries outside DoDIN control; responses depend on partner and private-sector coordination rather than unilateral action [S7]. (3) Mission assurance: map mission dependencies on links that traverse East Asian partner or subsidiary networks and treat them as potentially compromised; apply zero-trust controls and review subsidiary connections as the advisory recommends [S7]. (4) Coordination: the advisory was co-authored by US and Japanese agencies, so information sharing with Japan's NPA and NISC and with DC3/DIB partners is the natural channel for indicators and remediation status [S7].

provenance.importedSummary: BlackTech is a cyber espionage group operating against targets in East Asia, particularly Taiwan, and occasionally, Japan and Hong Kong. Based on the mutexes and domain names of some of their C&C servers, BlackTech’s campaigns are likely designed to steal their target’s technology. Following their activities and evolving tactics and techniques helped us uncover the proverbial red string of fate that connected three seemingly disparate campaigns: PLEAD, Shrouded Crossbow, and of late, Waterbear. PLEAD is an information theft campaign with a penchant for confidential documents. Active since 2012, it has so far targeted Taiwanese government agencies and private organizations. PLEAD’s toolset includes the self-named PLEAD backdoor and the DRIGO exfiltration tool. PLEAD uses spear-phishing emails to deliver and install their backdoor, either as an attachment or through links to cloud storage services. Some of the cloud storage accounts used to deliver PLEAD are also used as drop off points for exfiltrated documents stolen by DRIGO. PLEAD actors use a router scanner tool to scan for vulnerable routers, after which the attackers will enable the router’s VPN feature then register a machine as virtual server. This virtual server will be used either as a C&C server or an HTTP server that delivers PLEAD malware to their targets.

They have extensively used strategic web compromises to compromise victims.

identification.summary: CeranaKeeper is a China-aligned APT that has been active since at least early 2022, primarily targeting governmental institutions in Asian countries. The group employs custom backdoors like TONESHELL and OneDoor, leveraging cloud services such as Dropbox and OneDrive for data exfiltration. CeranaKeeper utilizes techniques like side-loading, brute-force attacks, and the deployment of BAT scripts to extend its reach within compromised networks. Their operations are characterized by a relentless pursuit of sensitive data, adapting their toolset and methods to evade detection.

Microsoft describes Charcoal Typhoon (formerly CHROMIUM) as a Chinese state-affiliated threat actor with a broad operational scope, targeting government, higher education, communications infrastructure, oil and gas, and information technology, mainly in Taiwan, Thailand, Mongolia, Malaysia, France and Nepal, and also institutions and individuals worldwide who oppose China's policies [S1]. In February 2024 Microsoft and OpenAI reported that the group had used large language models for research, scripting, translation and phishing content, and disabled its accounts [S1][S2]. In March 2025 the FBI said that activity of the PRC contractor i-Soon (Anxun Information Technology) is tracked by industry as Aquatic Panda, BRONZE UNIVERSITY, Charcoal Typhoon, Earth Lusca and RedHotel [S3][S4].
identification.firstObserved: Trend Micro (as summarized in a Singapore IMDA advisory): Earth Lusca active since at least April 2019 [S12]. Trend Micro had been tracking Earth Lusca since mid-2021 when it published its 2022 brief [S11]. The FBI places i-Soon intrusions from about 2016 to 2023 [S3][S4]. Microsoft does not give a first-observed date in the sources gathered [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Charcoal Typhoon (formerly CHROMIUM). Microsoft lists Aquatic Panda, ControlX, RedHotel and BRONZE UNIVERSITY as other researchers' names [S1]. The FBI's 2025 statement adds Earth Lusca to the i-Soon cluster [S3][S4]. ESET tracks FishMonger, which it says is operated by I-SOON and also tracked as Earth Lusca, TAG-22, Aquatic Panda and Red Dev 10 [S5]. Recorded Future's TAG-22 (2021) and RedHotel (2023) reports describe overlapping activity [S6][S7]. MITRE tracks Aquatic Panda as G0143 and Earth Lusca as a separate group, G1006 [S13]. The imported summary in this record is Earth Lusca text, not Microsoft's description of Charcoal Typhoon.

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China. Microsoft calls Charcoal Typhoon Chinese state-affiliated [S1]. US prosecutors (as reported in press coverage) allege that i-Soon, whose activity the FBI ties to Charcoal Typhoon, hacked at the direction of and in close coordination with the Ministry of State Security (MSS) and the Ministry of Public Security (MPS), and tried to sell stolen data to at least 43 MSS/MPS bureaus in at least 31 provinces and municipalities [S3][S4]. Recorded Future assessed that RedHotel's targeting, tooling and methods closely resemble other MSS-affiliated private contractor groups, and linked its infrastructure administration to Chengdu [S7].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft states the attribution as a Chinese state-affiliated actor [S1]. ESET assesses with high confidence that FishMonger conducted Operation FishMedley and says it independently confirmed FishMonger is operated by I-SOON [S5]. Trend Micro calls the Earth Lusca and i-Soon overlap significant but says its research was still ongoing [S10]. The US government brought formal criminal charges against i-Soon employees and MPS officers in March 2025 [S3][S4]; the FBI's mapping of vendor names to i-Soon is the government link to the Charcoal Typhoon name [S3][S4].
attribution.basis: Microsoft and OpenAI account telemetry [S1][S2]; DOJ indictment and FBI statements (via press coverage) [S3][S4]; Trend Micro overlaps in victims, tooling (ShadowPad, Winnti) and Chengdu source IPs with the leaked i-Soon data [S10]; ESET intrusion analysis [S5]; Recorded Future infrastructure analysis [S6][S7].

actors.objectives: Espionage that supports PRC government priorities: government, foreign-affairs, telecommunications and academic intelligence across Asia and globally, plus monitoring of people and institutions who oppose China's policies [S1][S9]. Recorded Future assessed that some targeting, such as Taiwan's ITRI and COVID-19 research, was likely industrial and economic espionage [S7]. Trend Micro reports possible financial motivation from attacks on gambling and cryptocurrency firms [S11]. Under the contractor model described by prosecutors, i-Soon both received tasking from officials and chose its own targets to sell stolen data to MSS/MPS bureaus [S3][S4].

capabilities.summary: Initial access through exploitation of internet-facing servers: Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) on VMware Horizon at an academic institution [S8], compromised GlassFish servers [S6], and 2019-2022 n-day flaws on public-facing servers [S9]; also spear-phishing, watering holes and geopolitical lure documents [S10][S11]. Post-exploitation includes Cobalt Strike, attempts to disable EDR, LSASS credential dumping and WinRAR staging for exfiltration [S8][S9]. Lateral movement uses Impacket with privileged access [S5]. Long-term access relies on shared PRC malware families (ShadowPad, Winnti, Spyder, SodaMaster) [S5][S6][S12] and the custom Linux backdoor SprySOCKS, derived from Trochilus [S9]. VPS reverse proxies hide C2 [S7]. Microsoft and OpenAI observed the group using LLMs to research companies, platforms, vulnerabilities and security tools, generate and debug scripts, translate, and draft phishing content; OpenAI judged this a limited, incremental uplift [S1][S2].

diamond.socioPolitical: Intelligence collection for PRC state customers through a hacker-for-hire market, where stolen data is sold to MSS/MPS bureaus [S3][S4]; monitoring of opponents of PRC policy [S1]; interest in Taiwan politics around elections [S10].
diamond.technology: Exposed and unpatched internet-facing services (VMware Horizon, GlassFish, other public-facing servers), Windows and Linux server estates, and endpoint security that the actor attempts to disable [S6][S8][S9].

gaps: Primary DOJ indictment, DOJ press release and FBI wanted notice could not be opened (government sites blocked); indictment details come from press coverage [S3][S4].

Microsoft's threat-actor naming table (learn.microsoft.com) could not be fetched to confirm the current Microsoft alias list; Microsoft's 2024 blog does not list Earth Lusca, TAG-22 or FishMonger as Charcoal Typhoon names [S1].

Cluster boundaries: MITRE keeps Aquatic Panda (G0143) and Earth Lusca (G1006) as separate groups, and the shared tooling (ShadowPad, Winnti) is used by multiple PRC actors [S6][S13]. Treat the merged victim and TTP picture as cluster-level, not confirmed single-actor.

ESET WeLiveSecurity FishMedley report, Trend Micro primary reports, Recorded Future RedHotel PDF and the CrowdStrike Log4Shell blog were not opened directly; details come from search-result summaries, translated copies or press coverage.
CrowdStrike's Aquatic Panda adversary profile (stated start date, dual intelligence and industrial-espionage mission) could not be read in full or dated.
Post-indictment activity (2025-2026) attributed to Charcoal Typhoon by Microsoft was not found in the sources gathered.
No public reporting gathered on any targeting of US military or Air Force networks beyond the DIA victim named in the indictment coverage [S3].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Key cyber terrain is internet-facing servers (VMware Horizon/Log4j, GlassFish, other n-day-exposed services) and the Linux and Windows hosts behind them in government, academic, telecom and defense-intelligence networks [S3][S6][S8][S9]. STEP 2 (effects): The actor relies on known, often older n-days, so patch latency on edge services defines the exposure window. Shared PRC malware complicates attribution [S6][S9]. STEP 3 (adversary template): edge exploitation, spear-phishing or a watering hole leads to Cobalt Strike, then EDR tampering, LSASS dumping and Impacket lateral movement, then ShadowPad, Winnti, Spyder or SprySOCKS for persistence and WinRAR-staged exfiltration through VPS reverse proxies [S5][S7][S8][S9]. STEP 4: MLCOA is persistent espionage against government, foreign-affairs, telecom and academic partners in the Indo-Pacific, with stolen data sold to MSS/MPS customers [S3][S7][S9]. MDCOA is long-dwell compromise of US defense-intelligence or partner-nation foreign-ministry networks around political events such as Taiwan elections [S3][S10]. Candidate indicators: Tomcat or Horizon processes spawning shells or wget/curl; attempts to stop EDR services; LSASS access followed by WinRAR archives; a libmonitor.so.2 loader on Linux; outbound beacons to VPS infrastructure [S8][S9].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: track vendor reporting under all mapped names (Charcoal Typhoon, Aquatic Panda, Earth Lusca, RedHotel, FishMonger, TAG-22) because public reporting is split across vendors [S1][S3][S5]. Authorities: the actor is a contractor indicted under US law and working for MSS/MPS [S3][S4]; defensive and law-enforcement equities (FBI) are active, so coordinate before any response actions beyond DoD networks. Mission assurance: prioritize patching and monitoring of edge services and Linux servers, and protect EDR from tampering, since the sourced intrusions began at exposed services and tried to disable EDR [S8][S9]. Coordination: partner-nation foreign ministries and telecoms in Southeast Asia, Taiwan, Nepal and Mongolia are repeat victims [S1][S3][S6][S9]; share indicators through combatant command and partner CERT channels.

provenance.importedSummary: Earth Lusca is a threat actor from China that targets organizations of interest to the Chinese government, including academic institutions, telecommunication companies, religious organizations, and other civil society groups. Earth Lusca's tools closely resemble those used by Winnti Umbrella, but the group appears to operate separately from Winnti. Earth Lusca has also been observed targeting cryptocurrency payment platforms and cryptocurrency exchanges in what are likely financially motivated attacks.

identification.summary: Chaya_004 is a Chinese threat actor identified through malicious infrastructure, including a network of servers hosting Supershell backdoors and various pen testing tools of Chinese origin. The actor's activities are linked to the exploitation of a specific vulnerability, with a focus on using Chinese cloud providers. Analysis of the infrastructure has revealed TTPs associated with Chaya_004, indicating a sophisticated approach to cyber operations. Mitigation recommendations and proactive response measures have been developed in light of these findings.

China-origin espionage actor that Microsoft tracks as Checkered Typhoon (formerly CHLORINE), mapping to it the vendor names DEEP PANDA, APT19, ATG50, TG-3551 and Red Gargoyle [S1]. Under the Deep Panda name, CrowdStrike reported intrusions into US national security think tanks in 2014 and a campaign against defense, healthcare, government and technology organizations using Sakula malware [S2][S3]. Security firms including CrowdStrike, RSA and ThreatConnect linked Deep Panda to the 2014-2015 Anthem and OPM breaches [S5]. Under the APT19 name, FireEye reported a 2017 phishing campaign against law and investment firms [S7]. Fortinet tied Deep Panda to 2022 Log4Shell exploitation of VMware Horizon servers [S10].
identification.firstObserved: Public reporting under the Deep Panda name dates to July 2014 [S2]. Symantec says Black Vine, a cluster press links to the Anthem breach, has been active since at least 2012 [S6]; Microsoft does not list Black Vine in its mapping [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Checkered Typhoon (formerly CHLORINE); 'Typhoon' denotes China origin in Microsoft's taxonomy [S1]. Microsoft's mapping lists only CHLORINE, DEEP PANDA, ATG50, APT19, TG-3551 and Red Gargoyle as other names [S1]. Other aliases in this record (Black Vine, Codoso/C0d0so0, Shell Crew, KungFu Kittens, PinkPanther, WebMasters, Sunshop Group, etc.) come from MISP/MITRE imports and are not confirmed by Microsoft; MITRE tracks Deep Panda (G0009) and APT19 (G0073) as separate group entries. The Forbes.com watering hole was attributed by iSIGHT and Invincea to 'Codoso Team', not by Microsoft [S4]. Sakula is described by CrowdStrike as a limited-release tool used by several adversaries, so Sakula use alone does not identify this actor [S3].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China (Microsoft assigns the actor to its China-origin 'Typhoon' family) [S1]. FireEye assesses APT19 is composed of freelancers with some degree of sponsorship by the Chinese government [S7]. CrowdStrike said in 2014 it believed Deep Panda works for or is funded by the Chinese government [S2].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft attributes the actor to China by family assignment but publishes no confidence level in its mapping [S1]. CrowdStrike's Dmitri Alperovitch expressed 'great confidence' the actors were state-sponsored (2014) [S2]. Researchers told Reuters in 2015 the group's exact affiliation with the Chinese government was not known and it might be a private contractor [S5]. The 2019 US indictment over the Anthem breach does not allege Chinese government involvement [S9]. China has denied involvement [S5].
attribution.basis: Vendor telemetry and malware analysis (CrowdStrike, FireEye, Fortinet, Symantec, ThreatConnect) [S2][S3][S5][S6][S7][S10]; shared tooling and stolen code-signing certificates across the OPM and Anthem intrusions [S5]; US criminal cases against Yu Pingan (Sakula supplier, 2017) and Fujie Wang (Anthem, 2019) [S8][S9].

actors.objectives: Espionage against foreign-policy and national security research organizations, including rapid re-tasking to Iraq and Middle East experts in June 2014 [S2]; theft of large personal-data holdings from health insurers and, per vendor and press reporting, the US Office of Personnel Management [S5][S9]; and theft of data from law and investment firms for competitive economic purposes [S7].

sectors: National security and foreign-policy think tanks [S2]
Financial, academic, cosmetics and travel (2022 opportunistic Log4Shell activity) [S10]
targeting.notes: Targeting has shifted with events: CrowdStrike observed a sharp move from Asia-focused think-tank experts to Iraq experts on 18 June 2014 [S2]. The 2022 Log4Shell activity was opportunistic rather than sector-specific [S10].

capabilities.summary: Initial access through spear-phishing (RTF exploiting CVE-2017-0199, macro-enabled Excel documents, regsvr32 'Squiblydoo' whitelisting bypass) [S7][S9], drive-by exploits [S2], strategic web compromise (Forbes.com, attributed to Codoso) [S4], and exploitation of public-facing services (Log4Shell on VMware Horizon) [S10]. Tooling includes Sakula disguised as Adobe Reader and Juniper VPN installers and loaded by DLL side-loading [S3], Cobalt Strike BEACON [S7], Mivast (Black Vine reporting) [S6], the Milestone backdoor and the Fire Chili kernel rootkit [S10]. The actor repeatedly uses code-signing certificates stolen from Korean and US software and game companies [S3][S5][S10], and look-alike credential-harvesting domains such as We11point.com and OPM-Learning.org [S5].

campaigns.name: Anthem breach
campaigns.summary: Intrusions starting February 2014 led to theft of data on about 78.8 million people; Symantec linked it to Black Vine and Mivast, vendors to Deep Panda, and DOJ indicted Fujie Wang in 2019.

campaigns.name: Think-tank intrusions and Iraq re-tasking
campaigns.summary: CrowdStrike reported Deep Panda compromises of several US national security think tanks and a shift on 18 June 2014 to targeting Iraq and Middle East experts.

campaigns.name: 'Ironman' Sakula campaign
campaigns.summary: CrowdStrike reported Deep Panda use of signed Sakula variants against defense, healthcare, government and technology organizations.

campaigns.name: Forbes.com watering hole (Codoso)
campaigns.summary: A Forbes.com widget was compromised 28 Nov to 1 Dec 2014 to serve Flash and IE zero-days; iSIGHT and Invincea attributed it to Codoso Team (an alias not in Microsoft's mapping).

campaigns.name: OPM breach linkage
campaigns.summary: CrowdStrike, RSA, ThreatConnect and others told Reuters they believed Deep Panda was behind both the OPM and Anthem breaches, citing shared Sakula use and a stolen DTOPTOOLZ certificate.

campaigns.name: APT19 law and investment firm phishing
campaigns.summary: FireEye observed phishing against at least seven global law and investment firms in May-June 2017, delivering Cobalt Strike BEACON.

campaigns.name: Arrest of Sakula supplier Yu Pingan
campaigns.summary: The FBI arrested Yu Pingan, alleged to have supplied malware including Sakula used against US companies from 2011 to 2014.

campaigns.name: Log4Shell / Fire Chili
campaigns.summary: Fortinet linked Log4Shell exploitation of VMware Horizon servers, the Milestone backdoor and the signed Fire Chili rootkit to Deep Panda.

diamond.adversary: PRC-attributed operators that Microsoft tracks as Checkered Typhoon [S1]; FireEye assesses APT19 is freelancers with some Chinese government sponsorship [S7]; individuals charged include Fujie Wang (Anthem) and malware supplier Yu Pingan [S8][S9].
diamond.capability: Sakula, Mivast, Cobalt Strike BEACON, Milestone backdoor, Fire Chili rootkit; Office exploits, macros, Log4Shell; stolen code-signing certificates [S3][S6][S7][S10].
diamond.infrastructure: Look-alike phishing and credential-harvest domains (We11point.com, OPM-Learning.org) [S5]; 2bunny[.]com and cloudsend[.]net domains for 2017 phishing and C2 [S7]; compromised legitimate websites used as watering holes [S4].
diamond.victim: US think tanks, defense contractors, health insurers, government personnel records, technology firms, and law and investment firms [S2][S3][S5][S7].
diamond.socioPolitical: Foreign-policy intelligence tied to world events (Iraq crisis 2014) [S2]; bulk personal data on US persons and federal employees [S5][S9]; competitive economic intelligence from law and investment firms [S7].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints, Microsoft Office, Internet Explorer/Flash, internet-facing VMware Horizon servers [S4][S7][S10].

gaps: Microsoft has published no actor profile, blog or confidence statement for Checkered Typhoon found in this research; the only Microsoft source is its name-mapping file [S1].

Cluster boundaries are unresolved: MITRE keeps Deep Panda (G0009) and APT19 (G0073) as separate groups, and Microsoft's mapping omits Black Vine, Codoso and Shell Crew, which press reporting associates with the Anthem and Forbes activity [S1][S4][S6].

The US government has not formally attributed OPM to this actor; the OPM link comes from vendor statements to Reuters and anonymous sources [S5]. The Anthem indictment does not allege PRC government involvement [S9].

Primary documents were not opened: CrowdStrike blogs (fetch blocked), Symantec's Black Vine white paper, Fortinet's Fire Chili blog, DOJ press releases and complaints (justice.gov blocked), and MITRE ATT&CK pages (fetch failed). Facts from them rely on press coverage.
The DOJ Anthem indictment date (2019-05) and the CrowdStrike Ironman date (2014-11) come from search-result coverage, not the opened documents.
No public reporting after 2022 attributed to Checkered Typhoon, Deep Panda or APT19 was found; current activity is unknown.
Fortinet noted overlaps between the 2022 activity and the Winnti group (shared stolen certificates and possibly C2) whose nature is unclear [S10].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Key terrain includes HR and personnel-records systems, health-benefit provider networks, cleared defense contractors, policy research partners, and internet-facing remote-access servers such as VMware Horizon [S3][S5][S10]. STEP 2 (effects): Theft of personnel and health records gives an adversary long-term targeting data on service members and cleared personnel; quick uptake of public exploits (Log4Shell) shrinks patch windows [S5][S9][S10]. STEP 3 (adversary template): Spear-phishing or exploitation of public-facing services, then signed implants (Sakula, BEACON, Milestone) loaded via side-loading or regsvr32, then rootkit concealment and data theft [S3][S7][S10]. STEP 4: MLCOA is quiet collection of policy and personal data from think tanks, contractors and benefit providers, re-tasked to world events [S2][S5]. MDCOA is bulk theft of DoD-adjacent personnel or medical data enabling targeting of cleared personnel. Candidate indicators: look-alike domains imitating benefit providers or OPM; binaries signed with stolen game- or software-company certificates; regsvr32 calling remote scrobj.dll scriptlets; PowerShell spawned from VMware Horizon/Tomcat processes; unknown kernel drivers [S5][S7][S10].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: include contractor and benefit-provider breaches in the common picture, since this actor's largest known thefts were outside government networks [S5][S9]. (2) Authorities: much victim data sits with private healthcare and legal firms, so response depends on law enforcement and partner reporting rather than DoD authorities [S7][S9]. (3) Mission assurance: personnel-data compromise is a lasting risk to force protection and counterintelligence; plan for long-tail impacts, not just remediation [S5]. (4) Coordination: work with DC3/DIB CS and FBI on stolen code-signing certificates and shared tooling that cross actor boundaries (Sakula, Winnti overlap) [S3][S10].

identification.summary: Chernovite is a highly capable and sophisticated threat actor group that has developed a modular ICS malware framework called PIPEDREAM. They are known for targeting industrial control systems and operational technology environments, with the ability to disrupt, degrade, and potentially destroy physical processes. Chernovite has demonstrated a deep understanding of ICS protocols and intrusion techniques, making them a significant threat to critical infrastructure sectors.

China-based human-operated ransomware actor that Microsoft (as DEV-0401) describes as running every stage of the attack itself, from initial access to ransomware development, rather than using an affiliate model or buying access [S1][S9]. It gains access by exploiting unpatched internet-facing software and frequently rebrands its ransomware payloads, so payload-based reporting can make it look like several different groups [S1]. Secureworks (BRONZE STARLIGHT) and MITRE assess that the ransomware may be a smokescreen and that the underlying motive may be intellectual-property theft or espionage rather than profit [S3][S9].
identification.firstObserved: Secureworks coverage: active since early 2021 [S4]. MITRE: active since at least 2021 [S9]. Microsoft's DEV-0401 payload timeline begins in 2021 [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Cinnamon Tempest (formerly DEV-0401); Microsoft's DEV-0401 reporting calls the group China-based [S1][S9]. MITRE tracks it as G1021 with associated names DEV-0401, Emperor Dragonfly and BRONZE STARLIGHT [S9]. Emperor Dragonfly is Sygnia's name; Sygnia linked the Night Sky and Cheerscrypt ransomware to it [S6]. Ransomware brands reported for the cluster: LockFile, AtomSilo, Rook, Night Sky, Pandora (Secureworks), LockBit 2.0 (Microsoft) and Cheerscrypt (Sygnia) [S1][S3][S6].

attribution.sponsor: China-based; no public source reviewed names a specific PRC government sponsor or unit [S1][S3]. Secureworks and SentinelLabs describe the actor as China-linked or China-aligned and suggest espionage aims, but neither ties it to a named state organization [S3][S7].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft states DEV-0401 is 'confirmed to be a China-based activity group' [S1]. Secureworks CTU assesses with moderate confidence that BRONZE STARLIGHT is located in China and that ransomware may be a smokescreen for IP theft or espionage [S3]. SentinelLabs says indicators point to BRONZE STARLIGHT but the exact grouping remains unclear given interconnected Chinese APT relationships [S7]. No government attribution was found.
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry of the full attack lifecycle and payload history [S1][S2]; Secureworks analysis of HUI Loader, which it has only seen used by likely China-based groups, plus PlugX and victimology [S3][S4]; Sygnia incident response linking Night Sky and Cheerscrypt TTPs and Chinese-language open-source tooling [S6]; MITRE's synthesis of victimology, short ransomware lifespans and use of malware tied to government-sponsored groups [S9].

actors.objectives: Overtly, ransomware extortion with name-and-shame leak sites [S1][S3]. Secureworks and MITRE assess that the real objective may be intellectual-property theft or cyber-espionage, citing victimology, the short lifespan of each ransomware brand and the use of state-associated malware [S3][S9]. SentinelLabs reporting on gambling-sector intrusions points to collection on Southeast Asian gambling operations of interest to China [S7].

sectors: Aerospace and defense (defense division of an Indian conglomerate) [S5]
Organizations running unpatched VMware Horizon, Exchange, ManageEngine ADSelfService Plus or Confluence (opportunistic) [S1][S2]
targeting.notes: Victim list comes from secondary summaries of the Secureworks report, not the primary text [S4][S5]. Secureworks notes the ransomware tended to hit a small number of organizations over a short period before each brand was dropped [S4]. Initial access is driven by exposed vulnerable software, so victims may partly reflect opportunity rather than tasking [S1].

capabilities.summary: Exploits unpatched public-facing software, including Exchange, ManageEngine ADSelfService Plus, Confluence and Log4j 2 (CVE-2021-44228) in VMware Horizon, and typically obtains elevated credentials at initial access [S1][S2]. Uses Cobalt Strike, often launched by DLL search-order hijacking; around June 2022 Microsoft saw it begin replacing Cobalt Strike with Sliver [S1]. Uses the custom HUI Loader to decrypt and run Cobalt Strike and PlugX [S3]. Moves laterally with a customized Impacket wmiexec.py and deploys ransomware from batch files via Group Policy, often staged in the domain controller NETLOGON share, which requires domain-admin-level credentials [S1]. Exfiltrates with Rclone to Mega cloud storage and runs ransomware against both Windows and VMware ESXi [S6]. Ransomware is rebuilt from leaked code (Babuk-derived Rook, Night Sky and Pandora) or bought in, as with LockBit 2.0 [S1][S3]. SentinelOne linked to DEV-0401 a LockBit intrusion that side-loaded Cobalt Strike through a signed VMware utility and evaded EDR, ETW and AMSI [S8]. Gambling-sector intrusions attributed to the group used DLL hijacking of Adobe, Edge and McAfee executables and a likely stolen code-signing certificate [S7].

campaigns.name: LockFile and AtomSilo ransomware operations
campaigns.summary: Secureworks reports LockFile and AtomSilo as the group's first ransomware strains, followed by Babuk-derived families [S3][S4].

campaigns.name: Night Sky via Log4j in VMware Horizon
campaigns.summary: Microsoft reports DEV-0401 exploiting CVE-2021-44228 on internet-facing VMware Horizon from as early as 4 January 2022, leading to Night Sky ransomware [S2].

campaigns.name: Cheerscrypt intrusion (Emperor Dragonfly)
campaigns.summary: Sygnia investigated a January 2022 intrusion that began with Log4Shell on VMware Horizon and ended with Rclone exfiltration to Mega and Cheerscrypt encryption, linking Cheerscrypt to Night Sky [S6].

campaigns.name: Pandora ransomware deployments
campaigns.summary: Microsoft observed Pandora deployed mainly through unpatched VMware Horizon systems vulnerable to Log4j 2 [S1].

campaigns.name: Shift to LockBit 2.0
campaigns.summary: Microsoft reports that DEV-0401 began deploying LockBit 2.0 in April 2022 [S1]. SentinelOne later tied to DEV-0401 a LockBit intrusion that side-loaded Cobalt Strike through VMwareXferlogs.exe [S8].

campaigns.name: Cobalt Strike to Sliver transition
campaigns.summary: Microsoft observed DEV-0401 starting to replace Cobalt Strike with Sliver around 6 June 2022 [S1].

campaigns.name: Secureworks HUI Loader disclosure
campaigns.summary: Secureworks publicly attributes the HUI Loader ransomware cluster to BRONZE STARLIGHT and assesses the ransomware may be a smokescreen [S3][S4].

campaigns.name: Southeast Asian gambling sector intrusions
campaigns.summary: SentinelLabs reports Cobalt Strike delivered through DLL hijacking against Southeast Asian gambling companies, with indicators pointing to BRONZE STARLIGHT, and links it to ESET's Operation ChattyGoblin [S7].

campaigns.name: RA World ransomware attack (low-confidence link)
campaigns.summary: Symantec, as reported by BleepingComputer, describes an RA World attack on a South Asian software firm that used PlugX and the NPS proxy tool, which Bronze Starlight has used before. Unit 42 linked RA World to Emperor Dragonfly/Bronze Starlight only with low confidence [S10].

diamond.adversary: China-based group tracked as Cinnamon Tempest / DEV-0401 / BRONZE STARLIGHT / Emperor Dragonfly that runs the whole intrusion and ransomware chain itself [S1][S3][S6][S9].
diamond.capability: N-day exploitation (Exchange, ManageEngine, Confluence, Log4j/VMware Horizon); HUI Loader, PlugX, Cobalt Strike, Sliver, Impacket, Rclone; Babuk-derived and purchased ransomware such as LockBit 2.0; Windows and ESXi encryptors [S1][S2][S3][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised internet-facing servers used for entry; Mega cloud storage for exfiltration; leak sites that sometimes led to default web pages; Alibaba-hosted staging and a likely stolen code-signing certificate in gambling-sector activity [S1][S6][S7].
diamond.victim: Pharmaceutical, electronics manufacturing, aerospace/defense, media and legal organizations in the US, Brazil, Lithuania, Japan and India; Southeast Asian gambling companies [S5][S7].
diamond.socioPolitical: Vendors assess the ransomware may cover IP theft or espionage that serves Chinese interests [S3][S9]. SentinelLabs ties gambling-sector targeting to China's interest in the region following its Macao gambling crackdown [S7].
diamond.technology: Unpatched VMware Horizon (Log4j), Exchange, Confluence and ManageEngine servers; Active Directory and Group Policy used for mass deployment; VMware ESXi hypervisors [S1][S2][S6].

gaps: Primary Secureworks, Sygnia, SentinelLabs, Symantec and MITRE pages could not be fetched (DNS or host blocked). Their content is taken from mirrors (Sophos for Secureworks), press releases, news coverage and search-result summaries; validate against the originals.
Microsoft's threat-actor naming page (learn.microsoft.com) could not be opened to confirm the DEV-0401 to Cinnamon Tempest mapping directly; the mapping relies on the record's import and MITRE [S9].
No public government attribution or named PRC sponsor or unit was found.
Whether the ransomware is a smokescreen for espionage is an analytic judgment by Secureworks and MITRE, not a demonstrated fact; Microsoft treats the group as a ransomware operator [S1][S3][S9].

Cluster boundaries: Secureworks attributes a separate HUI Loader cluster aimed at Japanese IP theft to BRONZE RIVERSIDE (APT10-linked), not BRONZE STARLIGHT [S3]. SentinelLabs says the exact grouping of the gambling-sector activity is unclear [S7]. The RA World link rests on Unit 42 low-confidence attribution and Symantec hypothesis, and the PlugX variant was tied to Fireant/Mustang Panda [S10].
SentinelOne's LockBit side-loading case was linked to DEV-0401 after the fact; the details of that linkage were not reviewed in primary form [S8].

The TeamT5 Black Hat Asia 2022 talk ('To Loot or Not to Loot') on state-nexus attacks against online entertainment is cited in the actor record, but its slides were not reviewed and its link to this specific cluster is unconfirmed.
No public reporting confirming activity attributed to Cinnamon Tempest by name after 2023 was found, apart from the low-confidence RA World link.
The share of victims by sector or country, and any data stolen for espionage purposes, are not public in the sources gathered.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Internet-facing VMware Horizon, Exchange, Confluence and ManageEngine servers, along with Active Directory and domain controllers (NETLOGON and Group Policy), are key cyber terrain. So are ESXi hypervisors hosting mission systems [S1][S2][S6]. STEP 2 (effects): N-day exploitation gives the actor elevated credentials at entry, which shortens the time to domain-wide ransomware deployment. ESXi encryption raises the impact on virtualized infrastructure [S1][S6]. STEP 3 (adversary template): Exploit an exposed server; load Cobalt Strike or Sliver through DLL hijacking or HUI Loader; move laterally with Impacket wmiexec; exfiltrate with Rclone to Mega; deploy a short-lived ransomware brand by GPO batch script [S1][S3][S6]. STEP 4: MLCOA is opportunistic exploitation of unpatched perimeter services in defense-industrial, aerospace, electronics or pharma networks, followed by data theft and ransomware that may mask collection [S1][S3][S5]. MDCOA is domain-wide encryption of Windows and ESXi supporting mission-critical systems after IP exfiltration, with the ransomware masking espionage and misdirecting incident response [S3][S6]. Candidate indicators: Log4j exploitation attempts against Horizon; signed binaries (VMware, Adobe, McAfee, Edge) loading unexpected DLLs; renamed wmiexec output files; Rclone or Mega traffic; new batch files in NETLOGON or GPO changes [S1][S6][S7][S8].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: track exposure and patch status of Horizon, Exchange, Confluence and ManageEngine instances across DODIN and DIB partner enclaves, since this actor relies on known vulnerabilities rather than bought access [S1][S2]. Authorities: a ransomware event linked to this cluster may be espionage rather than crime, so plan early coordination between DCO, counterintelligence and law-enforcement channels instead of treating it purely as criminal extortion [S3][S9]. Mission assurance: protect domain controllers, Group Policy and ESXi management planes, and keep offline backups of virtualized mission systems [S1][S6]. Coordination: share indicators with DIB and partner-nation CERTs in affected sectors and regions (US, Brazil, Lithuania, Japan, India, Southeast Asia), and deconflict cluster names (DEV-0401, BRONZE STARLIGHT, Emperor Dragonfly) when fusing vendor reporting [S5][S7][S9].

provenance.importedSummary: BRONZE STARLIGHT has been active since mid 2021 and targets organizations globally across a range of industry verticals. The group leverages HUI Loader to load Cobalt Strike and PlugX payloads for command and control. CTU researchers have observed BRONZE STARLIGHT deploying ransomware to compromised networks as part of name-and-shame ransomware schemes, and posted victim names to leak sites. CTU researchers assess with moderate confidence that BRONZE STARLIGHT is located in China based on observed tradecraft, including the use of HUI Loader and PlugX which are associated with China-based threat group activity. It is plausible that BRONZE STARLIGHT deploys ransomware as a smokescreen rather than for financial gain, with the underlying motivation of stealing intellectual property theft or conducting espionage.

identification.summary: Citrine Sleet is Microsoft's name for a North Korea-based actor that goes after financial institutions, especially organizations and individuals that manage cryptocurrency, for financial gain [S1]. Its usual methods are fake cryptocurrency trading sites, fake job applications and weaponized wallet or trading apps. Its most common trojan is AppleJeus [S1]. In August 2024 Microsoft attributed, with medium confidence, exploitation of a Chromium zero-day (CVE-2024-7971) to Citrine Sleet. The intrusion chained a Windows kernel exploit and deployed the FudModule rootkit [S1]. Overlapping vendor clusters are linked to the 2023 3CX cascading supply-chain compromise (Mandiant UNC4736) [S2], to 2024 poisoned PyPI packages (Unit 42 Gleaming Pisces) [S3], and to the October 2024 Radiant Capital theft of about $50M [S5].
identification.firstObserved: Trojanized AppleJeus applications have been in use since 2018, per the US government advisory as reported [S4]. Unit 42 says Gleaming Pisces has been active since at least 2018 [S3]. Microsoft gives no first-observed date [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Citrine Sleet. Microsoft says other security companies track this actor as AppleJeus, Labyrinth Chollima, UNC4736 and Hidden Cobra [S1]. Microsoft's naming map also lists Storm-0139 and Storm-1222 [S8]. MITRE tracks the group as AppleJeus (G1049) [S7]. Unit 42 equates Gleaming Pisces with Citrine Sleet [S3]. Mandiant links UNC4736 to AppleJeus with moderate confidence [S2]. Microsoft's December 2022 DEV-0139 report (Telegram lures against crypto investment funds) is listed here as a probable predecessor designation; the naming-map entry Storm-0139 suggests this, but no cited source explicitly confirms it [S6][S8]. 'Hidden Cobra' is a broad US government term for DPRK activity, not a precise cluster name.

attribution.sponsor: Democratic People's Republic of Korea. Microsoft says Citrine Sleet is based in North Korea and reportedly linked to Bureau 121 of the Reconnaissance General Bureau (RGB) [S1]. Press reporting of Mandiant's Radiant Capital findings describes UNC4736 as aligned to the RGB [S5].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft assesses with high confidence that the CVE-2024-7971 exploitation came from a North Korean actor, and with medium confidence that the actor was Citrine Sleet [S1]. Mandiant assessed with moderate confidence that UNC4736 (3CX) is related to the AppleJeus activity reported by CISA [S2]. As reported by the victim and press, Mandiant assessed with high confidence that the Radiant Capital attack was DPRK-nexus and attributed it to UNC4736 [S5]. Unit 42 assesses with medium confidence that PondRAT belongs to Gleaming Pisces [S3]. FBI, CISA and Treasury attributed AppleJeus malware to North Korean state-sponsored actors (the Lazarus Group) in February 2021 [S4].
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and exploit analysis [S1]. Mandiant incident response at 3CX, including a POOLRAT sample matching the AppleJeus CoinGoTrade app [S2]. Unit 42 code, encryption-key and C2 overlaps [S3]. A joint US government malware analysis advisory (AA21-048A) [S4]. Mandiant's Radiant Capital investigation as reported in press [S5].

actors.objectives: Revenue generation for the DPRK through theft of cryptocurrency and other financial assets [S1][S7]. The US government assesses that the modified trading apps are likely a way to get around international sanctions on North Korea [S4]. Unit 42 assesses that the PyPI campaign aimed to reach supply-chain vendors through developer endpoints, and then those vendors' customers [S3].

sectors: Cryptocurrency exchanges, funds, wallets and individuals managing crypto assets [S1][S6]
Decentralized finance (DeFi) protocols and their developers [S5]
Software vendors and supply chains (VoIP software, trading software) [S2]
Software developers via open-source package repositories (PyPI) [S3]
Finance, government, energy, technology and telecommunications (AppleJeus victims, per coverage of the US advisory) [S4]
regions: Global; cryptocurrency-theft targeting in over 30 countries in one year, per the US advisory as reported [S4]
Downstream customers of 3CX, a globally used VoIP software vendor [S2]
targeting.notes: Microsoft notes that one organization targeted in the 2024 Chromium campaign had previously been targeted by Sapphire Sleet [S1]. The US government assessed that North Korean actors like Citrine Sleet will likely keep targeting crypto technology firms, gaming companies and exchanges [S1]. The sector list for 2021 comes from secondary coverage of the CISA advisory, which describes the wider AppleJeus/Lazarus activity [S4].

capabilities.summary: Social engineering through fake trading sites, fake job offers and Telegram contacts posing as trusted peers or former contractors [S1][S5][S6]. Trojanized cryptocurrency trading and wallet apps (AppleJeus; seven named variants, including Celas Trade Pro, JMT Trading and CoinGoTrade) [S4]. Zero-day exploitation: Chromium V8 type confusion CVE-2024-7971 chained with Windows kernel CVE-2024-38106 for sandbox escape, then the FudModule rootkit, which uses direct kernel object manipulation (DKOM) to tamper with kernel security mechanisms [S1]. FudModule is also attributed to Diamond Sleet, and Microsoft suggests the two groups may share it [S1]. Software supply-chain compromise: a trojanized, validly signed X_TRADER installer led to compromise of 3CX's Windows and macOS build environments and a trojanized 3CX Desktop App. Associated tools include VEILEDSIGNAL, TAXHAUL, COLDCAT, SUDDENICON, ICONICSTEALER and POOLRAT [S2]. Cross-platform backdoors for Windows, macOS and Linux, including POOLRAT, its lighter variant PondRAT delivered through poisoned PyPI packages [S3], and the macOS backdoor INLETDRIFT [S5]. Use of compromised developer devices to sign fraudulent multisignature transactions [S5].

gaps: Microsoft's own attribution of the 3CX compromise was not found. The 3CX link to Citrine Sleet rests on Mandiant's UNC4736 cluster (moderate-confidence AppleJeus link) and on Microsoft listing UNC4736 as an alias [S1][S2].
Unit 42's Gleaming Pisces report could not be opened (DNS failure). Its content comes from search-result summaries [S3].
CISA AA21-048A could not be opened (government site blocked). Details come from search-result coverage, including McGuireWoods and other secondary reporting [S4].
Mandiant's Radiant Capital findings are known only through the victim's statement as reported in press. SecurityWeek could not be fetched, and the article's exact date is approximate [S5].
No cited source explicitly confirms that Microsoft's DEV-0139 (December 2022) is Citrine Sleet. The Microsoft blog itself was not opened [S6][S8].
Boundary with Diamond Sleet and Sapphire Sleet: the clusters share FudModule and infrastructure, and some victims overlap. Tool attribution may span actors [S1].
AppleJeus reporting in the 2021 US advisory refers broadly to the 'Lazarus Group'. Its victim-sector list may cover activity beyond the Citrine Sleet cluster [S4].
No public reporting on Citrine Sleet activity in 2025 or 2026 was found in this research pass.
The meaning and scope of Microsoft's Storm-1222 designation are not described in the cited sources [S8].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Key terrain includes developer endpoints, software build environments, update and code-signing chains, open-source package dependencies (PyPI), and the browser and kernel attack surface of Windows workstations [S1][S2][S3]. Personnel reached through Telegram and LinkedIn-style job lures are part of the human terrain [S5][S6]. STEP 2 (effects): One trojanized vendor installer can cascade into downstream supply-chain compromise of widely deployed enterprise software such as VoIP clients [S2]. Zero-day chains can bypass browser sandboxes and kernel defenses [S1]. STEP 3 (adversary template): social-engineering lure (fake job, trusted-contact impersonation, fake trading site) or zero-day watering hole, then cross-platform backdoor (AppleJeus, POOLRAT/PondRAT, INLETDRIFT, VEILEDSIGNAL), then credential and wallet access or build-system tampering [S1][S2][S3][S5]. STEP 4: The MLCOA is continued financially motivated theft from crypto and fintech entities, with no direct targeting of DoD. The MDCOA is a supply-chain implant in software also used by DoD or defense industrial base networks, giving incidental access that could be passed to espionage-focused DPRK units, as in the 3CX case where victims were downstream customers [S2]. Candidate indicators: unexpected child processes or DLL side-loading from signed vendor installers [S2]; installs of newly published or typosquatted PyPI packages on developer hosts [S3]; Chromium renderer crashes followed by kernel-mode tampering of security callbacks [S1]; connections to known C2 such as voyagorclub[.]space, jdkgradle[.]com and rebelthumb[.]net [S1][S3]; and macOS .app files posing as PDFs delivered over Telegram [S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track software bill-of-materials and vendor-compromise alerts, such as trojanized 3CX builds, across DODIN and mission partner networks, because this actor's supply-chain operations can reach DoD users incidentally [S2]. Monitor emergency Chromium and Windows kernel patches, since the 2024 chain was patched within days of discovery [S1]. (2) Authorities: activity is primarily financial theft by a state actor. Coordinate with FBI and Treasury, which have issued joint guidance on AppleJeus, and with law enforcement for any DIB victim [S4]. (3) Mission assurance: harden developer and build environments, enforce package allow-listing for PyPI, and verify code-signing provenance of third-party installers [S2][S3]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with DC3/DIB CS and commercial vendors. Note that vendor clusters (Citrine Sleet, UNC4736, Gleaming Pisces, Labyrinth Chollima) overlap but are not identical, and tools such as FudModule are shared with Diamond Sleet, so prioritize containment over precise attribution [S1][S2][S3].
