provenance.importedSummary: AppleJeus is a North Korean state-sponsored threat group attributed to the Reconnaissance General Bureau. Associated with the broader Lazarus Group umbrella of actors, AppleJeus has been active since at least 2018 and is closely aligned in resources with TEMP.hermit, another DPRK-affiliated group under the same umbrella. The group’s primary mission is to generate and launder revenue to provide financial support to the government. AppleJeus primarily targets the cryptocurrency industry and is most notably responsible for the 3CX Supply Chain Attack. The group traditionally deploys malicious cryptocurrency software in combination with Phishing. From these compromised environments, it selectively deploys additional backdoors to enable extended operations against high-value financial targets.

identification.summary: CL-STA-0043 is a Chinese state-nexus cyber-espionage actor tracked by Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, which promoted the activity cluster to the named threat actor Phantom Taurus in September 2025, having previously designated it TGR-STA-0043 and linked it to the Operation Diplomatic Specter campaign. The group targets government and telecommunications organizations, including ministries of foreign affairs, embassies and diplomatic missions, across Africa, the Middle East and Asia, with a focus on geopolitical and military intelligence collection. It typically gains access by exploiting internet-facing Internet Information Services (IIS) and Microsoft Exchange servers, then performs reconnaissance and privilege escalation using native Windows tooling. In more recent operations the actor deployed NET-STAR, a fileless .NET malware suite targeting IIS web servers that comprises the IIServerCore backdoor and the AssemblyExecuter V1 and V2 loaders.

CL-STA-0048 is a Chinese state-backed APT that targets strategic sectors in South Asia, particularly government and telecommunications entities, with a focus on espionage. The group has been linked to SAP NetWeaver intrusions and employs techniques such as DNS beaconing using ping commands and exploiting unpatched vulnerabilities in services like IIS, Apache Tomcat, and MSSQL. Analysts have observed its use of reverse shell commands and command-and-control traffic directed to specific IP addresses. The actor adapts its methods to evade detection and maintain persistent access to high-value networks.

CL-STA-1087 is a suspected state-sponsored espionage campaign operating out of China, targeting military organizations in Southeast Asia. The actor has demonstrated operational patience, maintaining dormant access for extended periods while focusing on precision intelligence collection and employing robust operational security measures. Their infrastructure includes the use of a legitimate cloud service for C2 operations, indicating a cloud-native approach. File timestamps and other indicators trace the campaign's activity back to 2020, suggesting a long-running operation.

CL-UNK-1068 is a Chinese threat actor that has targeted critical infrastructure in Asia, primarily focusing on cyberespionage. They utilize cross-platform tools, including the Xnote Linux backdoor and the GodZilla web shell, to maintain a persistent presence and execute credential theft. Their TTPs involve DLL side-loading, the use of custom malware, and batch scripts to bypass security measures. The group has demonstrated a capability for data exfiltration from SQL servers and has employed tools like DumpIt and Volatility for memory analysis.
Microsoft threat actor profile. Origin or category: China.

China-linked espionage actor that Microsoft tracks as Copper Typhoon and maps to Tonto Team, Earth Akhlut and Sharp-R [S1]. MITRE describes Tonto Team as a suspected Chinese state-sponsored espionage group that has mainly targeted South Korea, Japan, Taiwan and the United States since at least 2009, and that expanded to other Asian and Eastern European countries by 2020 [S2]. Its signature tooling is the long-lived Bisonal backdoor, delivered through spear-phishing documents, including documents built with the Royal Road weaponizer [S3][S4][S7][S8]. In 2020 Kaspersky reported that the group had also moved to more advanced tools such as ShadowPad [S4].
identification.firstObserved: MITRE: active since at least 2009, and linked to the Heartbeat Campaign (2009-2012) [S2]. Kaspersky describes CactusPete as active since at least 2012 [S4].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Copper Typhoon. Microsoft's public mapping lists only Tonto Team, Earth Akhlut and Sharp-R as other names [S1]. MITRE G0131 (Tonto Team) lists Earth Akhlut, BRONZE HUNTLEY, CactusPete and Karma Panda as associated names [S2]. Recorded Future tracks TAG-74 as a separate cluster that overlaps with Tonto Team/COPPER/CactusPete/Earth Akhlut/Karma Panda/Bronze Huntley; it is not a confirmed one-to-one match [S3]. Recorded Future also judges that a custom ReVBShell variant is likely shared with Tick Group, which is a different actor [S3].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China, People's Liberation Army (per vendor reporting). Recorded Future notes that Tonto Team has been publicly linked to the former Shenyang Military Region Technical Reconnaissance Bureau of the PLA Strategic Support Force, now part of the Northern Theater Command [S3]. In 2017 FireEye described Tonto Team as tied to China's military and based in Shenyang [S5].
attribution.confidence: Recorded Future assesses with moderate confidence that TAG-74 is aligned with the PLA Northern Theater Command, based on targeting patterns [S3]. MITRE calls Tonto Team a 'suspected' Chinese state-sponsored group [S2]. In the sources gathered, Microsoft gives no public confidence statement beyond assigning the Typhoon (China) name [S1]. No US government indictment or advisory naming this actor was found.
attribution.basis: Targeting pattern consistent with the Northern Theater Command's area of responsibility [S3]; FireEye statements reported in the press [S5]; exclusive use of Bisonal by Chinese APTs and Simplified Chinese document metadata [S7][S8]; Microsoft naming taxonomy [S1]. China's Ministry of Defense denied that the PLA supports hacking [S5].

actors.objectives: Long-term intelligence collection against military, government, defense-industrial and political targets in states bordering China's northeast, including South Korea, Japan and Russia [S2][S3]. Kaspersky judged that the 2019-2020 Eastern Europe campaign most likely sought confidential information from military and financial organizations [S4]. In 2017 the group targeted South Korean entities connected to the THAAD missile-defense deployment [S5].

targeting.notes: South Korea is the most consistent focus, from Heartbeat (2009-2012) through TAG-74 (2023) [S2][S3]. Russian targeting rose in 2022, though SentinelLabs' attribution of that activity to Tonto Team is tentative [S7]. Group-IB, a security vendor, was targeted in March 2021 and June 2022 [S8].

capabilities.summary: The primary tool is the Bisonal backdoor. Kaspersky linked more than 300 samples to the group from March 2019 to April 2020, about 20 new samples a month. Bisonal can run programs, terminate processes, manage files and support lateral movement [S4]. Group-IB documents the Bisonal.DoubleT variant and a new TontoTeam.Downloader (QuickMute) [S8]. For initial access the group uses spear-phishing with weaponized Office/RTF documents built with Royal Road [S7][S8], and in TAG-74 activity it used .chm files that launch a DLL search-order-hijacking chain to load a customized ReVBShell VBScript backdoor before Bisonal [S3]. In March 2021 ESET observed the group exploiting Exchange ProxyLogon vulnerabilities [S6]. Kaspersky reported a move to ShadowPad in 2020 [S4]. MITRE lists Mimikatz, gsecdump, LaZagne, NBTscan, Bisonal and ShadowPad as associated software [S2].

diamond.adversary: PRC-linked operators publicly associated with the PLA's former Shenyang Military Region technical reconnaissance bureau, now under the Northern Theater Command; Microsoft names the cluster Copper Typhoon [S1][S3][S5].
diamond.capability: Bisonal family (including DoubleT), ReVBShell, TontoTeam.Downloader, ShadowPad, Royal Road documents, CHM/DLL hijacking chains, ProxyLogon exploitation, and credential tools such as Mimikatz and LaZagne [S2][S3][S4][S6][S8].
diamond.infrastructure: Actor-controlled C2 for Bisonal and ReVBShell [S3][S4], and free webmail (GMX) sender accounts posing as legitimate firms [S8]. Detailed infrastructure patterns are not covered in the sources gathered.
diamond.victim: Government, military, defense-industrial, political and academic organizations in South Korea, Japan, Russia and Eastern Europe, plus security vendors [S2][S3][S4][S8].
diamond.socioPolitical: Regional security intelligence on the Korean Peninsula (e.g., THAAD), Japan and Russia, consistent with a Northern Theater Command focus [S3][S5].
diamond.technology: Microsoft Office and Equation Editor exploitation through Royal Road, Windows CHM handling and DLL search order, and on-premises Exchange servers [S3][S6][S8].

gaps: No Microsoft Threat Intelligence report on Copper Typhoon activity was found; Microsoft's public mapping gives only the name and its alias links [S1].
The MITRE and Microsoft naming pages could not be fetched directly (network blocked); MITRE details come from search-result summaries [S2].
Primary reports by Kaspersky (Securelist), Recorded Future (TAG-74 PDF), SentinelLabs, Trend Micro and ESET could not be fetched; this file relies on search-result coverage of them.

The 2022 Pakistan E-Office supply-chain attack that delivered ShadowPad (Trend Micro) appears in the imported references, but coverage found states that Trend Micro made no firm attribution; do not credit it to Copper Typhoon without the primary paper [S9].
The Cybereason PortDoor attack (2021) on Russia's Rubin Design Bureau used Royal Road, which Tonto Team and other groups share; it was not attributed to Tonto Team, so it is excluded.
TAG-74 (Recorded Future) overlaps with Tonto Team but is not confirmed as identical, and it likely shares tooling with Tick Group [S3].
No US government indictment, sanction or joint advisory naming Tonto Team/Copper Typhoon was found.
Operation Bitter Biscuit (2017) and the original Trend Micro HeartBeat paper were not reviewed.
Activity after 2023 attributable to this actor was not found.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Key terrain is user endpoints and email at government, military, defense-industrial and academic organizations in Northeast Asia, especially South Korea and Japan, along with exposed on-premises Exchange servers [S2][S3][S6]. STEP 2 (effects): Spear-phishing with Office/RTF exploits and CHM files depends on unpatched Office components and user execution, so patch status and attachment filtering shape the attack surface [S3][S8]. STEP 3 (adversary template): Royal Road document or CHM lure; DLL search-order hijack; ReVBShell or downloader; Bisonal backdoor; credential dumping and lateral movement [S2][S3][S4][S8]. STEP 4: MLCOA is sustained espionage against Korean Peninsula defense and policy entities, including those tied to US-ROK missile-defense cooperation such as THAAD [S3][S5]. MDCOA is opportunistic mass exploitation of a newly disclosed server vulnerability, as with ProxyLogon in 2021, to reach DoD-adjacent or coalition networks [S6]. Candidate indicators: CHM attachments spawning signed executables that side-load DLLs; RTF documents exploiting Equation Editor; Bisonal C2 beacons; Simplified Chinese metadata in lure documents; new web shells on Exchange [S3][S6][S8].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track Copper Typhoon/Tonto Team, TAG-74 and CactusPete as overlapping clusters with distinct confidence levels, not as a single fused entity [S1][S3]. (2) Authorities: reporting is vendor-sourced; no US government attribution was found, so attribution-dependent responses need IC validation [S2][S3]. (3) Mission assurance: USFK and coalition partners in South Korea and Japan, plus defense contractors supporting missile defense, are high-likelihood targets for phishing and should get priority for email and endpoint hardening against Office and CHM execution chains [S3][S5]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with ROK and Japanese partners and with DIB CS participants, because Tonto activity spans academic, political and defense-industrial targets outside DoD networks [S3][S4].

provenance.importedSummary: Tonto Team is a Chinese-speaking APT group that has been active since at least 2013. They primarily target military, diplomatic, and infrastructure organizations in Asia and Eastern Europe. The group has been observed using various malware, including the Bisonal RAT and ShadowPad. They employ spear-phishing emails with malicious attachments as their preferred method of distribution.

identification.summary: Coral Sleet (formerly Storm-1877) is Microsoft's name for a North Korean state actor. Microsoft groups it with Sapphire Sleet and Jasper Sleet as actors that often use financial-opportunity or job-interview lures to get initial access [S1]. Microsoft first described Storm-1877 in May 2024. It said the actor had used malicious npm packages since late 2023 to deliver JavaScript-based malware to software developers, and that Palo Alto Networks publicly reported this campaign as 'Contagious Interview' [S2]. Unit 42 first reported Contagious Interview in November 2023: fake employers persuade job seekers to install malware during online interviews, using the BeaverTail stealer/loader and the InvisibleFerret Python backdoor [S5]. In March 2026 Microsoft reported that Coral Sleet used AI coding tools to build and iterate malware components, including the OtterCookie malware, and used agentic AI for end-to-end lure development and infrastructure provisioning [S1]. In September 2026 Japanese, US, Australian and German agencies published a joint advisory on the same activity cluster (as 'WaterPlum' / Contagious Interview). The advisory, as reported, said the actors infected at least 30,000 devices in more than 100 countries and took funds or credentials from more than 7,000 cryptocurrency wallets [S11].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft says the Contagious Interview campaign has been active since at least December 2022 [S4]. Microsoft says Storm-1877 used malicious npm packages since late 2023 [S2]. Unit 42's first public report was November 2023 [S5], and ESET says the overlapping DeceptiveDevelopment cluster has been active since at least November 2023 [S7].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Coral Sleet. Microsoft explicitly gives 'Coral Sleet (formerly Storm-1877)' [S1]. Microsoft maps Storm-1877 to the npm campaign Palo Alto calls Contagious Interview [S2]. Unit 42 tracks Contagious Interview as CL-STA-0240 [S5][S6]. NTT Security tracks the cluster as WaterPlum and equates it with CL-STA-0240, DeceptiveDevelopment, DEV#POPPER, Famous Chollima, PurpleBravo and Tenacious Pungsan, as reported [S8]. ESET's DeceptiveDevelopment overlaps with Contagious Interview, DEV#POPPER, Famous Chollima, PurpleBravo and Tenacious Pungsan, as reported [S7][S13]. Trend Micro associates its Void Dokkaebi intrusion set, also known as Famous Chollima, with this campaign cluster [S10]. CLUSTER BOUNDARY: Microsoft tracks North Korean remote IT workers separately as Jasper Sleet (formerly Storm-0287). It says Storm-1877 is one of several other DPRK clusters that also pursue fraudulent employment [S3]. Unit 42 likewise separates the job-seeker IT-worker campaign Wagemole (CL-STA-0241) from Contagious Interview [S5]. CrowdStrike's Famous Chollima covers both the recruiter and IT-worker activity, so it is broader than Coral Sleet. The imported summary on this record describes WageMole (IT-worker fraud), which better matches Jasper Sleet than Coral Sleet. Microsoft's March 2026 Contagious Interview post describes the campaign but does not name Coral Sleet [S4].

attribution.sponsor: Democratic People's Republic of Korea. Microsoft describes Coral Sleet as a North Korean threat actor [S1]. The September 2026 multinational advisory, as reported, assesses (per Japan's National Police Agency and the FBI) that WaterPlum operators and some North Korean IT workers fall under the 313 General Bureau of the Munitions Industry Department of the Workers' Party of Korea Central Committee [S11][S12].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft names Coral Sleet as North Korean but gives no confidence level in the cited post [S1]. SentinelLABS attributes the CTI-platform activity it observed to North Korean Contagious Interview actors with high confidence [S9]. The 313 General Bureau assessment is from the NPA and FBI (government), as reported in press coverage. It was made against the WaterPlum / Contagious Interview cluster, not against Microsoft's Coral Sleet designation by name [S11][S12].
attribution.basis: Microsoft Threat Intelligence telemetry and reporting [S1][S2][S3]; Unit 42 telemetry and malware analysis [S5][S6]; ESET, NTT, SentinelLABS/Validin and Trend Micro vendor research [S7][S8][S9][S10]; joint government advisory from Japan, the US, Australia and Germany (reported via press) [S11][S12].

actors.objectives: Revenue generation for the DPRK through cryptocurrency theft. The 2026 joint advisory, as reported, says the actors took funds or credentials from more than 7,000 crypto wallets and moved about $10.7 million (about 1.7 billion yen) to North Korea [S11][S12]. Unit 42 assessed the goals as stealing cryptocurrency and using compromised targets as staging environments for future attacks [S5]. Microsoft notes the actors harvest API tokens, cloud credentials, signing keys, crypto wallets and password-manager artifacts. A compromised developer could therefore become a route into the employer's environment or software supply chain [S4][S11].

sectors: Software developers and job seekers in the technology sector [S2][S5]
Developers at enterprise solution providers and media and communications firms [S4]
regions: Global: at least 30,000 devices in more than 100 countries (December 2025 to July 2026, per the joint advisory as reported) [S11]
Japan, United States, Australia and Germany were the co-authoring governments [S11][S12]
targeting.notes: Targeting is individual-centric. The actors approach developers through fake recruiter personas, job postings on platforms such as LinkedIn and Upwork, and fake coding tests. Victim organizations are then exposed through the individual's device [S4][S7][S11]. SentinelLABS counted over 230 victims between January and March 2025 and said the true figure is likely higher [S9]. Recruiter lures have posed as cryptocurrency trading firms and AI solution providers [S4].

capabilities.summary: Social engineering through fake recruiters and technical interviews. Victims are asked to clone and run booby-trapped repositories (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket), install malicious npm packages, or follow 'quick fix' steps for supposed video-conferencing errors [S2][S4][S11]. Malware: the BeaverTail JavaScript stealer and loader, and the InvisibleFerret Python backdoor, which supports keylogging, file exfiltration and remote access via AnyDesk [S5][S6][S7]. Unit 42 reported Qt-compiled BeaverTail builds for Windows and macOS from July 2024 [S6]. Later families: the OtterCookie JavaScript backdoor (v3 and v4 in February and April 2025; v4 added VM detection and Chrome/MetaMask credential theft), a JavaScript beaconing agent, FlexibleFerret, and VS Code task-file abuse that runs code when a project is trusted [S4][S8]. The joint advisory coverage also lists OtterCandy and StoatWaffle [S11]. Microsoft says Coral Sleet uses AI coding tools to generate and revise malware, including OtterCookie, and uses agentic AI for lure websites and remote infrastructure provisioning [S1]. The operators watch threat intelligence platforms (Validin, VirusTotal) to spot their own exposed infrastructure and stand up replacements quickly [S9].

campaigns.summary: Japan, the US, Australia and Germany report at least 30,000 infected devices in over 100 countries (December 2025 to July 2026), more than 7,000 affected crypto wallets and about $10.7M moved to the DPRK. They attribute the activity to the 313 General Bureau (reported via press).

diamond.adversary: North Korean state actor (Microsoft: Coral Sleet, formerly Storm-1877) [S1]. NPA and FBI assess the WaterPlum operators fall under the 313 General Bureau of the Munitions Industry Department, as reported [S12]. Operators work in coordinated teams [S9].
diamond.capability: Fake-recruiter social engineering. Malware includes BeaverTail, InvisibleFerret, OtterCookie, OtterCandy, StoatWaffle and FlexibleFerret, delivered through npm packages, trojanized repositories and VS Code tasks. Malware is developed with AI assistance [S1][S4][S5][S8][S11].
diamond.infrastructure: Public code hosting (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket) and the npm registry; fake interview and company websites built on development platforms; URL shorteners redirecting to vercel.app [S1][S4]. Russian IP ranges behind VPN, proxy and RDP layers [S10]. Infrastructure is replaced quickly after exposure [S9].
diamond.victim: Software developers, freelancers, and Web3/crypto professionals, and their employers [S4][S7][S9][S11]. At least 30,000 devices in more than 100 countries [S11].
diamond.socioPolitical: Sanctions-evasion revenue for the DPRK through crypto theft. The advisory links the activity to the same bureau as DPRK IT workers [S11][S12].
diamond.technology: Developer workstations holding credentials, signing keys, cloud tokens and wallets. Trust in code repositories, package managers, IDE automation (VS Code tasks) and remote hiring workflows [S4][S11].

gaps: Microsoft has not published a dedicated Coral Sleet profile in the sources gathered. The Coral Sleet = Storm-1877 equivalence rests on one sentence in the March 2026 AI-tradecraft post [S1]. Microsoft's March 2026 Contagious Interview post does not name the actor [S4].

Cluster boundaries: Microsoft says Storm-1877 also pursues fraudulent employment [S3], and its March 2026 post groups Coral Sleet with Jasper Sleet [S1]. It is unclear how much IT-worker (WageMole) activity Microsoft folds into Coral Sleet versus Jasper Sleet. The imported record summary (WageMole) may belong to Jasper Sleet.

The September 2026 joint advisory primary text (FBI IC3 / NPA) could not be opened. Figures and the 313 General Bureau attribution come from press coverage [S11][S12]. The advisory names the cluster WaterPlum, not Coral Sleet.
Unit 42, SentinelLABS, Trend Micro, ESET and NTT primary reports could not be fetched (host blocked). Their content is taken from search-result summaries and press coverage.
MITRE ATT&CK G1052 page could not be fetched to confirm its group name and associated-group list.
No Microsoft confidence level for the Coral Sleet North Korea attribution was found.

Aliases Gwisin Gang, Nickel Tapestry, TAG-121 and UNC5267 in the imported record were not confirmed against cited sources for this cluster. Some (for example UNC5267) are commonly used for IT-worker activity.
ContagiousDrop tooling and the face-swap/deepfake claims in some advisory coverage were not verified against primary sources.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Key terrain is people, not networks. Individual developers and Web3 personnel on LinkedIn and Upwork, their personal and work devices, and the code repositories, npm registry and IDE automation they trust [S4][S7][S11]. DoD-adjacent software contractors and personnel using personal devices for job searches fall in scope. STEP 2 (effects): A single compromised developer exposes cloud tokens, signing keys and credentials that can be pivoted into the employer and its software supply chain [S4][S11]. AI-assisted development shortens the actor's retooling cycle [S1]. STEP 3 (adversary template): Recruiter persona approach, then a fake coding test or 'fix your camera' instruction, then a malicious repo, npm package or VS Code task, then BeaverTail or OtterCookie, then InvisibleFerret or a beaconing agent, then credential and wallet theft [S4][S5][S6][S8]. Infrastructure is replaced when CTI platforms expose it [S9]. STEP 4: MLCOA is high-volume, opportunistic theft of cryptocurrency and credentials from developers worldwide [S11]. MDCOA is pivoting from a compromised contractor developer into a defense software supply chain via stolen signing keys or cloud credentials, or handing access to other DPRK units [S4][S5]. Candidate indicators: unsolicited recruiter contact leading to repo clone or npm install on a work device; node or python child processes spawned from VS Code tasks.json; outbound connections to vercel.app or short-link redirects from developer hosts; AnyDesk installed unexpectedly; bulk reads of browser credential and wallet extension stores [S4][S5][S8].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: Fuse identity, endpoint and developer-tooling telemetry (IDE task execution, package installs) into the common operational picture. Network-centric sensors alone will miss an intrusion that starts on a personal or contractor device [S4]. (2) Authorities: The initial compromise usually occurs off the DODIN, on personal or contractor endpoints. Response depends on coordination with FBI, DC3 (a co-sealer of the 2026 advisory) and DIB CS partners rather than DoD-internal authorities alone [S11][S12]. (3) Mission assurance: Treat code-signing keys, CI/CD secrets and cloud tokens on developer workstations as mission-critical assets. Rotate them after any suspected Contagious Interview exposure [S4]. (4) Coordination: The cluster has many vendor names (Coral Sleet, Contagious Interview, WaterPlum, DeceptiveDevelopment, Famous Chollima), and some of these names also cover IT-worker activity. Normalize names on the Microsoft designation in reporting, and coordinate with allied partners (Japan, Australia, Germany) who co-authored the advisory [S1][S8][S11].

provenance.importedSummary: WageMole is a North Korean state-sponsored APT that employs social engineering and technology to secure remote job opportunities in Western countries, leveraging stolen personal data from the Contagious Interview campaign. Threat actors create fake identities, including passports and driver's licenses, and prepare study guides for interviews, often utilizing generative AI for well-structured responses. They target small to mid-sized businesses and utilize job platforms like Upwork and Indeed, while employing automation scripts for account creation. WageMole's activities include sharing code within their group and requesting payments through platforms like PayPal to conceal their identity.

identification.summary: In May 2018, we discovered a campaign targeting dozens of mobile Android devices belonging to Israeli citizens. Kaspersky spyware sensors caught the signal of an attack from the device of one of the victims; and a hash of the APK involved (Android application) was tagged in our sample feed for inspection. Once we looked into the file, we quickly found out that the inner-workings of the APK included a malicious payload, embedded in the original code of the application. This was an original spyware program, designed to exfiltrate almost all accessible information. During the course of our research, we noticed that we were not the only ones to have found the operation. Researchers from Bitdefender also released an analysis of one of the samples in a blogpost. Although something had already been published, we decided to do something different with the data we acquired. The following month, we released a private report on our Threat Intelligence Portal to alert our clients about this newly discovered operation and began writing YARA rules in order to catch more samples. We decided to call the operation “ViceLeaker”, because of strings and variables in its code.

Crimson Sandstorm (formerly CURIUM) is an Iran-based espionage actor [S1][S2]. Microsoft says it uses a network of fictitious social media accounts to build trust with targets and then delivers malware to exfiltrate data [S1]. Microsoft says it has targeted the defense, maritime shipping, transportation, healthcare and technology sectors, often using watering-hole attacks and social engineering to deliver custom .NET malware. Microsoft also notes earlier research on its malware that used email for command and control [S2]. Microsoft's 2021 CyberWarCon presentation describes CURIUM spending months posing as an attractive woman on LinkedIn or Facebook before sending a malicious document [S3].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft: active since at least 2017 [S2]. Symantec (as Tortoiseshell): active since at least July 2018 (summary of Symantec report via Malpedia) [S4].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Crimson Sandstorm (formerly CURIUM) [S1][S3]. Microsoft states other researchers track it as Tortoiseshell, Imperial Kitten and Yellow Liderc [S2]. Microsoft's profile also lists Houseblend and Tortoise Shell [S1]. PwC tracks it as Yellow Liderc and lists Imperial Kitten, Tortoiseshell, TA456 and Crimson Sandstorm as overlapping names (reported via press) [S8]. Proofpoint tracks TA456 and says it overlaps with Tortoiseshell and Imperial Kitten (reported via press) [S7]. Press coverage of Meta's 2021 takedown says researchers linked much of the activity to Mandiant's UNC1833, with some infrastructure overlap with APT35 [S6]. This is a press claim and is not used to merge clusters. CrowdStrike's IMPERIAL KITTEN is also mapped by Microsoft to Cuboid Sandstorm and Smoke Sandstorm, which Microsoft tracks separately. Facts from CrowdStrike IMPERIAL KITTEN reporting [S9] should therefore be read as the CrowdStrike cluster, not Microsoft's boundary.

attribution.sponsor: Iran. Microsoft assesses Crimson Sandstorm to be connected to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) [S2]. Meta (Facebook) said the malware used in the 2021 Tortoiseshell campaign was developed by Mahak Rayan Afraz, a Tehran IT company with ties to the IRGC (reported via press) [S6]. CrowdStrike assesses that IMPERIAL KITTEN likely fulfills Iranian strategic intelligence requirements associated with IRGC operations (reported via press) [S9].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft describes the actor as 'assessed to be connected to' the IRGC and gives no numeric confidence level [S2]. Its public profile names Iran as country of origin without naming a sponsor [S1]. CrowdStrike uses 'likely' [S9]. In 2019, Symantec and Cisco Talos declined to tie Tortoiseshell to a specific nation-state [S5]. No government attribution of this cluster was found in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and its 2024 OpenAI collaboration, which disabled Crimson Sandstorm accounts and assets [S2]. Meta platform investigation and malware-developer attribution [S6]. Vendor victimology and malware analysis from PwC, Proofpoint and CrowdStrike [S7][S8][S9].

actors.objectives: Strategic intelligence collection in support of Iranian (IRGC-associated) requirements [S2][S9]. Targets include US military and defense contractors, IT services firms, and Middle Eastern governments [S1]. The actor uses supply-chain access through IT, engineering and contractor firms to reach their downstream defense and intelligence customers [S1][S4][S7]. Since 2023 it has collected against Israeli and Mediterranean maritime, logistics and technology entities [S8][S9].

sectors: US military personnel and defense contractors [S1][S6]
Aerospace and defense, including smaller subsidiaries of contractors [S6][S7]
IT services and engineering providers to US defense and intelligence agencies [S1]
IT providers in Saudi Arabia (supply chain) [S4]
targeting.notes: Microsoft says that in 2021 the actor spear-phished companies providing IT and engineering services to US defense and intelligence agencies, probably to reach their customers [S1]. Focus shifted from Middle East IT firms (2018-2019) to US military and defense personnel (2019-2021) [S4][S5][S6]. It shifted again to Israeli and Mediterranean shipping, logistics and technology targets (2022-2023) [S8][S9].

capabilities.summary: The actor's signature is long-duration social engineering through fictitious personas on LinkedIn, Facebook and other platforms. It builds trust over months, sends benign media, and then sends a look-alike malicious file [S1][S3][S6][S7]. Lures include fake recruiting and job sites: 'Hire Military Heroes' (2019) delivered a reconnaissance downloader [S5], and a site spoofing a US Labor Department job site was used in 2021 [S6]. The actor runs watering-hole (strategic web compromise) operations that use JavaScript to fingerprint visitors and selectively serve malware [S2][S8][S9]. It also uses macro-laced Excel phishing, credential theft for VPN access, and one-day vulnerability exploitation [S9]. Custom .NET malware includes IMAPLoader, which uses email as C2 and AppDomain Manager Injection [S8], and StandardKeyboard, which uses email C2 and installs as a Windows service [S9]. LEMPO (an updated Liderc) handles persistence, reconnaissance, exfiltration to actor email accounts and artifact deletion [S7]. A Python reverse shell has also been observed [S9]. In 2023 Microsoft observed the actor using LLMs for phishing content, scripting, and defense-evasion code [S2]. In the Symantec-reported Saudi supply-chain intrusions it gained domain-admin access in at least two organizations [S4].

diamond.adversary: Iran-based operators that Microsoft assesses to be IRGC-connected [S2]. Meta tied malware development to Mahak Rayan Afraz (reported) [S6].
diamond.capability: Fictitious social-media personas, fake job sites, watering holes with visitor fingerprinting, and macro Excel phishing. Custom .NET malware with email C2 (IMAPLoader, StandardKeyboard, LEMPO/Liderc) [S1][S5][S7][S8][S9].
diamond.infrastructure: Fake persona accounts on Facebook and LinkedIn [S3][S6]. Spoofed recruiting and job domains [S5][S6]. Compromised legitimate websites used as watering holes [S8][S9]. Actor-controlled email accounts used for C2 and exfiltration [S7][S8][S9].
diamond.victim: US military personnel and defense and aerospace contractors. IT service providers in Saudi Arabia and the US defense supply chain. Israeli and Mediterranean shipping, logistics and technology firms. Middle Eastern governments [S1][S4][S6][S8][S9].
diamond.socioPolitical: Iranian strategic intelligence requirements tied to the IRGC. Activity against Israel intensified after the October 2023 Israel-Hamas war [S2][S9].
diamond.technology: Trust in professional social networks and recruiting, the email protocols abused for C2, and third-party IT and contractor access into defense customers [S1][S7][S8].

gaps: MITRE ATT&CK G1012 page could not be fetched (host unreachable); MITRE description and references not verified in this pass.
Primary vendor reports (Symantec 2019, Cisco Talos 2019, Proofpoint 2021, Meta 2021, PwC 2023, CrowdStrike 2023) could not be fetched; content is from press coverage and search-result summaries.

Cluster boundary: CrowdStrike IMPERIAL KITTEN is mapped by Microsoft to Crimson, Cuboid and Smoke Sandstorm. Not every IMPERIAL KITTEN fact (e.g., October 2023 Israel activity) is confirmed by Microsoft as Crimson Sandstorm.

Nimbus Manticore (Check Point, 2025) appears in this record's aliases, but Check Point describes it as overlapping UNC1549/Smoke Sandstorm. Its 2025 European aerospace campaign was excluded pending Microsoft confirmation.
No government (CISA/FBI/DOJ/Treasury) attribution or indictment specific to this cluster was found.
Victim counts and impacts beyond Symantec's 11 organizations and Meta's fewer-than-200 notified individuals are not public.
Activity after February 2024 attributable by Microsoft to Crimson Sandstorm was not found in sources gathered.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): The human and persona layer of cyberspace is key terrain. This includes LinkedIn and Facebook profiles of service members, recruiters and contractor staff, plus third-party IT and engineering providers with access into DoD and intelligence networks [S1][S3][S6]. STEP 2 (effects): Months-long trust building defeats one-time phishing awareness. Email-based C2 blends with normal mail traffic, and watering holes on sector websites let the actor select victims passively [S3][S7][S8][S9]. STEP 3 (adversary template): The template is a fake recruiter or attractive persona, or a compromised sector website with JavaScript fingerprinting. That leads to a lure file or fake job app, then a .NET implant with IMAP/SMTP C2, then reconnaissance and exfiltration to actor email [S5][S7][S8][S9]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued espionage against US defense personnel, contractor subsidiaries, and Israeli and Mediterranean logistics targets through persona-driven social engineering. MDCOA is leveraging compromised IT and engineering providers for supply-chain access into defense or intelligence customer networks, as seen in 2018-2021 [S1][S4]. Candidate indicators: unsolicited recruiter or persona contacts with Airmen or contractors that move to off-platform chat or file sharing [S6][S7]; downloads of 'job' applications [S5]; outbound IMAP from non-mail hosts [S8][S9]; AppDomain Manager Injection artifacts [S8]; and a new 'Keyboard Service' Windows service [S9].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: fuse platform-takedown reporting (Meta, LinkedIn), vendor IOCs for IMAPLoader and StandardKeyboard, and DIB partner reporting into the common operational picture, since the actor's entry points sit outside DoDIN boundaries [S6][S8][S9]. Authorities: persona engagement with personnel on commercial platforms and compromises of contractor networks fall to counterintelligence, the DC3/DIB program and platform providers rather than DODIN defenders alone. Coordinate early [S1][S6]. Mission assurance: prioritize hunting for email-protocol C2 egress and macro and Excel execution on mission systems. Identify contractor and IT service accounts with privileged access as supply-chain risk [S1][S4][S8][S9]. Coordination: share persona and fake-job-site indicators with force protection and OPSEC offices for awareness training on long-duration social engineering [S3][S5][S6].

provenance.importedSummary: A previously undocumented attack group is using both custom and off-the-shelf malware to target IT providers in Saudi Arabia in what appear to be supply chain attacks with the end goal of compromising the IT providers’ customers. The group, which we are calling Tortoiseshell, has been active since at least July 2018. Symantec has identified a total of 11 organizations hit by the group, the majority of which are based in Saudi Arabia. In at least two organizations, evidence suggests that the attackers gained domain admin-level access.

identification.summary: Curious Gorge, a group TAG attributes to China's PLA SSF, has conducted campaigns against government and military organizations in Ukraine, Russia, Kazakhstan, and Mongolia. The actor has remained active against government, military, logistics and manufacturing organizations in Ukraine, Russia and Central Asia. In Russia, long running campaigns against multiple government organizations have continued, including the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Over the past week, TAG identified additional compromises impacting multiple Russian defense contractors and manufacturers and a Russian logistics company.

Curly COMrades is a threat actor identified by Amazon Threat Intelligence and Bitdefender, believed to operate in support of Russian interests. They employ techniques such as Hyper-V abuse for EDR evasion and utilize proxy tools like Resocks, SSH, and Stunnel to gain access to internal networks. Their activities include repeated attempts to extract the NTDS database from domain controllers and establishing covert access through virtualization features on compromised Windows 10 machines.

One of the threat actors responsible for the denial of service attacks against U.S in 2012–2013. Three individuals associated with the group—believed to be have been working on behalf of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps—were indicted by the Justice Department in 2016.

Cyber Av3ngers is an Iranian IRGC Cyber-Electronic Command-affiliated threat actor that targets internet-exposed operational technology and industrial control systems. Public reporting documents disruptive targeting of Israeli-made Unitronics PLCs and HMIs, broader critical-infrastructure targeting, and use of the IOCONTROL malware against IoT and OT devices.

identification.summary: Cyber Islamic Resistance is a hacktivist collective ideologically aligned with Iran, engaging in operations such as website defacements, DDoS attacks, and data exfiltration targeting Israeli and Western entities. They have claimed breaches of Israeli cybersecurity firms and academic platforms, framing their actions as part of a broader narrative of retaliation. The group has also targeted critical infrastructure, asserting access to industrial control systems and operational technology environments. Their activities are often presented as part of a coordinated cyber mobilization campaign, emphasizing psychological and reputational impacts.

UAC-0255 is a threat actor that conducted a phishing campaign impersonating CERT-UA to distribute the AGEWHEEZE RAT, targeting organizations in Ukraine's public and private sectors. The campaign is part of a broader trend of using trusted identities to enhance victim engagement, as seen in previous activities like UAC-0190 and UAC-0252. CERT-UA identified UAC-0255 after discovering links to the CyberSerp Telegram channel, which claimed responsibility for the attack. The activity is documented under the identifier CERT-UA#21075, with detection rules available for cybersecurity analysts.

Cyber Toufan is a threat actor group that has gained prominence for its cyberattacks targeting Israeli organizations. The group's tactics suggest potential nation-state backing, possibly from Iran. They have been involved in hack-and-leak operations, data breaches, and data destruction, impacting over 100 organizations. Cyber Toufan's activities align with geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and their attacks are characterized by a combination of technical breaches and psychological warfare.

identification.summary: Operate since at least 2011, from several locations in China, with members in Korea and Japan as well. Possibly linked to Onion Dog. This threat actor targets government institutions, military contractors, maritime and shipbuilding groups, telecommunications operators, and others, primarily in Japan and South Korea.

BRONZE HIGHLAND has been observed using spearphishing as an initial infection vector to deploy the MgBot remote access trojan against targets in Hong Kong. Third party reporting suggests the threat group also targets India, Malaysia and Taiwan and leverages Cobalt Strike and KsRemote Android Rat. CTU researchers assess with moderate confidence that BRONZE HIGHLAND operates on behalf of China and has a remit covering espionage against domestic human rights and pro-democracy advocates and nations neighbouring China

The group usually targets vulnerable servers to breach information including internal data from companies or encrypts files and demands money. Their targets of attack are usually Windows servers that are poorly managed or are not patched to the latest version. Besides these, there are also attack cases that targeted email servers or MS-SQL database servers.

identification.summary: DEV-0147 is a China-based cyber espionage actor was observed compromising diplomatic targets in South America, a notable expansion of the group's data exfiltration operations that traditionally targeted gov't agencies and think tanks in Asia and Europe. DEV-0147 is known to use tools like ShadowPad, a remote access trojan associated with other China-based actors, to maintain persistent access, and QuasarLoader, a webpack loader, to deploy additional malware. DEV-0147's attacks in South America included post-exploitation activity involving the abuse of on-premises identity infrastructure for recon and lateral movement, and the use of Cobalt Strike for command and control and data exfiltration.

Microsoft threat intelligence teams have been tracking multiple ransomware campaigns and have tied these attacks to DEV-0270, also known as Nemesis Kitten, a sub-group of Iranian actor PHOSPHORUS. Microsoft assesses with moderate confidence that DEV-0270 conducts malicious network operations, including widespread vulnerability scanning, on behalf of the government of Iran.

North Korean state-sponsored actor that pursues espionage, data theft, financial gain and network destruction, typically targeting media, IT services and defense organizations worldwide [S1][S2]. implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: The OE includes software vendors and CI/CD infrastructure that supply DoD and DIB networks; supply-chain paths are key terrain. STEP 2: A validly signed installer defeats allow-listing based on signer trust, so terrain analysis must include update channels. STEP 3: The template is n-day exploitation of developer infrastructure or trojanized signed software, then credential theft (ForestTiger) and hijack-based persistence (RollSling), then espionage or destruction. STEP 4: MLCOA is espionage against defense and IT targets with opportunistic financial theft. MDCOA is a destructive attack, Sony-style, against a high-profile target during a Korean Peninsula crisis. Candidate indicators: unexpected child processes from vendor updaters, DLL search-order hijacks in IT tools, and newly exploited CI/CD CVEs [S1][S2].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Supply-chain visibility: JCC2 data should flag vendor-signed binaries behaving abnormally, not just unsigned code. (2) Coordinate with INDOPACOM and USFK on Korean Peninsula crisis I&W, since DPRK cyber activity can precede or accompany provocations. (3) Revenue-focused operations (crypto theft) are a Treasury, FBI and law-enforcement lead, but they finance regime programs and so are relevant to campaign-level assessment. (4) Naming discipline: reporting chains should carry the specific cluster (Diamond, Onyx, Jade, Sapphire Sleet), because 'Lazarus' aggregates distinct actors with different targets.

provenance.importedSummary: CryptoCore is a North Korean APT known for targeting cryptocurrency exchanges and financial institutions, employing spear-phishing techniques that lead to LONEJOGGER malware infections. The group has leveraged social engineering tactics, including deepfake technology and hijacked YouTube accounts, to execute sophisticated giveaway scams that deceive victims into sending cryptocurrencies. Their operations have involved the misuse of platforms like Gemini for reconnaissance and the development of fraudulent content. Additionally, CryptoCore has been linked to a variety of campaigns, including Dangerous Password and SnatchCrypto, focusing on financial gain through cryptocurrency theft.

identification.summary: DiceyF is an advanced persistent threat group that has been targeting online casinos and other victims in Southeast Asia for an extended period. They have exhibited overlapping activity with LuckyStar PlugX and Earth Berberoka/GamblingPuppet, as reported by various cybersecurity vendors. While their motivations remain unclear, previous incidents suggest a combination of espionage and intellectual property theft rather than immediate financial gain. DiceyF continuously evolves their codebase and adds encryption capabilities to enhance their stealthy cyberespionage activities.

An extensive surveillance operation targets specific groups of individuals with malicious mobile apps that collect sensitive information on the device along with surrounding voice recordings. Researchers with CheckPoint discovered the attack and named it Domestic Kitten. The targets are Kurdish and Turkish natives, and ISIS supporters, all Iranian citizens.

DragonSpark is a threat actor that has been conducting attacks primarily targeting organizations in East Asia. They utilize the open-source tool SparkRAT, which is a multi-platform and frequently updated remote access Trojan. The threat actor is believed to be Chinese-speaking based on their use of Chinese language support and compromised infrastructure located in China and Taiwan. They employ various techniques to evade detection, including Golang source code interpretation and the use of the China Chopper webshell.

DriftingCloud is a persistent threat actor known for targeting various industries and locations. They are skilled at developing or acquiring zero-day exploits to gain unauthorized access to target networks. Compromising gateway devices is a common tactic used by DriftingCloud, making network monitoring solutions crucial for detecting their attacks.

Earth Alux is a China-linked APT group known for conducting cyberespionage attacks across various sectors, including government, technology, and telecommunications. They primarily exploit vulnerable services in exposed servers to gain initial access, implanting web shells like GODZILLA and deploying backdoors such as VARGEIT and COBEACON. The group employs tools like RSBINJECT and MASQLOADER for lateral movement and network discovery, while also utilizing RAILSETTER for persistence through mspaint injection. Their operations have predominantly targeted the APAC region and have extended to Latin America, with a focus on exfiltrating sensitive information to attacker-controlled cloud storage.

Earth Baxia is a threat actor opearting out of China, targeting government organizations in Taiwan and potentially across the APAC region, using spear-phishing emails and exploiting the GeoServer vulnerability CVE-2024-36401 for remote code execution, deploying customized Cobalt Strike components with altered signatures, leveraging GrimResource and AppDomainManager injection techniques to deliver additional payloads, and utilizing a new backdoor named EAGLEDOOR for multi-protocol communication and payload delivery.

According to TrendMicro, Earth Berberoka is a threat group originating from China that mainly focuses on targeting gambling websites. This group's campaign uses multiple malware families that target the Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms that have been attributed to Chinese-speaking actors. Aside from using tried-and-tested malware families that have been upgraded, such as PlugX and Gh0st RAT, Earth Berberoka has also developed a brand-new complex, multistage malware family, which has been dubbed PuppetLoader.

Earth Freybug, identified as a subset of APT41, is a cyberthreat group active since at least 2012, engaging in espionage and financially motivated activities across various sectors worldwide. The tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) used in this campaign are similar to the ones from a campaign (Operation CuckooBees) described in an article published by Cybereason. They employ a diverse toolkit, including LOLBins and custom malware, to execute sophisticated cyberespionage attacks. The group's recent tactics involve DLL hijacking and API unhooking through a newly discovered malware named UNAPIMON, which prevents child processes from being monitored. This technique was observed in a vmtoolsd.exe process creating remote tasks to deploy malicious batch files for reconnaissance and backdoor access. UNAPIMON's simplicity and use of Microsoft Detours for defense evasion highlight the group's evolving methods and the need for vigilant security measures, such as restricting admin privileges and adhering to the principle of least privilege. Earth Freybug's persistence and creativity in refining their techniques underscore the ongoing threat they pose and the importance of proactive cybersecurity practices.

Earth Krahang is an APT group targeting government organizations worldwide. They use spear-phishing emails, weak internet-facing servers, and custom backdoors like Cobalt Strike, RESHELL, and XDealer to conduct cyber espionage. The group creates VPN servers on infected systems, employs brute force attacks on email accounts, and exploits compromised government infrastructure to attack other governments. Earth Krahang has been linked to another China-linked actor, Earth Lusca, and is believed to be part of a specialized task force for cyber espionage against government institutions.

Earth Lamia is a China-nexus APT that targets organizations across multiple sectors, including finance, logistics, and government, primarily in Latin America, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia. The actor exploits web application vulnerabilities, such as CVE-2025-55182, and employs techniques like SQL injection, DLL sideloading, and the deployment of custom backdoors like PULSEPACK and BypassBoss. Earth Lamia conducts reconnaissance, file operations, and credential theft, often utilizing tools like Cobalt Strike and VShell.

Earth Naga is an APT group that has persistently targeted high-value organizations, including government agencies, telecommunications, and military-related manufacturers, primarily in Taiwan and the broader APAC region. They have been linked to the use of Draculoader and ShadowPad C&C infrastructure, demonstrating sophisticated TTPs such as establishing SSH connections through compromised mail servers. Earth Naga has collaborated with Earth Estries, sharing access to facilitate continued exploitation, complicating detection and attribution efforts. Their operations reflect a growing interest in global intelligence collection, extending to NATO member countries and Latin America.

Earth Wendigo is a threat actor from China that has been targeting several organizations — including government organizations, research institutions, and universities in Taiwan — since May 2019, aiming to exfiltrate emails from targeted organizations via the injection of JavaScript backdoors to a webmail system that is widely used in Taiwan. The threat actor also sent spear-phishing emails embedded with malicious links to multiple individuals, including politicians and activists, who support movements in Tibet, the Uyghur region, or Hong Kong.

Edalat-e Ali is a hacktivist group known for disrupting Iranian state-run TV and radio transmissions during significant events, such as the Revolution Day ceremonies. They have also targeted government facilities, releasing security camera footage to expose abuses and draw attention to human rights violations. The group has used their hacks to call for protests against the Iranian regime and have displayed anti-government messages during their disruptions. Edalat-e Ali has been active in releasing sensitive information and footage to embarrass Iranian officials and highlight injustices within the country.

Educated Manticore is an Iranian APT group aligned with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, primarily engaged in espionage targeting government, military, and academic sectors. The group employs spear-phishing tactics, utilizing custom backdoors like POWERLESS and phishing kits designed as SPAs to harvest credentials. Their operations have included impersonating credible figures to lure victims and using ISO images to initiate infection chains. Educated Manticore's activities are characterized by rapid domain setup and aggressive spear-phishing campaigns, particularly against Israeli individuals.

ELUSIVE COMET is a threat actor responsible for significant cryptocurrency theft through sophisticated social engineering attacks, particularly leveraging Zoom's remote control feature. Their attack methodology involves manipulating legitimate workflows and exploiting human-centric vulnerabilities rather than technical flaws. The actor employs tactics such as social proof, time pressure, and interface manipulation to deceive targets. Organizations can mitigate risks by implementing technical controls to disable the remote control feature and deploying email boundary protections like DMARC, SPF, and DKIM.

Emerald Sleet (formerly THALLIUM) is a North Korean threat actor that Microsoft says stayed highly active through 2023. It spear-phishes prominent individuals with North Korea expertise and often impersonates academic institutions and NGOs [S1]. Microsoft says it targets diplomats and Korean Peninsula experts in government, think tanks and NGOs, media and education, and assesses the motive as intelligence collection [S2]. Since January 2025 Microsoft has seen the actor trick targets into running PowerShell as administrator and pasting code the actor supplies [S3]. Microsoft and OpenAI also observed it using large language models (LLMs) for reconnaissance, vulnerability research and phishing content [S1][S11].
identification.firstObserved: Kaspersky's 2013 'Kimsuky' report dates the earliest signs of activity to 2013-04-03 and the first Kimsuky Trojan samples to 2013-05-05 [S8]. Microsoft was tracking the group as THALLIUM by 2019 [S4].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Emerald Sleet (formerly THALLIUM). Microsoft says Emerald Sleet overlaps with the actors other researchers call Kimsuky and Velvet Chollima [S1]. Microsoft's naming map lists THALLIUM, VELVET CHOLLIMA, RGB-D5, Black Banshee, Kimsuky and Greendinosa as other names. It lists APT43 and Konni separately, under Opal Sleet [S5]. Material that vendors publish under Kimsuky, Springtail [S10] or TA427 [S9] is mapped to this record by alias, and boundaries may not match Microsoft's exactly. Mandiant's APT43 reporting is not merged here because Microsoft maps APT43 to Opal Sleet [S5]. MITRE tracks the group as Kimsuky (G0094) [S14].

attribution.sponsor: Democratic People's Republic of Korea. US Treasury describes Kimsuky as subordinate to the Reconnaissance General Bureau (RGB), the DPRK's primary foreign intelligence service [S7]. A May 2024 FBI, State Department and NSA advisory says Kimsuky is administratively subordinate to the 63rd Research Center, an element of the RGB [S6].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft calls Emerald Sleet a 'North Korean state actor' [S3]. In 2019 Microsoft said THALLIUM is 'believed to operate from North Korea' [S4]. US Treasury sanctioned Kimsuky as an RGB-subordinate entity on 2023-11-30 [S7]. These government statements name Kimsuky, which Microsoft maps to Emerald Sleet [S5]. Kaspersky's 2013 report only surmised North Korean origin from target profiles, Korean-language compile paths and registrant names [S8].
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and actor tracking, joint Microsoft and OpenAI LLM-abuse research, and a 2019 civil court action [S1][S2][S3][S4]. US Treasury designation [S7]. Joint FBI, State Department and NSA advisory [S6]. Vendor technical reporting from Kaspersky, Proofpoint and Symantec [S8][S9][S10].

actors.objectives: Microsoft assesses the motive as intelligence collection on North Korea-related policy, gathered from diplomats and Korean Peninsula experts [S2]. Through LLM-informed reconnaissance, the actor sought out think tanks, government organizations and experts focused on North Korean defense issues or its nuclear weapons program [S1]. Its 2022 impersonation campaign asked North Korea experts for their views on security issues and offered payment to review a document on the North Korean nuclear program [S12]. The 2024 joint US advisory describes Kimsuky posing as journalists, academics and East Asia experts to collect information for the regime [S6].

sectors: Government agencies and services, including diplomats [S2][S3]
Individuals working in international affairs, especially Northeast Asia [S3]
Nuclear non-proliferation, world-peace and human-rights organizations and experts [S4]
regions: North America, South America, Europe and East Asia (2025 PowerShell campaign) [S3]
United States, Japan and South Korea (2019 THALLIUM targets) [S4]
South Korea (2013 Kimsuky campaign; 2024 Gomir and GoBear activity) [S8][S10]
targeting.notes: Microsoft's victim set centers on people with North Korea or Northeast Asia expertise rather than on infrastructure [S1][S2][S3]. Treasury describes the group's targets as government, research and media figures, mainly in South Korea, Japan and the US [S7].

capabilities.summary: Social engineering is the core capability. The actor builds rapport over time while posing as officials, journalists, academics or think-tank staff, then sends spear-phishing emails [S1][S3][S6][S9][S12]. In 2019, THALLIUM's spoofed Microsoft-themed credential phishing led to mailbox access and forwarding rules that sent new mail to actor-controlled accounts [S4]. From December 2023 the group abused lax DMARC policies to spoof personas, and from February 2024 it added web beacons to profile targets [S6][S9]. In 2025 it ran ClickFix-style lures: victims were told to paste PowerShell as administrator, which installed a browser-based remote desktop tool and registered the device for actor access [S3]. Proofpoint saw similar lures deliver QuasarRAT [S13]. Its malware includes Linux (Gomir) and Windows (GoBear) backdoors spread through trojanized South Korean software installers [S10]. The 2013 Kimsuky malware included a module for stealing HWP documents [S8]. LLM use covers vulnerability research (CVE-2022-30190), basic scripting, phishing content and reconnaissance [S1][S11].

diamond.adversary: DPRK state actor tracked by Microsoft as Emerald Sleet (THALLIUM), which US Treasury and a joint US advisory place under the RGB [S3][S6][S7].
diamond.capability: Rapport-building spear-phishing and impersonation, credential phishing with mail-forwarding rules, PowerShell paste-and-run lures, remote desktop tooling, QuasarRAT, GoBear and Gomir backdoors, and LLM-assisted reconnaissance [S1][S3][S4][S10][S13].
diamond.infrastructure: Typosquatted and Microsoft-lookalike domains (50 seized in 2019), spoofed sender domains with weak DMARC policies, free webmail personas, web beacons, and remote servers that host certificates and register devices [S3][S4][S9].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): The key terrain is people, not networks: personal and work email of policy, diplomatic, academic and think-tank staff working on Korean Peninsula issues, plus organizational email domains with weak DMARC policies [S2][S3][S6]. STEP 2 (effects): Spoofed trusted personas undermine email-based trust. Compromised mailboxes with forwarding rules give persistent collection without implants [S4][S9]. STEP 3 (adversary template): Benign rapport-building email from a spoofed expert or official, then a lure (PDF, 'secure document', or 'device registration'), then credential capture or PowerShell paste-and-run, then remote desktop or RAT, then mail and document collection [S3][S4][S13]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued collection against DPRK-policy, nuclear and alliance-planning experts through impersonation and paste-and-run lures [S1][S3]. MDCOA is the compromise of a planner or liaison mailbox that gives sustained access to exercise, alliance or nuclear-policy correspondence [S4][S6]. Candidate indicators include unsolicited expert or official outreach that escalates to document review requests, instructions to run PowerShell as administrator, new inbox forwarding rules, spoofed domains failing DMARC alignment, and web-beacon tracking pixels in first-contact emails [S3][S4][S6][S9].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: Track Emerald Sleet lure themes and personas, such as South Korean officials, Japanese diplomats and think-tank staff. Monitor for PowerShell-as-admin and remote-desktop registration events and mailbox-rule changes [S3][S4][S9][S13]. Authorities: Most victims are civilian think tanks, academics and personal accounts outside the DODIN. Response relies on FBI and partner notification and on private-sector actions such as Microsoft's 2019 civil domain seizure and its account disablement with OpenAI [S1][S4][S6]. Mission assurance: Enforce DMARC quarantine or reject on mission-partner domains, restrict PowerShell for standard users, and train staff who handle Korean Peninsula topics to verify unsolicited expert contact out of band [S3][S6]. Coordination: Share indicators with USFK and INDOPACOM stakeholders and with ROK and Japanese partners, which mirrored the 2023 sanctions, and with industry reporters such as Microsoft and Proofpoint [S7][S9].

identification.summary: Femwar02 is a previously unknown pro-Russian ransomware threat actor that emerged in early 2026, linked to a major cyberattack on Italy's Sapienza University of Rome in February 2026, which caused a full network shutdown and operational disruptions. The group deploys Bablock (also known as Rorschach), a next-generation ransomware strain first identified in 2023 that features fast hybrid encryption (curve25519 and hc-128), partial file encryption for speed, direct system calls to evade detection, and domain-wide propagation via Group Policy on Windows Domain Controllers. Bablock shares code similarities with LockBit 2.0 but incorporates elements from other families like Babuk and DarkSide, often delivered via encrypted payloads, DLL sideloading with tools like DarkLoader, and exploits such as those in Zimbra or phishing. Notably, the malware skips encrypting files written in Russian, reinforcing its pro-Russian alignment, with no prior attributions or campaigns documented before the Sapienza incident.

Ferocious Kitten is an APT group that has been active against Persian-speaking individuals since 2015 and appears to be based in Iran. Although it has been active over a large timespan, the group has mostly operated under the radar until a lure document was uploaded to VirusTotal and was brought to public knowledge by researchers on Twitter. Subsequently, one of its implants was analyzed by a Chinese intelligence firm. Kaspersky then expanded some of the findings on the group and provided insights on additional variants. The malware dropped from the aforementioned document is dubbed MarkiRAT and is used to record keystrokes and clipboard content, provide file download and upload capabilities as well as the ability to execute arbitrary commands on the victims machine. Kaspersky were able to trace the implant back to at least 2015, along with variants intended to hijack the execution of the Telegram and Chrome applications as a persistence method. Interestingly, some of the TTPs used by this threat actor are reminiscent of other groups operating in the domain of dissident surveillance. For example, it used the same C2 domains across its implants for years, which was witnessed in the activity of Domestic Kitten. In the same vein, the Telegram execution hijacking technique observed in this campaign by Ferocious Kitten was also observed being used by Rampant Kitten, as covered by Check Point.

identification.summary: FireEye first identified this activity during a recent investigation at an organization in the financial industry. They identified the presence of a financially motivated threat group that they track as FIN1, whose activity at the organization dated back several years. The threat group deployed numerous malicious files and utilities, all of which were part of a malware ecosystem referred to as ‘Nemesis’ by the malware developer(s), and used this malware to access the victim environment and steal cardholder data. FIN1, which may be located in Russia or a Russian-speaking country based on language settings in many of their custom tools, is known for stealing data that is easily monetized from financial services organizations such as banks, credit unions, ATM operations, and financial transaction processing and financial business services companies.

Since 2017, Mandiant has been tracking FIN13, an industrious and versatile financially motivated threat actor conducting long-term intrusions in Mexico with an activity timeframe stretching back as early as 2016. Although their operations continue through the present day, in many ways FIN13's intrusions are like a time capsule of traditional financial cybercrime from days past. Instead of today's prevalent smash-and-grab ransomware groups, FIN13 takes their time to gather information to perform fraudulent money transfers. Rather than relying heavily on attack frameworks such as Cobalt Strike, the majority of FIN13 intrusions involve heavy use of custom passive backdoors and tools to lurk in environments for the long haul.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: In a Taiwan contingency, the cyberspace OE includes Taiwanese government and industrial networks and the global pool of compromised consumer and SOHO devices used as proxy terrain. STEP 2: A botnet of this scale lets adversary traffic appear to come from domestic residential and small-business addresses, which degrades geolocation-based attribution and blocklisting. STEP 3: The template is web shell, then privilege escalation, then RDP plus Sticky Keys, then a SoftEther VPN tunnel, then quiet access with no observed final action. STEP 4: MLCOA is persistent espionage access in Taiwanese and allied networks. MDCOA is using the botnet for DDoS against Taiwanese or US targets during a crisis while maintaining espionage footholds. Candidate indicators: new outbound SoftEther or VPN services masquerading as Windows binaries, changes to accessibility executables, and spikes in SOHO-sourced authentication attempts against DIB portals [S1][S2].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Shared situational awareness should include botnet infrastructure intelligence, such as FBI and partner-shared C2 and node lists, so that defensive cyber forces can recognize proxy-sourced traffic. (2) Coordinate with allied partners, Taiwan especially, through established channels. Flax Typhoon victims are predominantly non-US, so DoD visibility depends on partner sharing. (3) Disruption precedents: the 2024 court-authorized FBI operation shows that domestic botnet takedown is a law-enforcement lead. DoD options against foreign-hosted tiers fall under separate authorities and require deconfliction. (4) DDoS readiness: JCC2 planning should include upstream mitigation coordination for public-facing DoD and DIB services.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: The cyberspace OE includes commercial logistics providers, rail and port operators, and the IoT cameras along supply routes into Ukraine and NATO's eastern flank. These are intelligence collection points for the adversary. STEP 2: Compromised cameras turn the physical terrain itself into adversary ISR, which affects OPSEC for movements. (2) JCC2 situational awareness should take in partner and industry reporting on logistics-sector intrusions, since the victims are mostly private. (3) Authorities: hardening of commercial and allied camera networks is a partner-nation and owner responsibility. DoD influence is through contracts, requirements and liaison. (4) OPSEC: plan movement security assuming adversary visibility through compromised cameras on routes.

provenance.importedSummary: A 2015 report by F-Secure describe APT29 as: 'The Dukes are a well-resourced, highly dedicated and organized cyberespionage group that we believe has been working for the Russian Federation since at least 2008 to collect intelligence in support of foreign and security policy decision-making. The Dukes show unusual confidence in their ability to continue successfully compromising their targets, as well as in their ability to operate with impunity. The Dukes primarily target Western governments and related organizations, such as government ministries and agencies, political think tanks, and governmental subcontractors. Their targets have also included the governments of members of the Commonwealth of Independent States;Asian, African, and Middle Eastern governments;organizations associated with Chechen extremism;and Russian speakers engaged in the illicit trade of controlled substances and drugs. The Dukes are known to employ a vast arsenal of malware toolsets, which we identify as MiniDuke, CosmicDuke, OnionDuke, CozyDuke, CloudDuke, SeaDuke, HammerDuke, PinchDuke, and GeminiDuke. In recent years, the Dukes have engaged in apparently biannual large - scale spear - phishing campaigns against hundreds or even thousands of recipients associated with governmental institutions and affiliated organizations. These campaigns utilize a smash - and - grab approach involving a fast but noisy breakin followed by the rapid collection and exfiltration of as much data as possible.If the compromised target is discovered to be of value, the Dukes will quickly switch the toolset used and move to using stealthier tactics focused on persistent compromise and long - term intelligence gathering. This threat actor targets government ministries and agencies in the West, Central Asia, East Africa, and the Middle East; Chechen extremist groups; Russian organized crime; and think tanks. It is suspected to be behind the 2015 compromise of unclassified networks at the White House, Department of State, Pentagon, and the Joint Chiefs of Staff. The threat actor includes all of the Dukes tool sets, including MiniDuke, CosmicDuke, OnionDuke, CozyDuke, SeaDuke, CloudDuke (aka MiniDionis), and HammerDuke (aka Hammertoss). '

Ghost Blizzard is the Microsoft name for a Russia-origin actor that Microsoft maps to BROMINE, Berserk Bear, TG-4192, Koala Team, Blue Kraken, Crouching Yeti and Dragonfly [S1]. MITRE ATT&CK tracks it as Dragonfly (G0035): a cyber espionage group attributed to Russia's FSB Center 16 that has targeted defense and aviation companies, government entities, ICS-related companies and critical-infrastructure sectors worldwide through supply-chain, spearphishing and drive-by compromise [S2]. The group is best known for long-running access operations against Western energy companies, including trojanized ICS vendor software (2013-2014) [S3][S4] and the 'Dragonfly 2.0' campaign against energy firms in Europe and North America [S5][S6].

US and UK government statements describe the team as a unit within FSB Center 16, also known as Military Unit 71330 [S9][S10][S13]. A US grand jury in the District of Kansas indicted three FSB Center 16 officers (Pavel Akulov, Mikhail Gavrilov, Marat Tyukov) on 2021-08-26; the indictment was unsealed on 2022-03-24 [S9][S13]. In August 2025 the FBI attributed exploitation of Cisco devices to FSB Center 16 actors, and Cisco Talos assessed with high confidence that the related Static Tundra cluster is a subset of Berserk Bear [S11]. Microsoft's public mapping lists the actor as Russia-origin; no Microsoft confidence statement was found [S1].
attribution.basis: US criminal indictment and State Department Rewards for Justice offer [S9][S12][S13]; UK FCDO/NCSC attribution [S10]; joint DHS/FBI and CISA/FBI advisories [S6][S8]; German BSI/BfV/BND memo [S7]; vendor reporting from Symantec, F-Secure/Netresec and Cisco Talos [S3][S4][S5][S11].

actors.objectives: Long-term espionage and pre-positioned access to critical infrastructure, especially energy. Symantec assessed that Dragonfly 2.0 aimed both to learn how energy facilities operate and to gain access to operational systems, and that this access could enable disruption [S5]. The 2014 trojanized-software campaign was assessed by Symantec as giving the group a beachhead that could enable sabotage, though it focused on espionage at the time [S3]. German agencies warned in 2020 that the group sought to anchor itself permanently in IT networks and possibly reach OT networks [S7]. Public reporting has found no disruptive attack by this actor [S7][S8].

Nuclear (including Wolf Creek Nuclear Operating Corporation) [S6][S10][S12]
ICS / industrial equipment vendors and supply-chain suppliers [S3][S4][S6]
US state, local, territorial and tribal (SLTT) government; US federal agencies [S8][S9]
Telecommunications, higher education and manufacturing (Static Tundra sub-cluster) [S11]

targeting.notes: The US indictment alleges the Dragonfly 2.0 phase targeted more than 3,300 users at over 500 US and international companies and entities, including US government agencies [S9]. DHS/FBI described staging through smaller, less secure supply-chain organizations before reaching intended energy targets [S6].

capabilities.summary: Supply-chain compromise of ICS vendor websites to trojanize legitimate software installers with the Havex/Oldrea RAT (for example a European PLC maker's driver package available for at least six weeks in June-July 2013) [S3][S4]; custom malware Backdoor.Oldrea and Trojan.Karagany [S3]; spearphishing (including template-based credential harvesting with the Phishery toolkit) and watering-hole websites [S5][S6]; use of common administration tools rather than zero-days after initial access [S5]; network reconnaissance and collection of ICS information inside energy networks [S6]; exploitation of public-facing vulnerabilities including Citrix CVE-2019-19781, Fortinet CVE-2018-13379, Exchange CVE-2020-0688, Exim CVE-2019-10149 and Netlogon CVE-2020-1472 [S8]; and exploitation of Cisco Smart Install CVE-2018-0171 to collect configuration files from thousands of network devices and modify configurations for access [S11].
