provenance.importedSummary:
APT29 is threat group that has been attributed to Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR). They have operated since at least 2008, often targeting government networks in Europe and NATO member countries, research institutes, and think tanks. APT29 reportedly compromised the Democratic National Committee starting in the summer of 2015.

In April 2021, the US and UK governments attributed the SolarWinds Compromise to the SVR; public statements included citations to APT29, Cozy Bear, and The Dukes. Industry reporting also referred to the actors involved in this campaign as UNC2452, NOBELIUM, StellarParticle, Dark Halo, and SolarStorm.

identification.summary: Iranian state-sponsored actor associated with an intelligence arm of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). It runs long-term espionage through targeted phishing and social engineering against dissidents, journalists, academics, think tanks, policymakers and government officials. One subgroup rapidly weaponizes newly public vulnerabilities against critical-infrastructure targets [S1]. It targeted a 2024 US presidential campaign [S2][S3].
identification.firstObserved: FireEye identified APT35 operations dating back to 2014 (imported record). Microsoft reports a subgroup moving from reconnaissance to direct targeting of US critical infrastructure from late 2021 to mid-2022 [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Mint Sandstorm (formerly PHOSPHORUS). Microsoft maps CHARMING KITTEN, APT35, Newscaster and Parastoo to it [S5]. MITRE tracks it as Magic Hound (G0059) [S4]. Google/Mandiant's APT42 overlaps with part of this activity, and coverage of the 2024 election case uses 'Mint Sandstorm or APT42' interchangeably. This encyclopedia holds a separate APT42 record; vendor cluster boundaries differ.

attribution.sponsor: Islamic Republic of Iran: IRGC intelligence elements [S1]. The September 2024 indictment charged three individuals described as IRGC employees [S3].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft assesses the IRGC association, corroborated by Mandiant, Proofpoint and Secureworks; the US Treasury sanctioned elements of the group in 2022 citing IRGC sponsorship [S1]. Formal US attribution through the 2024 indictment of three named IRGC employees for the campaign hack [S3].
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and vendor corroboration [S1]; DOJ indictment [S3]; Treasury sanctions (2022), as cited by Microsoft [S1].

actors.objectives: Intelligence collection in support of IRGC priorities: monitoring dissidents and activists, collecting on foreign policy, defense and nuclear-related experts, and gaining access to critical infrastructure that could support retaliation [S1]. In 2024 it ran a hack-and-leak operation against a US presidential campaign, attempting to pass stolen material to people it believed were tied to the opposing campaign [S3].

sectors: Government and policy (current and former officials)
Critical infrastructure: seaports, energy, transit, a major US utility and gas entity (subgroup)
targeting.notes: Sector targeting from Microsoft [S1] and the 2024 indictment [S3]. Phishing against Israeli, North American and European think tanks and universities per Microsoft [S1].

capabilities.summary: Social engineering is the core tradecraft: tailored spear-phishing, impersonation and credential harvesting, including multi-week rapport building before delivery [S1][S3]. A subgroup weaponizes public proofs of concept within days: Zoho ManageEngine CVE-2022-47966 (exploited the day the PoC appeared), IBM Aspera Faspex CVE-2022-47986 (within five days) and Log4Shell [S1]. Custom tooling includes Drokbk and Soldier (.NET implants) and CharmPower (modular PowerShell backdoor delivered through template injection) [S1].

STEP 1: The OE includes the personal accounts and devices of staff, policy advisers and family members, because this actor works through people more than networks. Microsoft says it runs both financially motivated and espionage operations against software and IT, education and defense industrial base targets [S1]. Its signature tradecraft is social engineering through fake companies, fake job offers and personas on LinkedIn, Telegram and freelancing platforms. implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is the developer and contractor workforce: personal devices used for job hunting, npm and other package registries, and MSP management channels into DIB and aerospace suppliers [S1][S3][S6]. STEP 2: Recruiting platforms (LinkedIn, Telegram, freelance sites) and open package registries put the first contact outside DoD-controlled networks, which limits visibility before compromise [S1][S2]. STEP 3: The template is a persona and fake-company lure, then a trojanized tool, skills-test package or game, then a loader (SplitLoader or YouieLoad), then LSASS credential theft and IP theft, with ransomware optional (FakePenny or Qilin) [S1][S2]. STEP 4: The MLCOA is continued job-lure and npm-package intrusions against defense and aerospace contractors and developers to steal credentials and IP. The MDCOA is turning access at a software vendor or MSP into a supply-chain compromise or ransomware against DIB suppliers that support Air Force programs, a risk Microsoft flags [S1][S6]. Candidate indicators: Procdump run against LSASS; connections to known Moonstone Sleet domains; unsolicited job or skills tests that require running PuTTY or npm code; Defender detections such as SplitLoader, YouieLoad or PennyCrypt [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: fuse Microsoft and vendor npm and package-registry reporting into the JCC2 common operational picture for DIB and aerospace partners, because the first intrusion step happens off-network [S1][S3]. (2) Authorities: the activity mixes espionage with criminal ransomware (FakePenny, Qilin), so incidents may fall under law-enforcement as well as DoD and DC3 lanes. Classify carefully and coordinate early [S1][S2]. (3) Mission assurance: treat contractor developer workstations, build pipelines and MSP connections as mission-relevant terrain; ransomware against a key supplier could degrade sustainment [S1][S6]. (4) Coordination: work with the DIB CS program and industry partners on fake-recruiter and fake-company indicators; brief personnel about job and game lures [S1].

identification.summary: Mora_001 is a threat actor exhibiting a distinct operational signature that combines opportunistic attacks with ties to the LockBit ecosystem. The actor has been observed exploiting CVE-2024-55591 and CVE-2025-24472 vulnerabilities affecting Fortinet devices. The ransom note associated with Mora_001 includes the same TOX ID used by LockBit, indicating a potential affiliation or shared communication channels. Their post-exploitation patterns suggest a structured playbook that differentiates them from other ransomware operators, including LockBit affiliates.

Moshen Dragon is a Chinese-aligned cyberespionage threat actor operating in Central Asia. They have been observed deploying multiple malware triads and utilizing DLL search order hijacking to sideload ShadowPad and PlugX variants. The threat actor also employs various tools, including an LSA notification package and a passive backdoor known as GUNTERS. Their activities involve targeting the telecommunication sector and leveraging Impacket for lateral movement and data exfiltration.

China-based espionage actor that Microsoft tracks as Mulberry Typhoon (formerly MANGANESE) and that Mandiant and MITRE track as APT5 [S1][S8][S9]. MITRE says it primarily targets the telecommunications, aerospace and defense industries in the U.S., Europe and Asia and has a strong interest in compromising networking devices and their software, including with zero-day exploits [S8]. Microsoft reported in 2023 that Mulberry Typhoon targeted the US defense industrial base, most notably with a zero-day exploit against devices (CVE-2022-27518) [S1]. In December 2022 NSA published threat-hunting guidance on APT5's exploitation of Citrix ADC [S4][S5].
identification.firstObserved: MITRE: active since at least 2007 [S8]. 2019 press coverage of FireEye reporting also says the group has been active since 2007 [S7].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Mulberry Typhoon (formerly MANGANESE) [S1][S9]. MITRE associates Mulberry Typhoon, MANGANESE, BRONZE FLEETWOOD, Keyhole Panda and UNC2630 with APT5 [S8]. NSA-related coverage calls APT5 also UNC2630 and MANGANESE [S4][S6]. Mandiant itself only assessed UNC2630 as possibly tied to APT5, based on a trusted third party's evidence that it could not independently confirm [S2]. 2019 coverage of FireEye reporting describes APT5 as several subgroups with distinct tactics and infrastructure [S7].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China (suspected). Mandiant suspected UNC2630 operates on behalf of the Chinese government [S2]. Its May 2021 update says UNC2630 and UNC2717 are believed to be affiliated with the Chinese government [S3]. Coverage of the NSA guidance calls APT5 a Chinese state-sponsored group [S5][S6].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft describes Mulberry Typhoon as China-based [S1]. NSA publicly attributed the CVE-2022-27518 exploitation to APT5 in December 2022, according to press coverage of the advisory [S4][S5]. Mandiant held the UNC2630 to APT5 link at low-to-moderate confidence ('may have ties'; 'not able to definitively connect') [S2]. 2019 coverage notes that FireEye had not formally attributed APT5 to a nation-state [S7].

actors.objectives: Espionage aimed at defense, aerospace and telecommunications targets [S1][S8]. Mandiant judged that Pulse Secure-era activity sought to steal credentials, keep long-term persistent access to victim networks and access or exfiltrate sensitive data, in support of key Chinese government priorities [S3]. Earlier VPN-exploitation coverage reported spying on pricing and bidding information [S7].

sectors: Government, high tech, education, transportation and financial (broader Pulse Secure campaign, not UNC2630 alone) [S3]
targeting.notes: Microsoft groups Mulberry Typhoon with Circle Typhoon and Volt Typhoon as China-based groups targeting the US DIB. It says their targets occasionally overlap but they are distinct actors with different infrastructure and capabilities [S1]. capabilities.summary: Exploits edge and network appliances, including zero-days: Pulse Secure CVE-2021-22893 alongside older flaws [S2], Citrix ADC/Gateway CVE-2022-27518 [S1][S4], and, per 2019 coverage, Pulse Secure CVE-2019-11510 and Fortinet CVE-2018-13379 [S7]. CVE-2022-27518 allowed unauthenticated remote code execution on appliances configured as a SAML SP or IdP [S4]. UNC2630 deployed purpose-built Pulse Secure implants: SLOWPULSE, which modifies legitimate Pulse Secure files to bypass or log credentials in authentication flows, including some 2FA, plus RADIALPULSE, THINBLOOD, ATRIUM, PACEMAKER, SLIGHTPULSE and PULSECHECK [S2]. Later families include BLOODMINE, BLOODBANK, CLEANPULSE and RAPIDPULSE [S3]. Operators patched devices for persistence that survived upgrades, removed webshells to evade detection and cleared logs [S3]. MITRE also lists Mimikatz, Skeleton Key, PoisonIvy, gh0st RAT and PcShare [S8].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is the edge: SSL VPN concentrators, Citrix ADC/Gateway and SAML-integrated access appliances on DIB, aerospace and telecom networks that connect to DoD programs [S1][S2][S4]. STEP 2: These appliances often fall outside EDR coverage and retain few logs. The actor patches appliance binaries and clears logs, so absence of evidence is weak [S2][S3]. STEP 3: The doctrinal template is appliance exploit (zero-day or fresh n-day), then trojanized authentication components or a webshell, then credential harvest, then internal access and data staging [S2][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is quiet, long-term credential theft and data collection from DIB and telecom networks via edge devices [S3]. MDCOA is a rapid mass-exploitation wave against a newly discovered appliance zero-day across DoD-adjacent contractors, with implants that survive vendor patching and upgrades, giving persistent access to program data during a crisis [S1][S3]. Candidate indicators: modified Pulse Secure or Citrix system files and integrity-check failures, unexpected webshells on appliances, gaps or truncation in appliance logs, and authentication successes that bypass MFA [S2][S3][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: JCC2 should track edge-appliance inventory and patch state, plus vendor integrity-check results, for DoD and mission-partner networks, because this actor's entry point is the appliance [S2][S4]. (2) Authorities: most observed victims are DIB companies [S1][S2]. Response depends on DC3/DIB CS sharing, CISA and NSA advisories and contractor cooperation rather than DoD-owned terrain. (3) Mission assurance: an appliance patch alone does not remove a persistence patcher [S3]. Plan for rebuild or replacement and credential resets on systems behind compromised appliances. (4) Coordination: Mulberry, Circle and Volt Typhoon target the same DIB sector but are distinct actors [S1]. Deconflict hunts and reporting by actor, and avoid merging indicators across clusters.

As part of our investigations, we were also able to identify and contact one of the attackers to try and gain insights into the motivations behind these attacks.' Palo Alto Networks reported on continued activity by the attackers in 2014.

Prodaft researchers have published a report on Paperbug, a cyber-espionage campaign carried out by suspected Russian-speaking group Nomadic Octopus and which targeted entities in Tajikistan. According to Prodaft, known compromised victims included high-ranking government officials, telcos, and public service infrastructures. Compromised devices also included OT devices, besides your typical computers, servers, and mobile devices. In typical Prodaft fashion, the company also gained access to one of the group's C&C server backend panels.

Nylon Typhoon (formerly NICKEL) is a China-based espionage actor that Microsoft says uses exploits against unpatched systems to compromise remote access services and appliances, targeting government agencies, diplomatic organizations and NGOs in Central and South America, the Caribbean, Europe and North America [S1][S11]. MITRE ATT&CK tracks the same group as Ke3chang (G0004), attributed to actors operating out of China, which has targeted oil, government, diplomatic, military and NGO organizations since at least 2010 [S3]. Microsoft reports that the actor achieved long-term access to several victims and ran regularly scheduled data exfiltration [S1]. Symantec reported the group, which it tracks as Flea, still attacking foreign ministries in the Americas in late 2022 and early 2023 with a new Microsoft Graph-based backdoor, Graphican [S12][S13].
identification.firstObserved: MITRE: targeting since at least 2010 [S3]. Microsoft has tracked NICKEL since 2016 and tracked the operations it disclosed in 2021 since September 2019 [S1]. Latest dated public campaign found: late 2022 to early 2023 (Symantec, Flea) [S12][S13].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Nylon Typhoon (formerly NICKEL). Microsoft maps NICKEL, VIXEN PANDA, Playful Dragon, RedRiver, ke3chang, APT15 and Mirage to it [S4]. In 2021 Microsoft wrote that it 'observed some common activity' with actors known as APT15, APT25 and KeChang, which is an overlap statement rather than a one-to-one equivalence [S1]. Microsoft's Security Insider profile (dated 2024-01-25) lists APT15 and Vixen Panda as other names [S11]. Symantec's Flea is linked to APT15/Nickel in coverage of its 2023 report [S13]. MITRE lists Ke3chang, APT15, Mirage, Vixen Panda, GREF, Playful Dragon, RoyalAPT, NICKEL and Nylon Typhoon as associated names [S3]. The imported summary on this record described ESET's 'GREF' cluster (active since March 2017, Android BadBazaar campaigns against Uyghurs). That summary was not carried forward because no source gathered here ties that ESET cluster to Microsoft's Nylon Typhoon (see gaps).

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China (state nexus). Microsoft describes NICKEL as a China-based threat actor [S1][S4], and MITRE attributes Ke3chang to actors operating out of China [S3]. None of the sources gathered names a specific PRC agency or unit.
attribution.confidence: Microsoft attributes the activity to NICKEL / Nylon Typhoon by name and assesses that China-based actors will keep targeting government, diplomatic and NGO sectors, likely for economic espionage or traditional intelligence collection [S1]. Microsoft did not publish a numeric or worded confidence level for state sponsorship. The December 2021 domain seizure was a civil action by Microsoft's Digital Crimes Unit under a US District Court order, not a US government attribution [S1][S2]. Symantec assesses Flea as China-linked [S13]; that is a vendor assessment, not government attribution.
attribution.basis: Microsoft MSTIC telemetry and customer notifications, plus the DCU seizure of NICKEL-operated websites [S1][S2]; sign-in activity concentrated Monday to Friday, 08:00 to 17:00 China Standard Time [S1]; long-running vendor reporting summarized by MITRE ATT&CK (Mandiant, NCC Group, Intezer, ESET) [S3][S6][S7][S8][S9]; Symantec reporting on Flea/Graphican, as covered by the press [S12][S13]; Mandiant reporting on shared China-nexus ORB infrastructure [S5].

actors.objectives: Intelligence collection against foreign ministries, diplomatic entities, other government bodies and NGOs. Microsoft assesses this is likely in pursuit of economic espionage or traditional intelligence collection as China expands bilateral relations and Belt and Road partnerships [S1]. Mandiant's 2014 Operation Ke3chang report focused on attacks against Ministries of Foreign Affairs [S3][S9]. Symantec's 2022-2023 Flea victims were mainly foreign affairs ministries in the Americas, plus a government finance department, consistent with continued diplomatic intelligence collection [S12][S13].

Private corporation in Central and South America (2022-2023) [S13]

targeting.notes: Microsoft's December 2021 list of 29 targeted countries: Argentina, Barbados, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Brazil, Bulgaria, Chile, Colombia, Croatia, Czech Republic, Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, France, Guatemala, Honduras, Hungary, Italy, Jamaica, Mali, Mexico, Montenegro, Panama, Peru, Portugal, Switzerland, Trinidad and Tobago, United Kingdom, United States and Venezuela [S1]. In its 2021 Digital Defense Report summary, Microsoft names NICKEL among the four nation-state groups most active against the government sector from July 2020 to June 2021, mostly against government entities involved in international affairs [S10]. Symantec's 2022-2023 activity hit foreign ministries in the Americas, a corporation in Central and South America and one European victim [S12][S13].

capabilities.summary: Initial access through exploits against unpatched internet-facing Microsoft Exchange and SharePoint servers and remote-access appliances such as VPNs, including a Pulse Secure VPN vulnerability [S1]. MITRE also records VPN access using compromised accounts and stolen VPN certificates [S3][S6]. Credential theft uses keyloggers, Mimikatz, WDigest abuse and NTDSDump [S1]. Custom backdoors include Neoichor, Leeson, NumbIdea, NullItch and Rokum; several use the Internet Explorer COM interface for C2 hidden in legitimate-looking web pages, and implants are dropped into existing application paths to blend in [S1]. Stolen credentials are used for routine Microsoft 365 email collection through browser sign-ins and legacy Exchange Web Services, routed through commercial VPNs and actor infrastructure [S1]. Scheduled, incremental file collection is staged and archived with renamed RAR or 7-Zip [S1]. Earlier tooling includes RoyalCLI and RoyalDNS (DNS C2) and the SharePoint dumping tool spwebmember [S3][S6], the MirageFox RAT, an upgraded Mirage [S3][S7], and the Okrum backdoor, in use since December 2016 [S3][S8]. Mandiant reports that APT15 has used the provisioned ORB network SPACEHOP for reconnaissance scanning and vulnerability exploitation [S5]. In 2022-2023 the group (as Symantec's Flea) used Graphican, an evolution of the Ketrican backdoor (itself based on BS2005), which uses the Microsoft Graph API and OneDrive to retrieve encrypted C2 addresses and supports an interactive shell, file transfer, hidden process creation and hidden PowerShell execution [S12][S13]. The same campaign used the EWSTEW Exchange email-extraction backdoor, the Zerologon flaw CVE-2020-1472, Mimikatz, Pypykatz, Safetykatz and the public K8Tools toolkit [S12][S13].

diamond.adversary: China-based espionage operators that Microsoft tracks as Nylon Typhoon (NICKEL) [S1][S4]. Sign-in activity clusters on weekdays from 08:00 to 17:00 China Standard Time, with possible shift-based scheduling [S1].
diamond.capability: Exploits for Exchange, SharePoint and VPN appliances. Credential theft with Mimikatz, WDigest, NTDSDump and keyloggers. Custom backdoors Neoichor, Leeson, NumbIdea, NullItch and Rokum [S1]. Legacy tools RoyalCLI, RoyalDNS, MirageFox and Okrum [S3][S6][S7][S8]. Graphican (Graph API/OneDrive C2), EWSTEW, Zerologon exploitation and K8Tools in 2022-2023 [S12][S13].
diamond.infrastructure: Actor-operated websites used for C2, seized by Microsoft DCU in 2021 [S1][S2]. Hardcoded C2 servers return legitimate-looking HTML that hides Base64 shellcode [S1]. Commercial VPN providers carry account sign-ins [S1]. The SPACEHOP ORB network, provisioned by a single entity in China, uses relay servers hosted in Hong Kong or China [S5]. RoyalDNS used DNS for C2 [S3]. Graphican retrieves its C2 address from OneDrive through the Microsoft Graph API, hiding C2 lookup in legitimate cloud traffic [S12][S13].
diamond.victim: Foreign ministries and other government bodies, diplomatic entities and NGOs in Latin America, the Caribbean, Europe, North America and Mali [S1]. MITRE adds oil and military targets [S3]. Foreign ministries and a finance department in the Americas, plus one European victim, in 2022-2023 [S12][S13].

diamond.technology: Unpatched on-premises Exchange and SharePoint, remote-access VPN appliances, Microsoft 365 accounts reachable through legacy authentication (EWS), and Windows hosts where credentials are cached in memory [S1]. Microsoft 365 Graph API and OneDrive as C2 channels, and domain controllers unpatched for Zerologon [S12][S13].

gaps: No Microsoft reporting dated after 2021 with new Nylon Typhoon technical detail was found; the 2024 Security Insider profile is a summary [S11]. The latest dated campaign found is Symantec's 2022-2023 Flea/Graphican activity [S12][S13]. No 2024-2026 campaign reporting was found.
Microsoft's DCU announcement and the court filings could not be opened. Seizure details come from the MSTIC blog [S1] and press coverage reporting 42 domains [S2].

Symantec's Graphican report (S12) and most of its press coverage could not be opened (hosts blocked). Its details come from search-result summaries of Symantec and CSO Online coverage [S13]. Symantec's Flea name is not in Microsoft's mapping [S4], so the Flea-to-Nylon Typhoon link rests on Symantec's APT15/Nickel linkage.

Primary reports were not opened because their hosts were blocked: Mandiant Operation Ke3chang (2014), NCC Group RoyalCLI/RoyalDNS (2018), Intezer MirageFox (2018), ESET Okrum and Ketrican (2019), and Palo Alto Unit 42 TidePool. Their content is used only as summarized by MITRE ATT&CK.

Cluster boundary: ESET's 'GREF' (active since March 2017; Android BadBazaar trojanized Signal and Telegram apps targeting Uyghurs) appears in the imported summary, and MISP lists it as a separate entry from APT15. MITRE's GREF alias rests on older NCC Group reporting [S3]. No source gathered here establishes that ESET's GREF mobile activity belongs to Microsoft's Nylon Typhoon, so it is excluded.

Microsoft stated only 'common activity' with APT15, APT25 and KeChang in 2021 [S1]. APT25 is not in Microsoft's current Nylon Typhoon mapping [S4]. The exact boundary with Mandiant's APT15 and APT25 is unresolved.

Secureworks BRONZE PALACE, BRONZE DAVENPORT and BRONZE IDLEWOOD, plus the aliases Lurid, Metushy, Red Vulture, Social Network Team and Royal APT, are unverified. The Secureworks profile could not be opened.
No specific PRC sponsoring agency (MSS, PLA or contractor) and no US government indictment or advisory naming this actor was found.

Google Threat Intelligence's APT15 profile (sectors: trade, economic and financial, energy, military; ENFAL, BALDEAGLE, NOISEMAKER and MIRAGE malware) was read but carries no publication date, so it is not cited.
The Microsoft mapping file (S4) is a living document. Its date is the access date, not a publication date.

MITRE ATT&CK pages could not be opened directly this session. The G0004 description and aliases were confirmed through search results (version 3.1, modified 2025-04-04) [S3]; software and campaign C0052 details come from earlier reading of the ATT&CK bundle and were not re-verified.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (define the OE): Key cyber terrain is internet-facing Exchange, SharePoint and VPN appliances, plus Microsoft 365 tenants that still allow legacy authentication (EWS). It matters most for foreign-affairs, diplomatic and partner-nation government networks in Latin America, the Caribbean, Europe and North America [S1]. STEP 2 (describe effects): Exposed and unpatched remote-access edges are the entry point. Shared ORB relay networks such as SPACEHOP spread source infrastructure across commercial VPS providers, which weakens IP-based blocking and attribution [S1][S5]. STEP 3 (adversary template): Exploit edge service or VPN, then dump credentials (Mimikatz, NTDSDump, WDigest, keylogger), then deploy an IE-COM backdoor in a legitimate software path, then collect mailboxes through M365/EWS sign-ins over commercial VPNs, then run recurring, date-filtered file collection archived with renamed RAR or 7-Zip [S1]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is quiet, long-term diplomatic and government intelligence collection with scheduled exfiltration from partner-nation ministries [S1]. MDCOA is persistent access to partner-nation foreign-affairs and military networks, or to shared coalition email, exposing coalition planning or negotiating positions (analyst extrapolation from the targeting [S1][S3]). Graphican shows the actor moving C2 into Microsoft Graph/OneDrive traffic, which blends with normal M365 use [S12][S13]. Candidate indicators: unexpected Graph API or OneDrive access by non-browser processes on servers; Zerologon (CVE-2020-1472) exploitation attempts against domain controllers [S12][S13]; EWS or legacy-auth sign-ins from commercial VPN ranges during 00:00-09:00 UTC on weekdays; WDigest UseLogonCredential being enabled; executables such as AcroRd64.exe or FoxitRdr64.exe in unexpected application folders; IE registry changes (IEHarden=0, ClearBrowsingHistoryOnExit=1); renamed rar.exe or 7z.exe with keyboard-walk passwords [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: Fuse identity telemetry (legacy-auth and EWS sign-ins, VPN-sourced logons) with edge-device patch status. The actor relies on valid credentials after initial exploitation, so host-only sensing will miss mailbox collection [S1]. Track ORB/SPACEHOP-linked infrastructure as shared China-nexus terrain rather than as a single-actor indicator [S5]. Authorities: The 2021 disruption came through a private civil seizure (Microsoft DCU under a US District Court order), not government action [S1][S2]. Planners should not count such actions as DoD effects, and they should coordinate deconfliction with private-sector disruption efforts. Situational awareness should also cover cloud API telemetry, because Graph/OneDrive C2 bypasses traditional C2 domain blocking [S12][S13]. Mission assurance: Block legacy authentication, enforce MFA, apply the ASR rule against LSASS credential theft, and prioritize patching of Exchange, SharePoint and VPN appliances on DODIN and mission-partner enclaves [S1]. Coordination: Many victims are partner-nation and Western Hemisphere foreign ministries [S1]. Information sharing with partner nations and combatant commands, especially SOUTHCOM-area partners, is an analyst-inferred coordination need for protecting shared diplomatic and military communications.

provenance.importedSummary: GREF is a China-aligned APT group that has been active since at least March 2017. They are known for using custom backdoors, loaders, and ancillary tools in their targeted attacks. Recently, they have been attributed to two active Android campaigns that distribute the BadBazaar malware through malicious apps on official and alternative app stores. identification.summary:
Scattered Spider is a native English-speaking cybercriminal group active since at least 2022.   The group initially targeted customer relationship management (CRM) providers, business process outsourcing (BPO) firms, and telecommunications and technology companies before expanding in 2023 to gaming, hospitality, retail, managed service provider (MSP), manufacturing, and financial sectors. 
Scattered Spider relies heavily on social engineering, including impersonating IT and help-desk staff, to gain initial access, bypass multi-factor authentication (MFA), and compromise enterprise networks. The group has adapted its tooling to evade endpoint detection and response (EDR) defenses and used ransomware for financial gain.   
Scattered Spider had expanded into hybrid cloud and identity environments, using help-desk impersonation and MFA bypass to obtain administrator access in Okta, AWS, and Office 365.

identification.summary: Storm-1679 is a Russian disinformation group believed to be a spinoff of the Internet Research Agency, actively engaged in influence operations targeting the International Olympic Committee and the 2024 Olympic Games. The group has employed AI-generated content, including deepfake videos and fabricated narratives about violence, to discredit the IOC and instill fear among potential attendees. Their campaigns have been identified across multiple languages and platforms, utilizing techniques such as impersonation of media outlets and the creation of disinformation websites. Microsoft attributes significant disinformation activities related to the Olympics to Storm-1679, highlighting their focus on spreading falsehoods and promoting anti-Olympics messaging.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: The OE includes DIB contractors, military installations' IT and healthcare systems supporting military communities. This actor targets all three. provenance.importedSummary:
Andariel is a North Korean state-sponsored threat group that has been active since at least 2009. Andariel has primarily focused its operations--which have included destructive attacks--against South Korean government agencies, military organizations, and a variety of domestic companies; they have also conducted cyber financial operations against ATMs, banks, and cryptocurrency exchanges. Andariel's notable activity includes Operation Black Mine, Operation GoldenAxe, and Campaign Rifle.

Andariel is considered a sub-set of Lazarus Group, and has been attributed to North Korea's Reconnaissance General Bureau.

North Korean group definitions are known to have significant overlap, and some security researchers report all North Korean state-sponsored cyber activity under the name Lazarus Group instead of tracking clusters or subgroups.

identification.summary: This threat actor targets critical infrastructure entities in the oil and gas sector, primarily in Ukraine. The threat actors deploy the BugDrop malware to remotely access the microphones in their targets' computers to eavesdrop on conversations.

Operation DRBControl is a cyberespionage campaign targeting gambling companies in Southeast Asia, first identified in 2019. The operation involves the use of HyperBro malware and SysUpdate variants, with evidence of customer database and source code exfiltration. The threat actor has employed domain spoofing for command and control and has shown a consistent interest in the gambling industry. Trend Micro's analysis linked multiple tools and malware families to this campaign, indicating a sophisticated and evolving threat landscape.

Operation Emmental, also known as the Retefe gang, is a threat actor group that has been active since at least 2012. They primarily target customers of banks in countries such as Austria, Sweden, Switzerland, and Japan. The group has developed sophisticated malware, including a Mac alternative called Dok, to bypass two-factor authentication and hijack network traffic. They have also been observed using phishing emails to spread their malware. The group is believed to be Russian-speaking and has continuously improved their malicious codes over the years.

The threat actors compromised the update server of a remote support solutions provider to deliver a remote access tool called 9002 RAT to their targets of interest through the update process. They carried this out by first stealing the company’s certificate then using it to sign the malware. They also configured the update server to only deliver malicious files if the client is located in the range of IP addresses of their target organisations.

Operation Shadow Force is a group of malware that is representative of Shadow Force and Wgdrop from 2013 to 2020, and is a group activity that attacks Korean companies and organizations. The group's first confirmed attack was in March 2013, but considering the date of malware creation, it is likely to have been active before 2012. Since the malware used mainly by them is Shadow Force, it was named Operation Shadow Force, and it has not been confirmed whether the attacker is associated with a known group.

The PassCV group continues to be one of the most successful and active threat groups that leverage a wide array of stolen Authenticode-signing certificates. Snorre Fagerland of Blue Coat Systems first coined the term PassCV in a blog post. His post provides a good introduction to the group and covers some of the older infrastructure, stolen code-signing certificate reuse, and other connections associated with the PassCV malware. There are several clues alluding to the possibility that multiple groups may be utilizing the same stolen signing certificates, but at this time SPEAR believes the current attacks are more likely being perpetrated by a single group employing multiple publicly available Remote Administration Tools (RATs). The PassCV group has been operating with continued success and has already started to expand their malware repertoire into different off-the-shelf RATs and custom code. SPEAR identified eighteen previously undisclosed stolen Authenticode certificates. These certificates were originally issued to companies and individuals scattered across China, Taiwan, Korea, Europe, the United States and Russia. In this post we expand the usage of the term ‘PassCV’ to encompass the malware mentioned in the Blue Coat Systems report, as well as the APT group behind the larger C2 infrastructure and stolen Authenticode certificates. We’d like to share some of our findings as they pertain to the stolen certificates, command and control infrastructure, and some of the newer custom RATs they’ve begun development on.

identification.summary: Iranian nation-state threat actor that Microsoft tracks as Peach Sandstorm (formerly HOLMIUM), whose activity overlaps with public reporting on APT33, Elfin and Refined Kitten [S1]. Microsoft assesses that it operates on behalf of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and runs long-term intelligence-gathering operations [S2]. Since 2023 its typical tradecraft has been large-scale password spraying followed by cloud-focused post-compromise activity in Microsoft Entra ID and Azure, including command and control (C2) hosted in fraudulent Azure subscriptions [S1][S2]. Earlier Mandiant (FireEye) reporting describes a group focused on aviation and on energy and petrochemical targets in Saudi Arabia, the United States and South Korea [S3].
identification.firstObserved: Mandiant: cyber espionage since at least 2013, with the earliest TURNEDUP compile timestamp dated April 2013 [S3]. Microsoft cites a 2019 password-spray wave and spraying since at least February 2023 [S1][S2].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Peach Sandstorm (formerly HOLMIUM). Microsoft states overlap, not identity, with APT33 (Mandiant), Elfin (Symantec) and Refined Kitten (CrowdStrike) [S1]. MITRE tracks the group as APT33 (G0064) [S7]. Facts from APT33/Elfin-era reporting (2013-2019) stay attributed to their original vendors and are not merged into Microsoft's Peach Sandstorm findings. Microsoft notes that other Iranian groups, including Smoke Sandstorm, have used similar techniques, so tradecraft alone does not identify this actor [S2].

attribution.sponsor: Islamic Republic of Iran. Microsoft assesses that Peach Sandstorm operates on behalf of the IRGC [S2]. Mandiant (2017) assessed that APT33 works at the behest of the Iranian government [S3].
attribution.confidence: These are vendor assessments only. Microsoft bases its IRGC assessment on victimology and operational focus and states no confidence level [S2]. Its 2023 report says the spray campaign is 'likely' used for intelligence collection in support of Iranian state interests [S1]. Mandiant uses hedged language and calls APT33 'most likely government sponsored' [S3]. Press coverage of FalseFont says Microsoft did not tie that activity to a specific Iranian government entity [S6]. This pass found no US government attribution naming Peach Sandstorm or APT33.
attribution.basis: Victimology and operational focus [S2]. Activity in late May and June 2023 fell almost entirely within 09:00-17:00 Iran Standard Time [S1]. Mandiant also cited activity in a UTC+04:30 time zone and on Iran's Saturday-Wednesday workweek, use of Iranian hacker tools and hosting providers, Farsi artifacts in DROPSHOT/SHAPESHIFT, and the persona 'xman_1365_x', which open sources linked to the Nasr Institute [S3].

actors.objectives: Intelligence collection in support of Iranian state interests [S1][S2]. Targeting of satellite, defense, government and oil-and-gas organizations shows interest in military, space and energy information [S1][S2]. Mandiant judged the aviation focus may serve Iran's interest in military and commercial aviation, and the petrochemical focus its energy-sector interests [S3]. Earlier reporting also shows possible preparation for disruption. Mandiant found the SHAPESHIFT wiper in APT33's toolset but had not seen it used destructively [S3]. Microsoft in 2019 (as reported) suggested that targeting industrial control system (ICS) suppliers might be aimed at physically disruptive access, though it said motive remained unclear [S5].

sectors: Oil and gas, energy and petrochemical [S2][S3]
regions: Global (2023 spraying of thousands of organizations) [S1]
targeting.notes: Microsoft lists earlier targeting across aviation, construction, education, energy, financial services, healthcare, government and telecommunications [S1]. Peach Sandstorm used compromised education-sector accounts to buy Azure infrastructure, so universities are both victims and enablers [S2].

capabilities.summary: Microsoft-reported (2023-2024) capabilities: high-volume password spraying from TOR IPs with a 'go-http-client' user agent, and exploitation of public proof-of-concept exploits for Zoho ManageEngine (CVE-2022-47966) and Confluence (CVE-2022-26134) [S1]. Post-compromise, Microsoft reported Entra ID reconnaissance with AzureHound and ROADtools, and persistence through Azure Arc, new or abused Azure subscriptions and AnyDesk [S1]. It also reported the custom tunneling tool EagleRelay, a Golden SAML attack in March 2023, and DLL search-order hijacking [S1]. The custom multi-stage backdoor Tickler (2024) used Azure C2 nodes under azurewebsites.net in fraudulent subscriptions, Run-key persistence and SMB lateral movement [S2]. LinkedIn personas have been used for reconnaissance and possible social engineering since at least November 2021 [S2]. The FalseFont backdoor (late 2023) offers remote access, file execution and data exfiltration to C2 (as reported) [S6]. Mandiant-reported (2017) tooling includes the DROPSHOT dropper, TURNEDUP backdoor, SHAPESHIFT wiper, NANOCORE, NETWIRE and ALFA Shell, plus recruitment-themed spear-phishing with .hta files and domains impersonating Boeing, Alsalam Aircraft, Northrop Grumman Aviation Arabia and Vinnell Arabia [S3].

campaigns.name: Aviation and petrochemical espionage (Mandiant APT33)
campaigns.summary: A US aerospace organization was compromised from mid-2016 to early 2017. A Saudi conglomerate with aviation holdings and a South Korean petrochemical company were targeted with job-recruitment spear-phishing that delivered TURNEDUP. Domains impersonated defense and aviation firms.

campaigns.name: Narrowed password spraying against ICS suppliers (Microsoft, CYBERWARCON)
campaigns.summary: Microsoft (as reported) said the group narrowed spraying to about 2,000 organizations a month. About half of its top 25 targets were makers, suppliers or maintainers of ICS equipment.

campaigns.name: LinkedIn persona operations
campaigns.summary: Fake LinkedIn profiles posing as students, developers and recruiters targeted higher education and satellite sectors from at least November 2021 to mid-2024.

campaigns.name: Global password spray campaign
campaigns.summary: From February to July 2023, password spraying hit thousands of organizations. Follow-on activity included Entra ID reconnaissance, Azure Arc persistence and EagleRelay, a March 2023 Golden SAML intrusion, and data exfiltration in a small number of cases.

campaigns.name: FalseFont backdoor against defense industrial base
campaigns.summary: Microsoft (as reported) saw Peach Sandstorm attempting to deliver the new FalseFont backdoor to individuals at defense industrial base organizations. First use was observed in early November 2023.

campaigns.name: Tickler backdoor and Azure C2 operations
campaigns.summary: From April to July 2024, Tickler was deployed against satellite, communications equipment, oil and gas, and government targets in the US and UAE. Password spraying hit defense, space, education and government organizations in the US and Australia. Microsoft disrupted the fraudulent Azure subscriptions.

diamond.adversary: IRGC-aligned Iranian operators, per Microsoft's assessment [S2]. Mandiant linked the persona 'xman_1365_x' to the tooling [S3].
diamond.capability: Password spraying, public N-day exploits, Entra ID and Azure abuse (Golden SAML, Azure Arc) and custom backdoors (Tickler, FalseFont, TURNEDUP), plus the SHAPESHIFT wiper [S1][S2][S3][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: TOR exit IPs for spraying [S1]. Fraudulent Azure subscriptions bought with compromised education accounts and used for C2 [S2]. Earlier, dynamic-DNS domains impersonating aviation and defense firms [S3].
diamond.victim: Satellite, defense/DIB, government, oil and gas, aviation and pharmaceutical organizations in the US, Gulf states, Australia, Europe and South Korea [S1][S2][S3][S6].
diamond.socioPolitical: Intelligence collection for Iranian state interests [S1]. Microsoft tied a 2019 spray wave to rising US-Iran tensions [S1]. Mandiant linked the aviation focus to Iran's interest in military aviation capability [S3].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing cloud identity (Microsoft 365 and Entra ID) with weak passwords and no MFA, unpatched ManageEngine and Confluence servers, and cloud tenant trust relationships [S1][S2].

gaps: No US government attribution or advisory naming Peach Sandstorm or APT33 was located; IRGC sponsorship rests on Microsoft's assessment [S2].
FalseFont details come from press coverage of Microsoft's December 2023 social-media disclosure, which did not disclose the delivery method; no Microsoft blog post was opened [S6].
The Microsoft 2019 CYBERWARCON findings come from Axios coverage; no Microsoft primary document was found [S5].

A 2026 CloudSEK advisory (seen only in search excerpts; fetch failed) claims APT33 deployed a 'Shamoon 4.0' wiper against about 15,000 Saudi energy workstations in January 2026. It is single-source, unverified and NOT included as fact.
No Microsoft or Mandiant primary reporting on Peach Sandstorm activity in 2025-2026 was found. A November 2025 Brandefense forecast was seen but not used.
Mandiant's link between the persona and the Nasr Institute, and any ties to Shamoon/StoneDrill, remain unproven. Mandiant said it had not directly seen APT33 carry out destructive operations [S3].
Trend Micro (2019 narrow-targeting botnets) and Recorded Future (2019, more than 1,200 domains) reports were not opened in this pass.
It is unclear whether any ICS supplier targeted in 2019 was breached, or whether any damage resulted [S5].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): Key terrain is cloud identity (Entra ID and Microsoft 365 tenants) at satellite, space, defense-industrial-base and government organizations, along with Azure subscriptions and internet-facing ManageEngine and Confluence servers [S1][S2]. STEP 2 (effects): Weak passwords and missing MFA on DIB and space contractor tenants offer an indirect path to DoD program data. Compromised university accounts let the adversary stand up infrastructure on trusted cloud domains that blend with normal traffic [S2]. STEP 3 (adversary model): The pattern runs from LinkedIn persona reconnaissance, to low-and-slow password spraying from TOR, to Entra ID reconnaissance (AzureHound/ROADtools), to persistence (Azure Arc, AnyDesk, Golden SAML), to a custom backdoor (Tickler or FalseFont) with Azure-hosted C2, to SMB lateral movement and exfiltration [S1][S2][S6]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is continued credential-based intelligence collection against DIB, satellite and government tenants that rises with US-Iran tension [S1][S2]. MDCOA is using ICS-supplier and energy footholds for disruptive or wiper operations, given SHAPESHIFT in the toolset and 2019 ICS-supplier targeting [S3][S5]. Candidate indicators: bursts of failed sign-ins from TOR with 'go-http-client' user agents; unexpected Azure Arc enrollment or new Azure subscriptions; outbound traffic to newly created azurewebsites.net hosts; new SharePoint.exe Run-key entries; and AnyDesk installs on servers [S1][S2].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: identity telemetry (sign-in logs, conditional access failures, federation/SAML changes) from DIB and space-sector partners should be fused with DoD network sensing, because this actor's primary access vector is cloud identity, not the DODIN perimeter [S1][S2]. (2) Authorities: most targets are contractor- or university-owned tenants and Azure infrastructure, so response depends on partners and cloud providers (Microsoft disrupted the fraudulent subscriptions), not on DoD action [S2]. (3) Mission assurance: Prioritize MFA and password-spray detection for satellite, space and weapons-program contractors, and track defended-asset dependence on vendors such as ICS suppliers [S2][S5][S6]. (4) Coordination: Coordinate with DC3/DIB CS and cloud-provider threat intelligence, and raise the watch level during periods of US-Iran tension, which Microsoft linked to earlier spray waves [S1].

provenance.importedSummary: Our analysis reveals that APT33 is a capable group that has carried out cyber espionage operations since at least 2013. We assess APT33 works at the behest of the Iranian government.

identification.summary: Pearl Sleet is a nation state activity group based in North Korea that has been active since at least 2012. They primarily target defectors from North Korea, media organizations in carrying out their cyber espionage activities.

LIMINAL PANDA is a China-nexus APT that targets telecommunications entities, employing custom malware and publicly available tools for covert access, C2, and data exfiltration. The adversary demonstrates extensive knowledge of telecom networks, utilizing GSM protocols to retrieve mobile subscriber information and call metadata. LIMINAL PANDA exploits trust relationships and security gaps between providers to access core infrastructure, indicating a focus on SIGINT collection rather than financial gain. Their intrusion activity has primarily affected telecom providers in southern Asia and Africa, with potential for broader targeting based on network configurations.

Periwinkle Tempest (formerly DEV-0193) is what Microsoft calls a financially motivated cybercriminal group. It develops, distributes and manages several payloads, including Trickbot, BazaLoader and AnchorDNS [S1][S2]. Microsoft describes it as the most prolific ransomware-associated cybercriminal activity group it tracked. It managed the Ryuk ransomware-as-a-service program until Ryuk shut down in June 2021 and also managed Ryuk's successor, Conti, as well as Diavol [S1][S2]. As other malware operations shut down, the group hired developers from Emotet, Qakbot and IcedID [S1][S2]. Microsoft also tracks DEV-0365, which provides Cobalt Strike Beacon infrastructure as a service to other cybercriminals, as a subgroup of DEV-0193 [S2].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft has tracked DEV-0193 since October 2020 [S1][S2]. Per DOJ charges reported by TRM Labs, the Trickbot conspiracy began in November 2015 [S7].
identification.notes: Microsoft also associates the name 'Trickbot LLC' with this group [S1][S2]. Microsoft said DEV-0193 overlaps with activity Mandiant tracks as UNC1878 [S3]. Mandiant later promoted UNC1878 to FIN12, a Ryuk-deploying intrusion actor that 'worked closely with TrickBot-affiliated actors' [S10]. FIN12 is therefore best treated as a closely linked affiliate cluster, not a synonym for the Trickbot developers. German BKA reporting refers to the Trickbot group as 'Wizard Spider' [S9]. Microsoft's mapping places some Wizard Spider and Conti names under separate entries (Storm-0230, Conti Team 1, and Pistachio Tempest/DEV-0237, a Ryuk and Conti affiliate) [S2], so these boundaries should not be merged.

attribution.sponsor: No state sponsor is assessed. Microsoft classifies Periwinkle Tempest as financially motivated [S1]. The US and UK governments describe the Trickbot group as Russia-based [S7].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft attributes the Trickbot, BazaLoader, AnchorDNS, Ryuk, Conti and Diavol management roles to DEV-0193/Periwinkle Tempest based on its telemetry and says leaked Conti chats from February 2022 confirmed the scale of the activity [S2]. The US and UK sanctioned alleged members in February and September 2023, and DOJ unsealed indictments of nine Russian nationals in September 2023 [S7]. In 2025 Germany's BKA publicly named a suspected founder and leader known as 'Stern' [S9].
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and the Conti chat leak [S1][S2]; Microsoft's 2020 civil and technical action against Trickbot infrastructure [S4]; US Treasury and UK sanctions and DOJ indictments (via secondary coverage) [S7]; and the BKA's Operation Endgame identification (via secondary coverage) [S9].

actors.objectives: Financial gain. The group runs malware and ransomware services that enable ransomware extortion of large organizations, and earlier ran banking and credential theft [S1][S2][S7]. According to DOJ charges as reported by TRM Labs, Trickbot was used to steal money and personal information [S7].

sectors: National government institutions, e.g. Costa Rica's finance and customs systems (Conti) [S8]
regions: Global, opportunistic (inferred from RaaS and botnet model; not region-limited in Microsoft reporting) [S1][S2]
targeting.notes: Microsoft's profile lists education and healthcare [S1]. Treasury said the group targeted many US critical infrastructure and health care providers during the COVID-19 pandemic [S7]. A joint CISA/FBI/HHS advisory warned of an imminent Trickbot and Ryuk threat to US hospitals in October 2020 [S5]. Mandiant found that nearly 20% of directly observed FIN12 victims were in healthcare [S10], but FIN12 is a separate, affiliated cluster.

capabilities.summary: The group develops and operates modular malware and loaders (Trickbot, BazaLoader, AnchorDNS) and manages ransomware programs (Ryuk, Conti, Diavol) [S1][S2]. Its DEV-0365 subgroup provides Cobalt Strike Beacon command-and-control as a service [S2]. In the typical Trickbot/Ryuk chain described by CISA, FBI and HHS, a malicious email installs Emotet and/or Trickbot, Trickbot moves laterally, disables protections and steals data, and Ryuk then encrypts systems [S5]. In 2021 its infrastructure hosted BazaLoader and Trickbot payloads alongside oleObjects used in CVE-2021-40444 (MSHTML) exploitation [S3]. The group recruits talent from other malware operations (Emotet, Qakbot, IcedID) [S1][S2], and the BKA said the group had more than 100 members at times [S9]. MITRE ATT&CK tracks the broader Wizard Spider cluster as G0102 [S11].

campaigns.summary: Germany's BKA named Vitaly Nikolaevich Kovalev, alias 'Stern', as the suspected founder of the Trickbot group, during an Operation Endgame round (reported by Heise) [S9].

diamond.adversary: A Russia-based, financially motivated criminal enterprise (Trickbot LLC) whose BKA-named suspected leader is 'Stern' [S1][S7][S9]. The BKA said it had more than 100 members at times [S9].
diamond.capability: Trickbot, BazaLoader, AnchorDNS, Ryuk, Conti, Diavol, and Cobalt Strike Beacon as a service [S1][S2]. Infrastructure overlapped with CVE-2021-40444 exploitation [S3].
diamond.infrastructure: Trickbot botnet C2, which Microsoft and partners targeted in 2020 [S4]. DEV-0365 Cobalt Strike C2-as-a-service [S2]. Infrastructure that hosted MSHTML exploit documents also delivered BazaLoader and Trickbot payloads [S3].
diamond.victim: Healthcare and public health, education, US critical infrastructure, and government institutions (Costa Rica) [S1][S5][S7][S8].
diamond.socioPolitical: Ransomware-as-a-service gig economy relationships with affiliates and access brokers [S2]. Members operate from Russia beyond Western arrest [S9]. Pro-Russia stance by Conti in 2022 triggered an insider leak [S8].
diamond.technology: Windows enterprise networks reached via malicious email, commodity loaders and lateral movement before encryption [S5]. Microsoft Office/MSHTML exploitation (CVE-2021-40444) [S3].

gaps: Microsoft's current mapping splits Wizard Spider/Conti names across Periwinkle Tempest, Storm-0230 and Pistachio Tempest; how much of MITRE G0102 activity belongs to Periwinkle Tempest specifically is unresolved.

Primary US government documents (Treasury press releases, DOJ indictments, the CISA advisory page, the State Department reward notice) could not be opened; facts rely on secondary coverage or AHA's copy.
BKA primary statement not reviewed; the exact date of the Kovalev/Stern announcement (late May 2025) is unverified.
No sourced reporting found on Periwinkle Tempest-branded activity after 2024 (e.g., successor ransomware brands, current loaders).
FIN12/UNC1878 overlap: Microsoft says DEV-0193 overlaps UNC1878 [S3], but Mandiant treats FIN12 as a Ryuk-deploying affiliate; the precise relationship is unclear.
MITRE G0102 page not fetched for this file; the software list comes from the imported record.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Step 1 (operational environment): Treat the defense industrial base, base hospitals and medical treatment facilities, and education and training enclaves on commercial or DODIN-adjacent networks as in scope, since the group has hit healthcare, education and critical infrastructure [S1][S5][S7]. Step 2 (effects): Ransomware encryption of Windows enterprise systems can degrade medical, logistics and administrative mission support, and the Costa Rica case shows national government services can be disrupted [S5][S8]. Step 3 (adversary model): Email-delivered loaders (Emotet/Trickbot/BazaLoader) lead to Cobalt Strike, then lateral movement, then data theft, then Ryuk/Conti-family encryption. Access is often shared or sold to affiliates [S2][S5]. Step 4 (courses of action): The most likely course of action is opportunistic loader infection of a mission-partner or support network, followed by affiliate ransomware within days. The most dangerous is a time-sensitive ransomware event against healthcare or a critical-infrastructure dependency (power, water, comms supporting an installation) during a crisis or surge, timed for maximum leverage, as with the 2020 hospital threat [S5][S7]. Candidate indicators: Trickbot/BazaLoader/AnchorDNS artifacts; Cobalt Strike Beacon C2 matching DEV-0365 patterns; malicious Office documents exploiting MSHTML; and protection tampering before encryption [S2][S3][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: Fuse Microsoft, CISA/FBI and vendor indicators for Trickbot-lineage loaders and Cobalt Strike-as-a-service infrastructure into DODIN and mission-partner monitoring [S2][S3][S5]. Authorities: This is a criminal actor, so the primary responses are law enforcement (DOJ indictments, BKA/Operation Endgame), sanctions (OFAC/UK) and private civil action (Microsoft's 2020 court order) [S4][S7][S9]. Any DoD role should be coordinated through those lanes and existing defense-support authorities. Mission assurance: Prioritize backup integrity and recovery for medical and logistics systems and plan for loss of supporting civilian infrastructure, given healthcare and critical-infrastructure targeting [S5][S7]. Coordination: Coordinate with CISA, FBI, HHS (for medical facilities) and allied partners such as the UK and Germany, who have acted jointly against the group [S5][S7][S9].

provenance.importedSummary: GRIM SPIDER is a sophisticated eCrime group that has been operating the Ryuk ransomware since August 2018, targeting large organizations for a high-ransom return. This methodology, known as “big game hunting,” signals a shift in operations for WIZARD SPIDER, a criminal enterprise of which GRIM SPIDER appears to be a cell. The WIZARD SPIDER threat group, known as the Russia-based operator of the TrickBot banking malware, had focused primarily on wire fraud in the past. Similar to Samas and BitPaymer, Ryuk is specifically used to target enterprise environments. Code comparison between versions of Ryuk and Hermes ransomware indicates that Ryuk was derived from the Hermes source code and has been under steady development since its release. Hermes is commodity ransomware that has been observed for sale on forums and used by multiple threat actors. However, Ryuk is only used by GRIM SPIDER and, unlike Hermes, Ryuk has only been used to target enterprise environments. Since Ryuk’s appearance in August, the threat actors operating it have netted over 705.80 BTC across 52 transactions for a total current value of $3,701,893.98 USD. Grim Spider is reportedly associated with Lunar Spider and Wizard Spider.

identification.summary: Iranian threat actor that Microsoft tracks as Pink Sandstorm (also known as Agrius) [S2]; public reporting has linked it to Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS) [S3]. It is known for destructive wiper and fake-ransomware operations focused on Israeli targets since 2020 [S3][S4]. Over time its operations moved from wipers disguised as ransomware (DEADWOOD, Apostle) to supply-chain wiper deployment (Fantasy, 2022), new ransomware (Moneybird, 2023), and data theft followed by wiping in Israeli higher education and technology (2023) [S4][S6][S7][S9]. In December 2023 Israel's National Cyber Directorate named Agrius, working with Hezbollah's Lebanese Cedar, in a late-November 2023 attack on Ziv Medical Center [S10].
identification.firstObserved: SentinelLabs observed Agrius operating in Israel starting in 2020 [S4]. MITRE also dates the group's activity to 2020 [S3].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Pink Sandstorm (formerly AMERICIUM). Microsoft lists SPECTRAL KITTEN, Agrius, Deadwood, BlackShadow, SharpBoys, FireAnt and Justice Blade as other names [S2]. Palo Alto Unit 42 tracks the group as Agonizing Serpens and equates it with Agrius, BlackShadow, Pink Sandstorm and DEV-0022 [S9]. MITRE tracks it as Agrius (G1030) [S3]. Check Point says the group has operated under multiple aliases and leaked Moneybird victim data through one of its previous personas [S7][S8]. BlackShadow is the persona that extorted Israeli insurer Shirbit in 2020 [S8].

attribution.sponsor: Iran, Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS). MITRE notes that public reporting has linked Agrius to MOIS [S3]. Israel's National Cyber Directorate (INCD), as reported by the press, described Agrius as affiliated with the Iranian Ministry of Intelligence [S10].
attribution.confidence: SentinelLabs (2021) assessed with medium confidence that Agrius is of Iranian origin [S4]. Check Point (2023) said the group's affiliation was not fully clear [S8]. The INCD attribution of the Ziv Medical Center attack is an Israeli government statement reported by the press [S10]; no US government attribution was found in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Vendor incident response and malware analysis (SentinelLabs, ESET, Check Point, Unit 42) [S4][S6][S7][S9]; INCD statement on the Ziv Medical Center incident, based on a joint investigation with the IDF and Shin Bet [S10].

actors.objectives: Disruption and destruction against Israeli organizations, with ransomware used as cover rather than for profit; SentinelLabs judged it unlikely that Agrius is financially motivated [S4]. Espionage and data theft come before destructive operations [S4][S9].

sectors: HR consulting and IT support services [S6]
targeting.notes: Israel is the consistent focus across all vendor reporting [S3][S4][S9]. Victims outside Israel came through the 2022 supply-chain compromise of an Israeli software developer [S6]. Check Point did not specify which sectors Moneybird hit [S8].

capabilities.summary: Initial access usually comes through internet-facing web servers and known vulnerabilities, including FortiOS CVE-2018-13379, and is followed by ASPXSpy web shells [S5][S7]. After access the group uses public tools for lateral movement, credential harvesting and exfiltration [S7]. Its custom destructive tooling has evolved over time: the DEADWOOD wiper; the .NET Apostle wiper, which later gained working ransomware encryption; and the IPsec Helper .NET backdoor [S4]. Fantasy, a wiper built from Apostle code, was pushed through a compromised Israeli software vendor's updates; the campaign lasted under three hours [S6]. Moneybird is C++ ransomware using AES-256 GCM [S7][S8]. In 2023 the group used the MultiLayer, PartialWasher and BFG Agonizer wipers and the Sqlextractor database-theft tool. It also switched between public proof-of-concept tools and custom code to evade EDR [S9].

gaps: No Microsoft reporting on Pink Sandstorm operations was verified during fact-check; Microsoft detail here is limited to the naming page [S2].
Microsoft alias list includes Justice Blade, SharpBoys and FireAnt, but no cited source describes the operations behind those personas [S2].

Attribution of the Ziv Medical Center incident: the INCD named Agrius with Lebanese Cedar, while a separate 'Malek Team' persona claimed a data leak; press reporting does not settle whether these are one operation [S10].
No 2024-2026 Pink Sandstorm operational reporting (for example during the 2025 Israel-Iran conflict) was found in the searches run.
The SentinelLabs confidence assessment is medium, and Check Point in 2023 called the affiliation not fully clear; no US government attribution was located [S4][S8].
The Unit 42 alias DEV-0022 and the Malpedia aliases DEV-0227 are not confirmed against Microsoft's current mapping [S2][S9].
Vendor profiles of UAE targeting were seen in search results but not verified from primary reporting, so the UAE is excluded from regions.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): Key terrain includes internet-facing web servers and VPN appliances, software vendors' update channels and database servers at Israeli and partner organizations [S5][S6][S7][S9]. The environment also includes the information space, where leak personas publish stolen data [S8]. STEP 2 (effects): Unpatched public-facing applications and trusted update paths let the actor turn one intrusion into many victims within hours [S6]. Ransomware branding hides state intent and complicates attribution and response priorities [S4]. STEP 3 (threat model): web-server exploit, then ASPXSpy web shell, then credential harvesting and lateral movement with public tools, then data theft (including Sqlextractor), then wiper or ransomware deployment and a leak via a persona [S7][S9]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is continued data theft followed by wiping or fake ransomware against Israeli education, technology and healthcare targets, amplified through hack-and-leak during periods of Israel-Iran tension [S9][S10]. MDCOA is a supply-chain wiper push through a trusted vendor, or a joint operation with Hezbollah-linked cyber actors such as Lebanese Cedar, hitting healthcare or partner-nation organizations at scale, including entities outside Israel [S6][S10]. Candidate indicators: ASPXSpy web shells on IIS servers; exploitation of known FortiOS or web-application CVEs; credential harvesting tools appearing weeks before a destructive event [S6]; new ransomware families with no payment infrastructure; and leak-persona claims after intrusions [S5][S7][S8].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: Track Israeli INCD and vendor reporting (Unit 42, Check Point, ESET), because the group's operations are usually first exposed through incident response [S6][S7][S9][S10]. Treat a 'ransomware' event at an Israel-linked or partner organization as possibly state-directed destruction [S4]. Authorities: The 'ransomware' framing can steer cases toward criminal channels. Coordinating early with intelligence and partner-nation cyber authorities supports a correct attribution and response posture [S4][S10]. Mission assurance: Prioritize patching internet-facing servers, monitoring for web shells, verifying the integrity of third-party software updates and maintaining offline backups for mission-relevant databases [S6][S7][S9]. Coordination: The INCD attributed the Ziv Medical Center attack to Agrius working with Hezbollah's Lebanese Cedar, so combined Iran-proxy activity needs coordination across CCMD and partner-nation boundaries, with information sharing with Israeli partners [S10].

identification.summary: PlushDaemon is a China-aligned APT group that has conducted cyberespionage operations against targets in China, Taiwan, Hong Kong, South Korea, the United States, and New Zealand. They executed a supply chain attack on the South Korean VPN provider IPany, compromising its installer to deploy the SlowStepper backdoor, which features a toolkit of over 30 components. puNK-003 is a North Korean APT group known for deploying the Lilith RAT, a sophisticated C++ remote access trojan, and its AutoIt variant, CURKON, which functions as a downloader. The group primarily distributes malware through targeted phishing attacks using malicious LNK files. Analysis indicates that puNK-003 shares similarities with the KONNI group, particularly in the use of AutoIt scripts and specific coding functions. Key indicators of infection include unusual network activity and system slowdowns, with removal methods involving specialized antivirus software and manual techniques.

China-based cyber-espionage actor that Microsoft tracks as Purple Typhoon (formerly POTASSIUM), mapped to APT10, menuPass, Stone Panda and Red Apollo [S1]. US prosecutors allege APT10 intrusions from about 2006 through 2018 aimed at intellectual property and confidential business information, including against managed service providers (MSPs), more than 45 technology companies and US government agencies [S2]. The group is best known for Operation Cloud Hopper, a sustained campaign against global MSPs and their clients [S4][S3], and has repeatedly targeted Japanese organizations [S5][S6][S7].
identification.firstObserved: DOJ indictment alleges activity from about 2006 [S2]; FireEye stated it had tracked APT10 since 2009 [S6]; Unit 42 reported Japanese targeting since at least 2014 [S5].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Purple Typhoon (formerly POTASSIUM); Microsoft's mapping lists POTASSIUM, STONE PANDA, GOLEM, Evilgrab, AEON, LIVESAFE, ChChes, APT10, Haymaker, Webmonder, Foxtrot, Foxmail, MenuPass and Red Apollo [S1]. Symantec tracks the actor as Cicada [S7][S8]. Several mapped names (ChChes, Evilgrab, Haymaker) are malware family names rather than vendor cluster names [S1][S5]. MirrorFace / Earth Kasha is assessed by Japan's NPA as a sub-group within the APT10 umbrella [S9]; it is kept as a related cluster here, not merged.

Later campaigns collected information from government, legal, religious and NGO organizations [S8]; the MirrorFace sub-group is assessed to target Japanese national-security and advanced-technology information [S9].

gaps: Primary DOJ indictment text and gov.uk statement were seen only in search results and summaries, not opened; quoted wording comes from search-result excerpts [S2][S3].
Microsoft has published little public reporting under the Purple Typhoon name; this profile relies on Microsoft's naming mapping plus other vendors' reporting [S1].

Cluster boundaries: Trend Micro describes APT10 as an umbrella with Earth Kasha (LODEINFO, NOOPDOOR) and Earth Tengshe (SigLoader, SodaMaster) sub-clusters; MirrorFace/Earth Kasha's relation to Purple Typhoon in Microsoft's taxonomy is not stated in the sources gathered. Trend Micro's original reports were not retrieved.
Start date of Cloud Hopper differs: UK NCSC says since at least 2016, while other reporting cites 2014 [S3].

Symantec's original 2020 and 2022 Cicada blogs, the ESET AkaiRyu blog and the Japanese NPA report could not be fetched (host resolution errors); details come from coverage and vendor press releases [S7][S8][S9][S11].
Activity attributed specifically to Purple Typhoon after 2022 (outside the MirrorFace sub-group) is not documented in the sources gathered.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key cyber terrain includes MSP and IT-outsourcing remote-administration channels, domain controllers and Exchange/mail servers supporting defense and DIB networks [S4][S7][S8]. STEP 2: Trust relationships with service providers bypass perimeter defenses; unpatched Zerologon and Exchange exposure shorten time-to-compromise [S4][S7][S8]. STEP 3: Doctrinal template is spear-phishing or public-facing exploit, then DLL side-loaded RAT (PlugX, ANEL, Hartip), credential theft, lateral movement via MSP access, and staged exfiltration of IP and policy documents [S4][S5][S6][S7][S8]. STEP 4: MLCOA is long-dwell espionage against contractors and allied (especially Japanese) partners through MSP and mail-server access to collect technology and national-security information [S2][S7][S9]. MDCOA is simultaneous compromise of multiple shared service providers to gain persistent access across many DoD-adjacent customers before a crisis [S4][S3]. Candidate indicators: anomalous MSP admin-account logons outside maintenance windows, legitimate binaries (e.g., VLC) loading unsigned DLLs from user paths, Zerologon exploitation events on domain controllers, password-protected macro documents with diplomatic or maritime lures, and VS Code tunnel traffic from servers [S6][S7][S8][S11].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: map which mission systems depend on third-party MSPs and track their compromise reporting, since victims in Cloud Hopper were reached through providers [S4]. (2) Authorities: activity against contractor and MSP networks falls outside DODIN boundaries; coordinate via DC3/DIB CS, FBI and partner-nation agencies (NCSC, NPA) that have attributed this actor [S2][S3][S9]. (3) Mission assurance: prioritize patching and monitoring of domain controllers and Exchange servers, the observed entry points [S7][S8]. (4) Coordination: Japan-focused targeting makes combined information sharing with Japanese partners relevant for INDOPACOM-supporting networks [S7][S9][S11].
