identification.summary: Russian state cyber-espionage actor that Microsoft tracks as Secret Blizzard and other vendors track as Turla, Snake, Uroburos, Venomous Bear and Waterbug [S1][S2][S4]. Microsoft says it seeks long-term access to systems for intelligence collection, generally looking for information of political importance, and it targets foreign affairs ministries, embassies, government offices and defense organizations worldwide [S2]. It regularly takes over the tools and infrastructure of other threat actors; Microsoft counts at least six such actors over seven years [S2]. Its flagship Kazuar backdoor has grown into a modular peer-to-peer botnet [S4]. In 2025 Microsoft confirmed for the first time that it can operate adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) attacks at the internet service provider (ISP) level inside Russia [S1].
identification.firstObserved: ESET describes Turla as operating since at least 2004 [S5]. The French C4 says it has observed Turla targeting France since 2010 [S7].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Secret Blizzard. Microsoft lists the overlapping names VENOMOUS BEAR, Uroburos, Snake, Blue Python, Turla, Wraith, ATG26 and Waterbug [S1]. MITRE tracks the group as Turla (G0010). 'Snake' names both the actor (in some vendor reporting) and its long-running implant, which the US disrupted in 2023 [S6]. Kaspersky's WhiteBear is described as a parallel project or second stage of its Skipper Turla cluster, with a separate target focus [S9]. Microsoft tracks Storm-0156, Storm-1919 (Amadey), Storm-1837 and Aqua Blizzard as separate actors whose access Secret Blizzard has piggybacked on; they are not aliases [S2][S3][S4].

attribution.sponsor: Russian Federation, Federal Security Service (FSB) Center 16. Microsoft cites CISA's attribution of Secret Blizzard to FSB Center 16 [S1][S2][S4], and US court documents in Operation MEDUSA attribute the Snake malware to a unit within FSB Center 16 [S6]. France's Cyber Crisis Coordination Centre (C4) attributes Turla to the FSB's 16th Centre [S7].
attribution.confidence: US government: attribution to FSB Center 16, stated in the 2023 MEDUSA court-authorized operation and the joint advisory, as reported by press [S6]. France: formal national attribution by the C4 on 2026-07-13, issued the same day as a French Foreign Ministry attribution statement and an EU High Representative statement [S7][S8]. Microsoft relies on CISA's attribution rather than stating its own confidence level [S1][S4]. ESET assesses with high confidence that Gamaredon collaborates with Turla [S5].
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and joint analysis with Lumen Black Lotus Labs [S2][S3]; FBI technical operation against the Snake peer-to-peer network [S6]; French C4 and Foreign Ministry attribution statements [S7][S8]; ESET telemetry from Ukrainian machines [S5]; Kaspersky reporting on WhiteBear [S9].

actors.objectives: Strategic political and military intelligence collection through long-term, covert access [S2]. Priorities include foreign ministries, embassies and diplomats, including foreign embassies in Moscow [S1][S2]; Ukrainian military devices, including front-line systems [S3]; and government, diplomatic and defense targets in Europe and Central Asia [S4]. US court documents describe the group stealing sensitive documents from hundreds of systems in at least 50 countries [S6].

sectors: Foreign affairs ministries and embassies / diplomatic entities [S1][S2][S9]
Defense and military organizations, including Ukrainian military devices [S2][S3]
Intelligence services (Afghan General Directorate of Intelligence) [S2]
regions: At least 50 countries, including the United States, per US court documents (as reported) [S6]
targeting.notes: Tasking is selective. ESET saw Turla on only seven machines in Ukraine over about 18 months, against much wider Gamaredon compromise [S5]. Microsoft saw a custom survey tool deployed selectively to devices connecting from Starlink IP addresses, which Microsoft describes as a common signature of Ukrainian front-line military devices [S3]. In India, Secret Blizzard mostly harvested data that Storm-0156 had already staged rather than deploying malware directly [S2].

capabilities.summary: Kazuar is a modular peer-to-peer botnet built from Kernel, Bridge and Worker modules. A single elected Kernel leader limits outbound traffic, internal traffic uses Window Messaging, Mailslot and named pipes, and external C2 uses HTTP, WebSockets or Exchange Web Services [S4]. Delivery uses droppers such as Pelmeni, whose payload is often encrypted against the target's hostname [S4]. The group hijacks other actors' access: Storm-0156 C2 servers since November 2022 (using TwoDash, Statuezy, MiniPocket and a TinyTurla fork) [S2], Amadey bots and a Storm-1837 backdoor in Ukraine in 2024 to install Tavdig and KazuarV2 [S3], and Gamaredon tools that launched or installed Kazuar in 2025 [S5]. ApolloShadow malware, delivered through ISP-level AiTM and a captive-portal redirect, installs a trusted root certificate disguised as a Kaspersky installer, enabling TLS stripping; it also creates a local admin account named UpdatusUser [S1]. Microsoft assesses that this AiTM position is likely enabled by lawful-intercept systems, possibly SORM [S1]. The Snake implant ran a covert peer-to-peer network across compromised computers until the FBI disabled it in 2023 [S6]. Earlier operations used hijacked satellite connections and compromised websites for C2 [S9].

The French Foreign Ministry and the EU High Representative issued attribution statements the same day; the Foreign Ministry cites targeting of Armed Forces Ministry email accounts since 2017, the French Embassy in Moscow network (2018) and a judicial-sector server (2019).

diamond.adversary: FSB Center 16 operators tracked as Secret Blizzard / Turla [S1][S6][S7].
diamond.capability: Kazuar P2P botnet, Tavdig, TwoDash, Statuezy, MiniPocket, TinyTurla variants, ApolloShadow and the Snake implant; hijacking other actors' footholds; ISP-level AiTM [S1][S2][S3][S4][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: Commandeered C2 and footholds belonging to Storm-0156, Amadey (Storm-1919), Storm-1837 and Gamaredon [S2][S3][S5]; Kazuar P2P relays with HTTP, WebSocket and EWS C2 [S4]; Snake's covert P2P network [S6]; ISP-level interception position in Russia [S1]; compromised websites and hijacked satellite links in earlier activity [S9].
diamond.victim: Foreign ministries, embassies and diplomats (including in Moscow), government ministries, defense organizations and defense research, Ukrainian front-line military devices, and Afghan and Indian government and military targets [S1][S2][S3][S7][S8].
diamond.socioPolitical: Russian strategic intelligence requirements on foreign policy, NATO and European governments, and the war in Ukraine [S1][S3][S4][S7].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints and Exchange Web Services [S4]; TLS trust stores and captive-portal flows on ISP-provided connections [S1]; Starlink-connected field devices [S3].

gaps: Primary US documents (the DOJ MEDUSA announcement and the joint Snake advisory) were not opened; their details come from press coverage [S6]. The advisory identifier AA23-129A and the Ryazan facility detail were not verified.

The French C4 statement and the CERT-FR report (CERTFR-2026-CTI-004/005) could not be fetched; details come from search summaries of the C4 and French Foreign Ministry statements [S7][S8]. Press mentions of a specific FSB unit number (Unit 61240), a twelve-country scope and Polish water and energy sabotage are unverified. The sabotage claims may belong to a different FSB Center 16 activity set or EU statement, so do not attach them to Turla without the primary text.
The ESET Gamaredon x Turla report was not opened; findings come from search summaries of the ESET blog and press release [S5].
How Secret Blizzard gained control of the Storm-1837 backdoor and Amadey bots was still under investigation at the time Microsoft published [S3].
Microsoft's assessment that SORM or lawful-intercept systems enable the ISP-level AiTM is a likelihood judgement, not a confirmed mechanism [S1].
A CrowdStrike report dated July 2026 appeared in aggregator results but was not reviewed.
The Kaspersky WhiteBear URL and content come from the imported actor record; the publication month (2017-08) was not re-verified [S9].
Most aliases in the imported record (e.g., ATK13, ITG12, SIG23, UAC-0003/0024/0144, UNC4210) were not confirmed by the sources gathered here.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (environment): key terrain includes diplomatic and government networks, defense research enclaves, Exchange/EWS services, TLS trust stores, and host-nation ISP links serving deployed or diplomatic personnel, especially inside Russia [S1][S4][S8]. STEP 2 (effects): host-nation telecommunications cannot be trusted; ISP-level AiTM plus a rogue root certificate exposes credentials and tokens in transit [S1]. Footholds left by lower-tier actors (criminal botnets, other APTs) can become entry points for this actor [S2][S3][S5]. STEP 3 (threat model): access is gained by piggybacking on an existing foothold or by AiTM/captive-portal lure, followed by a loader (Tavdig, Pelmeni) and then the Kazuar P2P botnet, with an elected leader keeping C2 traffic low, and selective collection [S1][S3][S4]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is quiet, long-term collection from a small number of high-value diplomatic, government and defense hosts, plus selective targeting of front-line military devices in Ukraine [S2][S3][S5]. MDCOA is covert interception of coalition planning traffic through compromised ISP or host-nation infrastructure and in-memory implants on mission-relevant networks, giving persistent awareness of intentions during a crisis [S1][S4]. Candidate indicators: unexpected root certificates (including fake Kaspersky-branded installers), a local account named UpdatusUser, captive-portal redirects to unfamiliar domains, internal Mailslot or named-pipe chatter between hosts paired with a single host making outbound HTTP/WebSocket/EWS connections, and Tavdig/Kazuar artifacts on hosts already infected with commodity malware [S1][S3][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: treat any detection of commodity malware (e.g., Amadey) or another APT's implant on mission or partner networks as a possible Secret Blizzard staging point, and escalate hunting accordingly [S2][S3][S5]. (2) Authorities: the 2023 MEDUSA operation shows US law-enforcement authorities can disrupt this actor's infrastructure [S6]. Coordinate DoD defensive actions with FBI/DOJ and with allied attributions such as France's 2026 statement [S7]. (3) Mission assurance: personnel and devices operating on host-nation networks in Russia or contested regions should tunnel all traffic to trusted networks, as Microsoft recommends, and certificate-store monitoring should be part of baseline hardening [S1]. Starlink-connected tactical devices are a demonstrated reconnaissance filter for this actor [S3]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with State Department and embassy IT, allied CERTs (e.g., CERT-FR), Ukrainian partners and DIB partners, because victims span diplomatic, defense-industrial and coalition military domains [S1][S3][S7][S8].

sources.title: Introducing WhiteBear

provenance.importedSummary: As a part of our Kaspersky APT Intelligence Reporting subscription, customers received an update in mid-February 2017 on some interesting APT activity that we called WhiteBear. Much of the contents of that report are reproduced here. WhiteBear is a parallel project or second stage of the Skipper Turla cluster of activity documented in another private intelligence report “Skipper Turla – the White Atlas framework” from mid-2016. Like previous Turla activity, WhiteBear leverages compromised websites and hijacked satellite connections for command and control (C2) infrastructure. As a matter of fact, WhiteBear infrastructure has overlap with other Turla campaigns, like those deploying Kopiluwak, as documented in “KopiLuwak – A New JavaScript Payload from Turla” in December 2016. WhiteBear infected systems maintained a dropper (which was typically signed) as well as a complex malicious platform which was always preceded by WhiteAtlas module deployment attempts. However, despite the similarities to previous Turla campaigns, we believe that WhiteBear is a distinct project with a separate focus. We note that this observation of delineated target focus, tooling, and project context is an interesting one that also can be repeated across broadly labeled Turla and Sofacy activity. From February to September 2016, WhiteBear activity was narrowly focused on embassies and consular operations around the world. All of these early WhiteBear targets were related to embassies and diplomatic/foreign affair organizations. Continued WhiteBear activity later shifted to include defense-related organizations into June 2017. When compared to WhiteAtlas infections, WhiteBear deployments are relatively rare and represent a departure from the broader Skipper Turla target set. Additionally, a comparison of the WhiteAtlas framework to WhiteBear components indicates that the malware is the product of separate development efforts. WhiteBear infections appear to be preceded by a condensed spearphishing dropper, lack Firefox extension installer payloads, and contain several new components signed with a new code signing digital certificate, unlike WhiteAtlas incidents and modules.

identification.summary: SHADOW-EARTH-053 is a China-aligned threat group exploiting unpatched Microsoft Exchange Server vulnerabilities, specifically CVE-2021-26855, to conduct cyberespionage against government and defense-linked targets across Asia and Europe. The group primarily deploys ShadowPad malware, utilizing techniques such as credential dumping, tunneling tools, and lateral movement via WMIC. They have also been observed installing web shells for persistence and leveraging a custom ExchangeExport tool to extract high-value mailbox contents. Additionally, low-confidence associations with Noodle RAT and CVE-2025-55182 have been noted in their operations.

The cyberattack campaign that Microsoft uncovered was launched by a China-linked hacking group called Storm-0062. According to the company, the group is launching cyberattacks by exploiting a vulnerability in the Data Center and Server editions of Confluence. Those are versions of the application that companies run on-premises.

ShaggyPanther is a threat actor that primarily targets government entities in Taiwan and Malaysia. They have been active since 2008 and utilize hidden encrypted payloads in registry keys. Their activities have been detected in various locations, including Indonesia and Syria.

Shahid Hemmat is an IRGC-CEC affiliated hacking group linked to cyberattacks targeting U.S. critical infrastructure, including the defense industry and international transportation sectors. The group has been implicated in the hack of a booster station at the Municipal Water Authority in Aliquippa, Pennsylvania, which disrupted drinking water supply. Key figures within Shahid Hemmat include Manouchehr Akbari, Amir Hossein Hoseini, Mohammad Hossein Moradi, and Mohammad Reza Rafatnejad. The U.S. government is offering a $10 million reward for information on these individuals.
Shamoon Group is an Iran-linked threat actor associated with destructive Shamoon wiper operations targeting organizations in the Middle East, especially in the energy sector.

This group's activity was first observed in November 2013. It leverages a banking Trojan more commonly known as Shylock which aims to compromise online banking credentials and credentials related to Bitcoin wallets.

SharpPanda, an APT group originating from China, has seen a rise in its cyber-attack operations starting from at least 2018. The APT group utilizes spear-phishing techniques to obtain initial access, employing a combination of outdated Microsoft Office document vulnerabilities, novel evasion techniques, and highly potent backdoor malware.

Last Friday, Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein announced the indictment of nine Iranians who worked for an organization named the Mabna Institute. According to prosecutors, the defendants stole more than 31 terabytes of data from universities, companies, and government agencies around the world. The cost to the universities alone reportedly amounted to approximately $3.4 billion. The information stolen from these universities was used by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) or sold for profit inside Iran. PhishLabs has been tracking this same threat group since late-2017, designating them Silent Librarian. Since discovery, we have been working with the FBI, ISAC partners, and other international law enforcement agencies to help understand and mitigate these attacks.

Silk Typhoon (formerly HAFNIUM) is a Chinese espionage group. Microsoft describes it as well-resourced and technically efficient, able to quickly operationalize exploits for zero-day vulnerabilities in edge devices, and holding one of the largest targeting footprints among Chinese threat actors [S1]. It is best known for exploiting four on-premises Exchange Server zero-days in early 2021 [S1][S2]. Since late 2024 Microsoft has observed it shift toward IT supply-chain compromise: it steals API keys and credentials from privileged access management (PAM), remote monitoring and management, cloud application and cloud data management providers, then uses them to reach those providers' downstream customers [S1].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft says it has tracked the actor since 2020 and observed Exchange zero-day exploitation beginning in January 2021 [S1]. The US indictment of two alleged HAFNIUM operators covers intrusions from February 2020 to June 2021, as reported by the press [S3].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Silk Typhoon (formerly HAFNIUM) [S1]. CrowdStrike tracks MURKY PANDA, active since at least 2023, and says that cluster's activity aligns with what industry tracks as Silk Typhoon. This is an overlap statement, not an identity [S5][S6]. MITRE tracks the group as HAFNIUM (G0125) [S10]. Some press coverage of the March 2025 APT27 / i-Soon indictments labels Yin Kecheng and Zhou Shuai 'Silk Typhoon', while other coverage of the same indictments uses APT27 and lists aliases such as Emissary Panda and Lucky Mouse. Those aliases sit under Linen Typhoon in this encyclopedia; see gaps [S9].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China, Ministry of State Security (MSS). A US indictment unsealed in July 2025 alleges that Xu Zewei and Zhang Yu acted at the direction of the MSS Shanghai State Security Bureau. Xu allegedly worked through Shanghai Powerock Network Co. Ltd., which prosecutors called an 'enabling' company (as reported by the press) [S3][S4].
attribution.confidence: In 2021 Microsoft attributed the Exchange campaign to HAFNIUM with high confidence, as a group assessed to be state-sponsored and operating out of China [S2]. In 2025 Microsoft called Silk Typhoon a Chinese state actor but stated no confidence level [S1]. The US government has charged alleged HAFNIUM operators criminally, which is an indictment, not a conviction [S3][S4]. Linking the 2024 Treasury breach to Silk Typhoon rests on Bloomberg reporting citing people familiar with the incident [S7].
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and incident analysis [S1][S2]; a DOJ indictment and the extradition of Xu Zewei from Italy, known here through press coverage [S3][S4]; and CrowdStrike reporting on the overlapping MURKY PANDA cluster [S5][S6].

actors.objectives: Espionage. Microsoft says the data it seeks overlaps with China-based interests, US government policy and administration, and legal process and documents tied to law enforcement investigations [S1]. In 2020 the group allegedly sought COVID-19 vaccine, treatment and testing research from US universities, including one in Texas (as reported from the indictment) [S3][S4]. In the 2024 Treasury intrusion the group reportedly accessed unclassified information on potential sanctions actions [S7].

sectors: IT services and infrastructure, including MSPs and RMM providers [S1]
PAM, identity management, cloud application and cloud data management providers [S1][S5]
Government, including US federal (Treasury) and state and local [S1][S7]
Healthcare and infectious-disease or COVID-19 researchers [S1][S2][S3]
regions: Worldwide; Microsoft says targets are in the US and worldwide [S1]
targeting.notes: Microsoft says downstream victims of the late-2024 supply-chain activity were mostly state and local government and the IT sector [S1]. The FBI said the 2021 Exchange campaign victimized more than 12,700 US organizations (as reported in press coverage of the DOJ case) [S4].

capabilities.summary: Edge-device and server exploitation: Exchange CVE-2021-26855, -26857, -26858 and -27065 (2021); Citrix NetScaler CVE-2023-3519 and zero-days (early 2024); Palo Alto GlobalProtect CVE-2024-3400 (March 2024); and an Ivanti Connect Secure zero-day, CVE-2025-0282 (January 2025) [S1][S2]. CrowdStrike says MURKY PANDA also used zero-days against SaaS providers, and coverage of its report includes a Commvault product zero-day [S5][S6]. Credential access includes password spraying and corporate passwords leaked on public repositories such as GitHub [S1]. Post-exploitation includes web shells, Active Directory dumping, theft of key-vault secrets, and LSASS dumping with Procdump [S1][S2]. In 2021 the group used Covenant C2, Nishang and PowerCat, staged data with 7-Zip and exfiltrated to MEGA [S2]. The group moves from on-premises to cloud through AADConnect/Entra Connect servers. It abuses service principals and OAuth apps (including by adding credentials to already-consented apps) to pull mail, OneDrive and SharePoint data through Microsoft Graph and EWS, and it creates Entra ID apps disguised as legitimate services [S1]. It has abused delegated administrative privileges held by a Microsoft cloud solution provider [S5][S6]. For anti-forensics it clears logs and modifies timestamps [S1][S5]. Its toolset includes the Neo-reGeorg web shell and a Golang Linux RAT that CrowdStrike calls CloudedHope [S5][S6].

campaigns.name: COVID-19 research intrusions
campaigns.summary: The alleged operators Xu Zewei and Zhang Yu targeted US universities and immunology and virology researchers, including a Texas university, to obtain COVID-19 research, reportedly under MSS Shanghai State Security Bureau direction (as reported from the indictment).

campaigns.name: Exchange Server zero-day campaign (ProxyLogon chain)
campaigns.summary: Microsoft attributes exploitation of four on-premises Exchange zero-days, followed by web shells, LSASS dumping and mailbox exfiltration, to HAFNIUM. The FBI later said more than 12,700 US entities were victimized.

campaigns.name: Citrix NetScaler and GlobalProtect exploitation
campaigns.summary: Microsoft observed exploitation of NetScaler zero-days and of CVE-2023-3519, and in March 2024 zero-day exploitation of Palo Alto GlobalProtect CVE-2024-3400.

campaigns.name: US Treasury breach via BeyondTrust API key
campaigns.summary: A stolen BeyondTrust Remote Support SaaS API key gave access to Treasury workstations, including OFAC. Bloomberg attributed the breach to Silk Typhoon, citing people familiar with the incident. In January 2025 Treasury sanctioned Yin Kecheng over the Departmental Offices compromise; Treasury did not name Silk Typhoon in the sources gathered.

campaigns.name: IT supply-chain compromise
campaigns.summary: Microsoft says the group used API keys and credentials stolen from PAM, cloud application and data-management providers to access downstream tenants, mostly state and local government and IT-sector victims.

campaigns.name: Ivanti Connect Secure zero-day (CVE-2025-0282)
campaigns.summary: Microsoft observed zero-day exploitation by Silk Typhoon and reported the flaw to Ivanti, which fixed it.

campaigns.name: APT27 / i-Soon indictments (naming conflict)
campaigns.summary: DOJ charged alleged APT27 hackers Yin Kecheng and Zhou Shuai. Some press labeled them 'Silk Typhoon', but this encyclopedia does not adopt that mapping.

campaigns.name: Arrest of Xu Zewei in Milan
campaigns.summary: Italian authorities arrested Xu on 3 July 2025 at US request, and a nine-count US indictment against Xu and Zhang Yu was unsealed. Zhang remains at large.

campaigns.name: MURKY PANDA trusted-relationship cloud compromises
campaigns.summary: CrowdStrike reported that the cluster used SaaS-provider zero-days and Entra ID secrets to read downstream customer email, and abused a Microsoft cloud solution provider's delegated admin privileges.

campaigns.name: Extradition of Xu Zewei
campaigns.summary: Xu was extradited from Italy and appeared in US District Court in Houston, Texas.

diamond.adversary: MSS-directed operators, including contractors. Xu Zewei of Shanghai Powerock Network Co. and Zhang Yu were allegedly tasked by the Shanghai State Security Bureau [S3][S4]. Microsoft calls the group a Chinese state actor [S1].
diamond.capability: Rapid zero-day and n-day exploitation of edge devices and servers (Exchange, NetScaler, GlobalProtect, Ivanti), web shells, credential and secret theft, and Entra ID / OAuth / service-principal abuse for cloud data theft [S1][S2]. The overlapping MURKY PANDA cluster adds Neo-reGeorg and CloudedHope [S5][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: No dedicated infrastructure. The group relies on covert networks of compromised Cyberoam appliances, Zyxel routers and QNAP devices, plus proxies, VPNs and short-lease VPS [S1]. In 2021 it operated mainly from leased US VPS and exfiltrated to MEGA [S2].
diamond.victim: US government at federal, state and local levels; IT service providers and SaaS vendors as stepping stones; and defense, healthcare and research, legal, higher education, think tanks, NGOs and energy [S1][S2][S7].
diamond.socioPolitical: Intelligence on US government policy and administration, legal and law-enforcement matters, sanctions deliberations and pandemic research, reflecting PRC state interests [S1][S3][S7].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing appliances and on-premises servers, hybrid identity (Entra Connect), multi-tenant and OAuth apps, and trust relationships between providers and customers (API keys, delegated admin privileges) [S1][S5].

gaps: No primary DOJ, Treasury or FBI documents could be opened (blocked); indictment and sanctions details come from press coverage [S3][S4][S7][S8].
The CrowdStrike MURKY PANDA blog post could not be fetched; details come from secondary coverage. CrowdStrike frames MURKY PANDA as aligning with Silk Typhoon, not as identical to it [S5][S6].
The Silk Typhoon attribution of the Treasury breach rests on Bloomberg's anonymous sourcing; the government sources gathered name Yin Kecheng, not Silk Typhoon [S7][S8].

Naming conflict: some press labels the March 2025 APT27 indictees (Yin Kecheng, Zhou Shuai) 'Silk Typhoon', while those aliases (APT27, Emissary Panda, Lucky Mouse) map to Linen Typhoon in this encyclopedia. The primary indictment text was not reviewed [S9].

Some press links Silk Typhoon or HAFNIUM to Mandiant's UNC5221, the cluster Google associated with Ivanti exploitation. This was not confirmed in a vendor primary source, so UNC5221 is not added as an alias.
Imported aliases ATK233, Operation Exchange Marauder, Red Dev 13 and 'timmy' were not verified in sources gathered.
The full extent of downstream victims of the 2024-2025 supply-chain activity and of the Commvault-related intrusions is not public in the sources gathered.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain includes internet-facing VPN and edge appliances (Ivanti, NetScaler, GlobalProtect), hybrid identity servers (Entra Connect), and third-party IT, PAM, RMM and SaaS providers that hold API keys or delegated admin rights into DoD and DIB tenants [S1][S5]. STEP 2: The group can turn new edge-device CVEs into exploits within days. Its use of covert networks of compromised SOHO devices and short-lease VPS undermines IP-reputation blocking [S1]. STEP 3: The template is edge-device or provider compromise, then web shell, credential and key-vault theft, then a pivot to Entra ID through service principals or OAuth apps, then mail and SharePoint/OneDrive exfiltration via Graph or EWS, with log clearing [S1][S2]. STEP 4: MLCOA is persistent collection of policy, legal and sanctions-related email and documents from government and contractor tenants through compromised providers [S1][S7]. MDCOA is mass zero-day exploitation of a widely deployed edge product across DoD-adjacent networks during a crisis, as in the Exchange 2021 campaign with more than 12,700 US victims, to harvest planning data at scale [S2][S4]. Candidate indicators: new or renamed Entra ID apps with Office 365-themed names; new credentials added to consented apps; Graph or EWS mail access by service principals; unexpected web shells on edge devices or servers; admin-account resets through provider APIs; and logons from SOHO-device IP space [S1][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: fuse edge-appliance patch status and third-party provider access (API keys, delegated admin privileges) into the common operating picture, because the actor enters through these trust paths [S1][S5]. (2) Authorities: the activity crosses DoD, DIB, commercial SaaS and federal civilian networks (Treasury), so response requires coordinating DC3, CISA and FBI lanes rather than unilateral DoD action [S1][S7]. (3) Mission assurance: inventory and minimize standing provider privileges and multi-tenant app consents, and plan for credential and key rotation at the provider level after a compromise [S1]. (4) Coordination: law-enforcement actions (the Xu Zewei arrest and extradition) have not been assessed as stopping operations, so keep defensive posture independent of indictment news [S3][S4].

HAFNIUM, G0125

provenance.importedSummary: HAFNIUM primarily targets entities in the United States across a number of industry sectors, including infectious disease researchers, law firms, higher education institutions, defense contractors, policy think tanks, and NGOs. Microsoft Threat Intelligence Center (MSTIC) attributes this campaign with high confidence to HAFNIUM, a group assessed to be state-sponsored and operating out of China, based on observed victimology, tactics and procedures. HAFNIUM has previously compromised victims by exploiting vulnerabilities in internet-facing servers, and has used legitimate open-source frameworks, like Covenant, for command and control. Once they’ve gained access to a victim network, HAFNIUM typically exfiltrates data to file sharing sites like MEGA.In campaigns unrelated to these vulnerabilities, Microsoft has observed HAFNIUM interacting with victim Office 365 tenants. While they are often unsuccessful in compromising customer accounts, this reconnaissance activity helps the adversary identify more details about their targets’ environments. HAFNIUM operates primarily from leased virtual private servers (VPS) in the United States.

identification.summary: SilkSpecter is a Chinese financially motivated threat actor that orchestrates phishing campaigns targeting e-commerce shoppers, particularly during peak shopping seasons. They exploit legitimate payment processors like Stripe to exfiltrate Cardholder Data and Personally Identifiable Information through convincing fake e-commerce sites created using the oemapps SaaS platform. Their phishing infrastructure relies on Chinese-hosted CDN servers and utilizes deceptive elements such as the "trusttollsvg" icon and a "/homeapi/collect" endpoint to track victim interactions. Analysts have linked SilkSpecter to over 89 IP addresses and more than 4,000 domain names associated with phishing activities, predominantly using .top, .shop, .store, and .vip TLDs.

Sima is a group of suspected Iranian origin targeting Iranians in diaspora. In February 2016, Iran-focused individuals received messages purporting to be from Human RightsWatch's (HRW) Emergencies Director, requesting that they read an article about Iran pressing Afghanr efugees to fight in Syria. While referencing a real report published by HRW, the links provided for the Director’s biography and article directed the recipient to malware hosted elsewhere. These spear-phishing attempts represent an evolution of Iranian actors based on their social engineering tactics and narrow targeting. Although the messages still had minor grammatical and stylistic errors that would be obvious to a native speaker, the actors demonstrated stronger English-language proficiency than past intrusion sets and a deeper investment in background research prior to the attempt. The actors appropriated a real identity that would be expected to professionally interact with the subject, then offered validation through links to their biography and social media, the former of which itself was malware as well. The bait documents contained a real article relevant to their interests and topic referenced, and the message attempted to address to how it aligned with their professional research or field of employment. The referenced documents sent were malware binaries posing as legitimate files using the common right-to-left filenames tactic in order to conceal the actual file extension. All of these techniques, while common pretexting mechanisms, are a refinement compared to a tendency amongst other groups to simply continually send different forms of generic malware or phishing, in the hopes that one would eventually be successful.

SLIME88 is a China-nexus APT that has exploited the critical vulnerability CVE-2026-34197 in Apache ActiveMQ to deploy SoxAgent RAT, compromising Linux devices and establishing an ORB network tracked as GOBLIN14. The group has targeted IT and manufacturing entities in the US, South Korea, India, and France. Additionally, SLIME88 has aimed at Taiwan’s energy sector using phishing emails and fake certificate installers to deploy backdoor programs like AdaptixC2 and CobaltStrike. They often utilize Cloudflare to obscure their C2 IP addresses, evading detection.

The Smishing Triad is a Chinese-speaking threat group known for targeting postal services and their customers globally through smishing campaigns. They leverage compromised Apple iMessage accounts to send fraudulent messages warning of undeliverable packages, aiming to collect personally identifying information and payment credentials. The group offers smishing kits for sale on platforms like Telegram, enabling other cybercriminals to launch independent attacks. "Smishing Triad" has expanded its operations to target UAE citizens, using geo-filtering to focus on victims in the Emirates.

Microsoft describes Smoke Sandstorm as an Iranian nation-state actor, formerly tracked as BOHRIUM and DEV-0056. In September 2021 it compromised email accounts at a Bahrain-based IT integration company whose Bahrain Government clients were likely the ultimate target [S1]. Microsoft maps Mandiant's UNC1549 and CrowdStrike's IMPERIAL KITTEN to Smoke Sandstorm [S8]. Google Threat Intelligence (Mandiant) describes UNC1549 as an Iran-nexus espionage group targeting aerospace, aviation and defense organizations and their third-party suppliers [S3][S4]. Check Point tracks the overlapping cluster as Nimbus Manticore and reported a new backdoor, MiniFast, in 2026 [S7].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft: earliest dated activity September 2021 [S1]. Mandiant: UNC1549 active since at least June 2022 [S3]. CrowdStrike: IMPERIAL KITTEN active since at least 2017 (reported by The Hacker News) [S6].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Smoke Sandstorm (formerly BOHRIUM, DEV-0056) [S1]. Microsoft's mapping lists IMPERIAL KITTEN and UNC1549 under Smoke Sandstorm [S8]. MITRE tracks NIMBUS MANTICORE as G1059 and lists UNC1549 and TA455 as associated names [S9]. The Hacker News lists GalaxyGato, Nimbus Manticore and Subtle Snail as other names for UNC1549 [S5]. Mandiant's 2024 report noted overlaps with both Tortoiseshell and Smoke Sandstorm/BOHRIUM [S3]. Cluster scopes differ by vendor; see gaps.

attribution.sponsor: Iran. Microsoft lists Iran as the country of origin [S1]. CrowdStrike assesses that IMPERIAL KITTEN likely fulfills Iranian strategic intelligence requirements associated with IRGC operations (as reported by The Hacker News) [S6]. Check Point and press coverage describe Nimbus Manticore as IRGC-affiliated [S7].
attribution.confidence: Mandiant assessed the Iran nexus of UNC1549 with moderate confidence, citing overlaps with Tortoiseshell, which has been linked to the IRGC [S3]. The 2025 GTIG report calls UNC1549 a suspected Iran-nexus, Iranian-backed group and does not name the IRGC [S4]. The IRGC link rests on vendor assessments; no government attribution was found in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and its 2022 civil legal action against BOHRIUM infrastructure [S1][S2]; Mandiant/GTIG incident response [S3][S4]; CrowdStrike and Check Point reporting, relayed by press coverage [S6][S7].

actors.objectives: Espionage. GTIG says UNC1549 primarily seeks network and IT documentation, intellectual property and email, and uses compromised organizations as pivots into their industry partners [S4]. Microsoft assesses that its Middle East targeting serves sectors of interest to the Iranian regime, including government, defense and transportation [S1].

targeting.notes: Microsoft's BOHRIUM reporting stresses supply-chain-style access through IT integrators [S1]. GTIG emphasizes abuse of trusted third parties to reach defense primes [S4]. CrowdStrike's IMPERIAL KITTEN reporting focuses on Israeli transportation, logistics and technology firms [S6].

capabilities.summary: Social engineering with fake recruiter personas and job lures, used by BOHRIUM in 2022 and by UNC1549 through 2025 [S2][S3][S4]. Initial access through trusted third-party relationships and VDI breakouts from Citrix, VMware and Azure Virtual Desktop environments provided to partners [S4]. Custom backdoors and tunnelers: MINIBIKE and MINIBUS [S3]; TWOSTROKE, DEEPROOT, POLLBLEND, GHOSTLINE and LIGHTRAIL [S4]; MiniFast (2026) [S7]. Credential theft through DCSync (DCSYNCER.SLICK), Kerberoasting, AD CS abuse, browser-credential theft (CRASHPAD) and a fake Outlook prompt (TRUSTTRAP) [S4]. Heavy use of Microsoft Azure infrastructure for C2, including more than 125 Azure subdomains in 2024, and lookalike aerospace career domains [S3][S4]. Defense evasion through DLL search-order hijacking of legitimate vendor binaries, unique per-payload hashes, legitimately signed backdoors, reverse SSH tunnels and dormant backdoors that reactivate after eradication [S4]. CrowdStrike reports watering holes, VPN credential theft, one-day exploitation and IMAPLoader malware under IMPERIAL KITTEN [S6]. Check Point assesses that MiniFast code appears AI-assisted [S7].

diamond.adversary: Iranian state-linked operators that Microsoft tracks as Smoke Sandstorm [S1]. Vendors link the overlapping clusters to the IRGC at varying confidence [S3][S6][S7].
diamond.capability: Recruiter and job lures; MINIBIKE/MINIBUS, TWOSTROKE, DEEPROOT, LIGHTRAIL and MiniFast; DCSync, Kerberoasting, AD CS abuse and RDP hijacking [S3][S4][S7].

gaps: Cluster boundaries: Microsoft maps IMPERIAL KITTEN to Smoke Sandstorm [S8], but CrowdStrike's IMPERIAL KITTEN reporting (IMAPLoader, watering holes, since 2017) overlaps with Tortoiseshell-associated activity, and Mandiant noted overlaps with both Tortoiseshell and Smoke Sandstorm [S3][S6]. Do not merge IMPERIAL KITTEN facts into Smoke Sandstorm without vendor confirmation.
MITRE G1059 (NIMBUS MANTICORE) also lists Proofpoint's TA455; Microsoft's mapping does not name TA455 under Smoke Sandstorm. The encyclopedia keeps TA455 as a separate record [S8][S9].

Check Point's 2025 report on Nimbus Manticore expanding into Europe (MiniJunk, MiniBrowse) was referenced in searches but could not be opened (host unreachable), and its date was not confirmed. It is not cited.

Secondary coverage says Check Point observed three Nimbus Manticore waves from February to April 2026, coinciding with the US 'Operation Epic Fury', and a first use of SEO poisoning that impersonated Oracle SQL Developer. Sources for this were undated aggregator pages and were not verified against the primary report.
Kaspersky reporting (NodeRabbit, PollCat, fake coding tests) and Nextron reporting (a fake Ebix recruiter) on Nimbus Manticore surfaced only in search snippets and were not verified.
Dark Reading reported 2025 targeting expansion to the US, UAE, Qatar, Spain and Saudi Arabia; the article date was not confirmed, so it is not cited.
Primary documents not opened: Microsoft's 2022 BOHRIUM blog and civil action filing, CrowdStrike's IMPERIAL KITTEN report, and Check Point's research posts.
No government (USG) attribution or advisory specific to Smoke Sandstorm was found in the sources gathered.
Unit 42 reportedly found no confirmed breaches of targeted oil, gas or aviation firms in the 2026 activity (secondary snippet only, unverified).

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): Key terrain includes defense-industrial-base suppliers, IT integrators and partner-facing VDI (Citrix, VMware, AVD) that bridge into prime contractors and government clients, as well as Active Directory and Azure AD Connect [S1][S4]. STEP 2 (effects): Supplier and integrator compromises let the actor bypass hardened primes, and Azure-hosted C2 blends with legitimate cloud traffic [S3][S4]. STEP 3 (adversary model): Recruiter or job lure, or a supplier pivot, then a custom backdoor (MINIBUS, TWOSTROKE, DEEPROOT, MiniFast), then DCSync and Kerberoasting, then RDP lateral movement, then collection of IT documentation, IP and email [S3][S4][S7]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is persistent espionage against aerospace, aviation and defense suppliers supporting US and partner programs, timed with regional conflict [S4][S7]. MDCOA is the use of supplier access and domain-controller credential resets to cause outages or set up follow-on disruption during an Iran-related crisis; GTIG notes that DC account password resets have already caused outages [S4]. Candidate indicators: job-themed archives from lookalike career domains; DLL side-loading of signed Fortinet, VMware, Citrix or NVIDIA binaries from unusual paths; new reverse SSH tunnels, ZeroTier or ngrok after remediation; DCSync from non-DC hosts; unexpected azurewebsites.net or cloudapp.azure.com beacons [S3][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: fuse DIB supplier compromise reporting with DoD network telemetry, because the actor reaches targets through third parties and partner VDI [S4]. (2) Authorities: much of the relevant terrain sits in contractor and cloud-provider space, so response depends on DC3 and the DIB CS program, cloud-provider takedowns (Microsoft's 2022 domain seizure is a precedent) and law-enforcement partners rather than DoD actions alone [S2][S4]. (3) Mission assurance: dormant backdoors reactivate after eradication, so restoration plans must include full credential and trust resets (including AD CS and Azure AD Connect) and post-remediation hunts [S4]. (4) Coordination: activity has tracked Middle East conflict cycles, so share indicators with coalition partners in Israel, the Gulf and Europe during escalation periods [S3][S7].

provenance.importedSummary: NIMBUS MANTICORE is a State Sponsored cyber espionage group associated with the Iranian Regime specifically the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). NIMBUS MANTICORE has employed social engineering attacks to include HR related themes and has leveraged custom malware against its victims. NIMBUS MANTICORE has sought sensitive information in victims’ environments to include network/IT documentation, intellectual property and emails. NIMBUS MANTICORE has also leveraged compromised organizations as pivot points to access other organizations of interest. NIMBUS MANTICORE has been active since 2021 and has targeted critical infrastructure organizations to include aviation, aerospace, telecommunications and defense and information technology related organizations within the United States, Australia, Midde East and Europe.

relatedRecords.note: MITRE's NIMBUS MANTICORE (G1059) lists Proofpoint's TA455 alongside UNC1549, which Microsoft maps to Smoke Sandstorm. Kept as separate records pending vendor-level confirmation.

identification.summary: SneakyChef is a threat actor known for using the SugarGh0st RAT to target government agencies, research institutions, and organizations worldwide. They have been active since at least August 2023, with a focus on leveraging old and new command and control domains. The group has been observed using lures in the form of scanned documents related to Ministries of Foreign Affairs and embassies. Talos Intelligence assesses with medium confidence that the operators are likely Chinese-speaking based on language preferences and specific targets.

Solntsepek is a threat actor group with ties to the Russian military unit GRU. They have claimed responsibility for a cyberattack on Kyivstar, a Ukrainian mobile operator, and have been linked to previous attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure. Solntsepek has been associated with the Sandworm hacking group, known for their destructive cyberattacks, including the NotPetya worm. They have also engaged in hostile activities, such as revealing personal details of Ukrainian soldiers.

SpaceBears is a ransomware group believed to be based in Moscow, Russia, that has taken credit for several high-profile cyberattacks while primarily operating as a Data Broker. They currently list eight organizations on their Data Leak Site, focusing on medium to small-sized targets. Their methods suggest a reliance on basic extortion strategies rather than sophisticated malware tactics, with no advanced techniques or indicators of ransomware detected.

Spandex Tempest is Microsoft's name for the financially motivated cybercrime actor that Proofpoint tracks as TA505 and CrowdStrike as MONTY SPIDER [S1]. Proofpoint describes TA505 as responsible for the largest malicious spam campaigns it had ever observed, distributing Dridex, Locky, Jaff, The Trick and other malware at high volume through the Necurs botnet [S2]. From late 2018 the group shifted from ransomware-first spam toward backdoors and RATs (ServHelper, FlawedGrace, Get2/SDBbot) aimed heavily at financial institutions [S3][S4]. Fox-IT reported in 2020 that the group had moved toward running most of its operation itself, from initial infection through monetization, including a Clop data-leak site [S5].
identification.firstObserved: Proofpoint's timeline begins with Dridex campaigns in 2014 [S2]; the Proofpoint profile was published in September 2017 [S2].
identification.notes: Microsoft maps Spandex Tempest to MONTY SPIDER and TA505 and labels it 'Financially motivated' [S1]. Microsoft separately tracks Lace Tempest (DEV-0950), which it named as the actor behind the 2023 MOVEit Transfer exploitation linked to the Clop extortion operation [S1][S8]. US government advisories use 'CL0P Ransomware Gang, also known as TA505' [S7], so the industry label TA505 spans activity that Microsoft splits between Spandex Tempest and Lace Tempest. Mandiant tracks related activity as FIN11 and several UNC clusters, which it has treated as overlapping with but not identical to TA505 [S9][S11]. MITRE ATT&CK tracks the group as TA505 (G0092).

attribution.sponsor: No state sponsor identified in the sources gathered; Microsoft classifies Spandex Tempest as financially motivated [S1]. 2019 reporting on CyberInt research describes TA505 as believed to be Russian-speaking [S10].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft's mapping assigns TA505 and MONTY SPIDER to Spandex Tempest [S1]. The 'Russian-speaking' characterization is a vendor belief reported in press coverage, not a government attribution [S10].
attribution.basis: Microsoft naming taxonomy [S1]; Proofpoint campaign tracking from 2014 onward [S2][S3][S4][S6][S12]; Fox-IT analysis of Get2/SDBbot samples [S5]; CyberInt research as reported by SecurityWeek [S10].

actors.objectives: Financial gain through banking-trojan fraud, ransomware, remote-access tooling on financial and retail networks, and data-theft extortion [S1][S2][S3][S5]. Proofpoint describes the actor as opportunistic and trend-setting, changing tactics to follow the most profitable targets [S6].

regions: Global, not focused on a single region [S3]
Financial institutions in Greece, Singapore, UAE, Georgia, Sweden and Lithuania (Sept 2019) [S4]
Financial institutions in Chile, India, Italy, Malawi, Pakistan and South Korea, and US retailers (Dec 2018 to Feb 2019) [S10]
targeting.notes: Proofpoint assessed in 2019 that TA505 focused on financial institutions while alternating with wider campaigns against other verticals [S4]. Victim counts in the CISA Clop advisory (3,000+ US and 8,000+ global organizations) are attributed to the 'CL0P Ransomware Gang, also known as TA505' and should not be assigned to Spandex Tempest alone given Microsoft's separate Lace Tempest cluster [S7][S1].

capabilities.summary: High-volume malspam via the Necurs botnet delivering Dridex, Locky, Jaff, GlobeImposter and Philadelphia [S2][S12]. FlawedAmmyy RAT delivered through Quant Loader in 2018 [S12]. Delphi-based ServHelper backdoor and the full-featured FlawedGrace RAT (first observed November 2017), delivered by Word, Publisher and PDF lures in late 2018 [S3]. Get2 downloader from September 2019 delivering FlawedAmmyy, FlawedGrace, Snatch and the C++ SDBbot RAT [S4]. Abuse of the commercial Remote Manipulator System remote-administration tool against banks and retailers [S10]. HTML redirects in the infection chain and a 'CL0P^_- LEAKS' data-leak site by 2020 [S5]. In 2021, intermediate loaders written in Rebol and KiXtart (tracked by Morphisec as MirrorBlast) replaced Get2 and delivered an updated FlawedGrace [S6].

gaps: Microsoft has not published, in sources found, a dedicated Spandex Tempest profile; the Microsoft name is supported only by the MSTIC naming mapping [S1].

Cluster boundary: Microsoft separates Spandex Tempest (TA505) from Lace Tempest (DEV-0950, Clop/MOVEit), while CISA treats the CL0P gang as 'also known as TA505' and Mandiant uses FIN11/UNC clusters. Accellion, GoAnywhere and MOVEit activity is not confirmed as Spandex Tempest by Microsoft [S1][S7][S8][S9][S11].
Russian-speaking assessment comes from vendor reporting via press; no government attribution of nationality or state nexus located [S10].

Primary documents could not be opened (fetch blocked or DNS failure): Proofpoint blogs, Fox-IT/NCC Group article, CISA AA23-158A, Canadian Centre for Cyber Security TA505/Cl0p profile; details rely on search-result summaries.
Activity attributable specifically to Spandex Tempest after 2021 is not established in the sources gathered.
Imported actor record lists country RU; this is not confirmed by Microsoft, which labels the group only as financially motivated [S1].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: The operational environment is email gateways, user Windows endpoints and, for support functions, financial and payment systems such as finance offices, base retail and contractor payroll [S3][S10]. STEP 2: High-volume campaigns of tens to hundreds of thousands of emails can overwhelm filtering, and the actor swaps loaders and payloads often, which shortens the useful life of signatures [S4][S6]. STEP 3: The doctrinal template is an Office, PDF or MSI lure, then a loader (Get2, Rebol/KiXtart), then a RAT (FlawedGrace, SDBbot, ServHelper, FlawedAmmyy, RMS), followed by monetization through fraud, ransomware or Clop-branded data-leak extortion [S3][S4][S5][S6][S10]. STEP 4: MLCOA is opportunistic phishing that reaches DoD-adjacent finance or contractor users for credential and remote-access theft. MDCOA is ransomware or data-leak extortion against a mission-support contractor that degrades logistics or payroll during an operation. Candidate indicators: macro-enabled Excel or Word lures themed on invoices or insurance claims; MSI execution spawning Rebol or KiXtart interpreters; unexpected RMS/TektonIT remote-admin binaries; HTML redirect chains in phishing links [S3][S6][S10].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: include commodity-crime loader and RAT families in DODIN threat reporting, because this actor's tooling changes yearly [S4][S6]. (2) Authorities: this is a criminal, financially motivated actor [S1], so response will be primarily DCO-IDM and law-enforcement coordination rather than an adversary-state military response. (3) Mission assurance: prioritize contractors and support functions that handle payment and personnel data, given the actor's banking and retail focus and its data-leak extortion model [S3][S5]. (4) Coordination: track vendor naming differences (Spandex Tempest, TA505, Lace Tempest, FIN11, CL0P) in joint reporting to avoid double-counting or merging separate clusters [S1][S7][S9].

provenance.importedSummary: TA505, the name given by Proofpoint, has been in the cybercrime business for at least four years. This is the group behind the infamous Dridex banking trojan and Locky ransomware, delivered through malicious email campaigns via Necurs botnet. Other malware associated with TA505 include Philadelphia and GlobeImposter ransomware families.

identification.summary: Russian nation-state actor focused on email credential theft through tailored, rapport-building spear-phishing of individuals in international affairs, defense, logistics support to Ukraine, think tanks, academia, NGOs and government, mainly in NATO countries [S1][S2][S5]. Microsoft says its activity has historically supported both espionage and cyber-influence objectives [S1]. The UK NCSC and allied agencies assess it is almost certainly subordinate to FSB Centre 18 [S5][S6]. Since at least 2022-2023 it has added selective custom malware (SPICA, LOSTKEYS, and the NOROBOT/MAYBEROBOT chain) to its phishing operations [S4][S9][S11].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft has tracked the actor since 2017 [S2]. NCSC reporting (via coverage) describes activity since at least 2015, including spear-phishing of UK parliamentarians [S6].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Star Blizzard (formerly SEABORGIUM; renamed April 2023) [S2]. Microsoft says its indicators and tactics overlap with Callisto Group (F-Secure), TA446 (Proofpoint) and COLDRIVER (Google) [S2]. Google lists COLDRIVER as also known as UNC4057, Star Blizzard and Callisto [S4]. The December 2023 joint advisory (per search summary) lists SEABORGIUM, Callisto Group, TA446, COLDRIVER, TAG-53 and BlueCharlie as aliases [S5]. Ukraine's SSU associated Callisto with Gamaredon (ACTINIUM), but Microsoft said it had not observed technical intrusion links supporting that association [S2]. Citizen Lab's COLDWASTREL is assessed as a distinct actor targeting similar communities and must not be merged with Star Blizzard [S10][S12].

attribution.sponsor: Russian Federation, Federal Security Service (FSB). The UK NCSC and partners assess Star Blizzard is almost certainly subordinate to FSB Centre 18 [S5][S6]. DOJ described the group as an operational unit within FSB Center 18 (per coverage of the October 2024 seizure) [S8].
attribution.confidence: Government: NCSC uses 'almost certainly' for Centre 18 subordination (December 2023), jointly with US and other Five Eyes agencies [S5][S6]. Microsoft calls it a Russian nation-state actor without a formal confidence rating [S1]. Google calls COLDRIVER 'Russian government-backed' without naming an agency [S4].
attribution.basis: Joint advisory and NCSC attribution statement [S5][S6]. US charges (December 2023) against Ruslan Peretyatko, described as an FSB Center 18 officer, and Andrey Korinets, with US Treasury and UK sanctions and a State Department reward of up to $10 million (per press coverage) [S7]. Microsoft and Google telemetry and infrastructure analysis [S1][S2][S4]. Microsoft civil action and DOJ domain seizures in October 2024 [S8].

actors.objectives: Intelligence collection in support of Russia's strategic interests, per Google [S4]. Microsoft assesses it likely supports traditional espionage and information operations rather than financial goals [S2]. In a small number of cases stolen material has been leaked, including hack-and-leak operations against UK officials and an NGO, and NCSC links it to leaks intended to interfere in UK politics [S4][S6]. It also targets exiled Russian opposition figures and Western civil society [S10].

sectors: Government and diplomacy, current and former officials [S3][S4]
Defense and intelligence consultancies; defense-industrial firms (from 2022) [S2][S5]
US government agencies including the intelligence community, DoD and defense contractors, State Department and Department of Energy facilities (2016-2022, per indictment coverage) [S7]
Think tanks and Russia-focused international-relations researchers [S2][S3]
NGOs, IGOs and civil society, including funders [S2][S8][S10]
regions: United States and United Kingdom (most targeted) [S2][S5]
Other NATO countries, with occasional Baltic, Nordic and Eastern European targeting [S2][S5]
targeting.notes: The actor mainly targets personal or NGO email accounts rather than corporate ones [S4][S5]. About 30% of Microsoft's nation-state notifications for this actor went to consumer email accounts [S2]. Microsoft observed targeting of more than 30 organizations in 2022 and more than 30 civil-society organizations between January 2023 and August 2024 [S2][S8].

capabilities.summary: Core tradecraft: reconnaissance of targets, fake social-media profiles and new webmail accounts impersonating trusted contacts, then benign rapport-building emails, often referencing a non-existent attachment, before any malicious link [S2][S5]. It harvests credentials with Evilginx adversary-in-the-middle pages, which capture passwords and MFA tokens [S1][S2]. Lures include custom PDFs, password-protected PDFs or Proton Drive links, and altered OneDrive notifications (July-August 2024) [S1]. Evasion includes HubSpot and MailerLite redirect URLs, multiple registrars, link shorteners, open redirects, Microsoft Safe Links abuse, browser fingerprinting, hCaptcha, a DNS/reverse-proxy service and randomized domains [S1]. Microsoft says it adopts TTPs for brief periods and changes them once they are publicly known [S1]. After compromise it exfiltrates mail and sets forwarding rules to dead-drop accounts [S2]. In November 2024 it used QR codes to link targets' WhatsApp accounts to actor-controlled devices, its first use of WhatsApp [S3]. Selective malware: the Rust backdoor SPICA, delivered as a fake PDF decryption tool and believed in use since November 2022 [S9]; LOSTKEYS, a VBS file stealer delivered through a ClickFix fake CAPTCHA and PowerShell chain (January-April 2025) [S4]; and, after LOSTKEYS was exposed, the COLDCOPY lure, NOROBOT DLL, YESROBOT Python backdoor and MAYBEROBOT PowerShell backdoor (May-June 2025) [S11].

diamond.adversary: FSB Centre 18-linked operators (NCSC: almost certainly) [S5][S6]. US charges name Ruslan Peretyatko, described as an FSB officer, and Andrey Korinets [S7].
diamond.capability: Evilginx AiTM credential and MFA-token theft; PDF, Proton Drive and OneDrive-themed lures; WhatsApp device linking; SPICA, LOSTKEYS and NOROBOT/YESROBOT/MAYBEROBOT malware [S1][S3][S4][S9][S11].
diamond.infrastructure: Actor-registered domains across multiple registrars, VPS servers running Evilginx, a DNS/reverse-proxy service, email marketing platforms (HubSpot, MailerLite) as redirectors, link shorteners, and newly created webmail sender accounts (often Proton) [S1][S2]. Over 100 domains were seized in October 2024 [S8].
diamond.victim: Government, defense, think-tank, academic, NGO, journalist and politician targets in the US, the UK and NATO, often through personal email; Russian exiles [S2][S4][S5][S10].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection on Russia, Ukraine and NATO policy; selective leaks intended to interfere in UK politics; targeting of Russian dissidents abroad [S4][S6][S10].
diamond.technology: Consumer and cloud email, phishable MFA, WhatsApp linked-device features, and Windows scripting (PowerShell via the Run dialog, rundll32) [S1][S3][S4][S11].

gaps: Primary government documents were not opened: the joint advisory, NCSC news pages, DOJ press release, indictment and Treasury designation were blocked. Their content comes from search summaries and press coverage [S5][S6][S7][S8].

Original Google TAG SPICA blog, GTIG October 2025 ROBOT-chain report, Citizen Lab 'Rivers of Phish' report and Zscaler's BAITSWITCH/SIMPLEFIX report were not opened; details come from search results and secondary coverage [S9][S10][S11].

Vendor naming: TAG-53 and BlueCharlie (Recorded Future), IRON FRONTIER (Secureworks) and GOSSAMER BEAR (CrowdStrike) come from the imported record or advisory alias lists and were not checked against the vendors' own reporting.
COLDWASTREL (Citizen Lab) and PwC's related tracking are assessed as distinct from COLDRIVER; the relationship is unresolved [S10][S12].
The SSU-proposed link to Gamaredon (ACTINIUM) is unconfirmed by Microsoft [S2].
Google could not confirm whether December 2023 Maltego-themed LOSTKEYS samples belong to COLDRIVER [S4].
The year of the Institute for Statecraft compromise differs across reports (2018 vs 2019) [S6].
No public reporting on activity after October 2025 surfaced in searches; search results showed NCSC PDFs re-hosted under 2026 paths, but their content could not be opened.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is the personal email, cloud accounts and messaging apps (WhatsApp) of senior leaders, policy advisers, defense-industrial staff, Ukraine-assistance logistics personnel and their outside contacts. Much of this sits outside DoD network boundaries [S1][S3][S5]. STEP 2: Reliance on credible impersonation and phishable MFA makes identity the operating environment. Rapid TTP and infrastructure turnover after public exposure shortens indicator lifespan [S1][S3][S8]. STEP 3: The template is reconnaissance and a fake persona, a benign rapport email, a PDF, link or QR lure, Evilginx credential and token capture or WhatsApp device linking, then mailbox exfiltration and forwarding rules. A selective malware branch runs from a ClickFix fake CAPTCHA through PowerShell to LOSTKEYS or the NOROBOT/MAYBEROBOT chain [S1][S2][S3][S4][S11]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued credential phishing of personal accounts of US, UK and NATO defense and policy figures for intelligence on Ukraine support and Russia policy. MDCOA is a timed leak of stolen planning or political correspondence during a crisis or election to undermine allied cohesion [S4][S6]. Candidate indicators: unsolicited mail from known contacts on new webmail addresses; mail citing a missing attachment; password-protected PDFs or Proton Drive links; Safe Links-wrapped shortened URLs; new inbox forwarding rules; unexpected WhatsApp linked devices; PowerShell or rundll32 launched from the Run dialog after a CAPTCHA page [S1][S2][S3][S4][S11].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: victims are mostly personal and NGO accounts, so DoD sensors will miss much of this activity. JCC2 pictures should include partner reporting from NCSC, Microsoft and Google [S2][S4][S5]. (2) Authorities: personal accounts and commercial messaging platforms fall outside DODIN defensive authorities. Response there relies on FBI, DOJ and industry actions such as the October 2024 domain seizures [S7][S8]. (3) Mission assurance: phishing-resistant MFA and personal-account hygiene for key leaders and Ukraine-support staff reduce exposure to AiTM credential theft. Script-execution restrictions reduce ClickFix risk [S1][S4]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with Five Eyes partners and the DIB, and expect rapid infrastructure rebuilding after exposure [S5][S8].

provenance.importedSummary: The Callisto Group is an advanced threat actor whose known targets include military personnel, government officials, think tanks, and journalists in Europe and the South Caucasus. Their primary interest appears to be gathering intelligence related to foreign and security policy in the Eastern Europe and South Caucasus regions.

identification.summary: Storm-0133 is Microsoft's name for the cluster that other vendors track as HEXANE, Lyceum, Siamesekitten and Spirlin. Microsoft lists its origin as Iran [S1]. Secureworks CTU disclosed the group as LYCEUM in August 2019. CTU said it had been active since about April 2018 against organizations of strategic national importance, including oil and gas and possibly telecommunications [S2][S3]. Dragos separately disclosed it as HEXANE at Black Hat 2019 [S4]. Later public reporting covers telecom and ISP intrusions in the Middle East and Africa in 2021 [S5][S6], Israeli IT-sector targeting via fake job lures in 2021 [S7], and a custom DNS backdoor used against Middle Eastern energy and telecom targets in 2022 [S8][S9].
identification.firstObserved: 2018 (Secureworks: active since about April 2018; earliest campaign mid-2018 against South African targets) [S2]; Dragos also says active since 2018 [S4].
identification.notes: Microsoft's mapping equates Storm-0133 with HEXANE, Lyceum, Siamesekitten and Spirlin [S1]. The imported summary says the group has been 'active since at least 2014' and is 'linked to APT34'. Neither claim is supported by the sources gathered here, so both are excluded (see gaps). Storm-#### is Microsoft's designation for an emerging or developing cluster [S1].

attribution.sponsor: Iran (Microsoft lists Iran as origin) [S1]. No specific Iranian government organization is named in the sources gathered.
attribution.confidence: Microsoft lists the cluster's origin as Iran [S1]. At disclosure in 2019, Secureworks CTU saw tradecraft resembling the Iranian groups COBALT GYPSY and COBALT TRINITY. CTU found no direct malware or infrastructure links and said technical evidence was insufficient for an attribution assessment [S2]. ClearSky described Siamesekitten/Lyceum as Iranian [S6][S7]. Zscaler ThreatLabz reporting describes the group as Iran-linked [S8].
attribution.basis: Vendor tradecraft comparison (Secureworks) [S2]; ClearSky campaign analysis [S7]; Zscaler analysis of an Iranian-military-themed lure [S8]; Microsoft naming taxonomy [S1]. No government attribution was found in the sources gathered.

actors.objectives: Espionage and access against strategically important energy and telecommunications organizations [S2][S5][S6]. Dragos assessed that telecom access could serve as a stepping stone to network-focused man-in-the-middle attacks [S4]. ClearSky assessed that 2021 targeting of Israeli IT and communications firms was most likely meant to enable supply-chain attacks [S7].

sectors: IT and communications service providers (supply chain) [S7]
Government (an African ministry of foreign affairs) [S6]
targeting.notes: Targeting staff in the 2019 Secureworks reporting were executives, HR staff and IT personnel [S2]. Victim names in the 2021 ISP and telecom intrusions were not disclosed [S6].

capabilities.summary: Initial access through credential harvesting by password spraying or brute force, followed by spearphishing with malicious Excel attachments that install the .NET RAT DanBot [S2]. Earlier tooling included PowerShell scripts alongside DanBot [S5]. In 2021 Kaspersky reported a shift from PowerShell scripts and DanBot to new C++ malware it named James and Kevin [S5]. In 2021 ClearSky reported a chain of fake-recruiter social engineering and impersonation of real Israeli firms on LinkedIn, with Excel lures dropping the Milan backdoor (which fetched DanBot), later replaced by the .NET backdoor Shark [S7]. Zscaler reported a custom .NET DNS backdoor in 2022 (DnsSystem, modified from open-source DIG.net). It was delivered by a macro-laden Word document posing as Iranian military news, persisted via the Startup folder, and used DNS hijacking with TXT-record command retrieval and A-record exfiltration [S8][S9].

diamond.adversary: Iran-origin cluster per Microsoft (Storm-0133). Tracked as HEXANE, Lyceum, Siamesekitten and Spirlin [S1]. The sponsoring organization is not publicly identified in the gathered sources [S2].
diamond.capability: Password spraying and brute force; Excel and Word macro lures; DanBot, Milan, Shark, James/Kevin and DnsSystem backdoors with DNS-based C2 [S2][S5][S7][S8].
diamond.infrastructure: Actor-controlled DNS servers used for DNS tunneling and hijacking C2 [S8]. Phishing sites mimicking Israeli IT companies and fake LinkedIn profiles [S7]. A HivePro advisory lists IOCs such as the cyberclub[.]one domain [S9].
diamond.victim: Energy (oil and gas), telecom operators and ISPs, IT service providers, aviation, and a foreign ministry. Victims are located in the Middle East, North Africa, South Africa and Israel [S2][S4][S5][S6][S7].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection against regional energy and communications infrastructure. Possible use of telecom access for man-in-the-middle operations (Dragos assessment) [S4]. Supply-chain access to Israeli organizations (ClearSky assessment) [S7].
diamond.technology: Reliance on DNS protocol C2 that blends with normal traffic [S8]. Exposure of single-factor enterprise accounts to password spraying [S2]. Trust in recruiters and HR channels [S7].

gaps: Primary documents not opened: Secureworks/Sophos blog (fetch blocked), Kaspersky VB2021 paper, ClearSky Siamesekitten report, Accenture CIFR/Prevailion PACT report, Zscaler ThreatLabz blog, Dragos HEXANE profile, Google 'Tool of First Resort' PDF (fetch failed). Facts rely on search-result summaries of secondary coverage.
Several source dates are approximate. The Kaspersky/Dark Reading item (S5) and the Heimdal/ClearSky item (S7) are dated by event timing, not a verified publication date.

No sponsoring Iranian organization (e.g., MOIS or IRGC) is named in any gathered source. Secureworks said evidence was insufficient for attribution in 2019. Do not upgrade vendor assessments to government attribution.
Imported summary claims 'active since at least 2014' and a link to APT34. Neither is supported by the gathered sources and both were excluded pending verification.

Aliases Chrono Kitten (CrowdStrike), MYSTICDOME and UNC1530 (Mandiant) come from the imported record. They were not confirmed in sources read here. The Google 'Tool of First Resort' report on Israel-Hamas war cyber activity may cover UNC1530 but could not be opened.
No public reporting from 2023 onward was found in this research pass. Current activity status is unknown.
ATT&CK G1001 page could not be fetched (DNS failure); technique and software lists come from the imported MITRE data, not this research.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): Key terrain is regional telecom operators, ISPs, energy companies and IT service providers in the Middle East and North Africa. Partner-nation and host-nation networks supporting deployed forces likely transit these providers [S4][S6]. STEP 2 (effects): Compromised ISPs and telecoms could expose communications that transit them to interception or man-in-the-middle activity (Dragos assessment) [S4]. Compromised IT suppliers could provide downstream access (ClearSky assessment) [S7]. STEP 3 (threat model): Password spraying or recruitment-themed social engineering, then macro-laden Office lures, then a .NET or C++ backdoor with DNS-based C2 [S2][S7][S8]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is persistent espionage access inside regional telecom and energy organizations for collection [S2][S6]. MDCOA is use of telecom or ISP access to intercept or manipulate traffic of partner or US-associated networks during a regional crisis [S4]. Candidate indicators: bursts of failed logons consistent with password spraying [S2]; Office documents with AutoClose macros writing to Startup folders [S8]; anomalous DNS TXT-record query volume to rare domains [S8]; recruiter outreach impersonating legitimate firms [S7].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: Track the security posture of partner-nation telecom and ISP carriers in the AOR, because this actor focused on that layer [S4][S6]. (2) Mission assurance: Assume transit over regional carriers may be observed. Rely on end-to-end encryption and avoid dependence on carrier-provided DNS [S4][S8]. (3) Detection: Prioritize DNS analytics and password-spray detection on DoD-adjacent and partner enclaves [S2][S8]. (4) Coordination and authorities: Activity against partner-nation infrastructure falls under host-nation and private-sector authorities. Coordinate through combatant command, partner CERTs and vendor reporting channels rather than acting unilaterally.

provenance.importedSummary: Lyceum is an Iranian APT group that has been active since at least 2014. They primarily target Middle Eastern governments and organizations in the energy and telecommunications sectors. Lyceum is known for using cyber espionage techniques and has been linked to other Iranian threat groups such as APT34. They have developed and deployed malware families like Shark and Milan, and have been observed using DNS tunneling and HTTPfor command and control communication.

identification.summary: Proofpoint researchers detected campaigns from a relatively new actor, tracked internally as TA2101, targeting German companies and organizations to deliver and install backdoor malware. The actor initiated their campaigns impersonating the Bundeszentralamt fur Steuern, the German Federal Ministry of Finance, with lookalike domains, verbiage, and stolen branding in the emails. For their campaigns in Germany, the actor chose Cobalt Strike, a commercially licensed software tool that is generally used for penetration testing and emulates the type of backdoor framework used by Metasploit, a similar penetration testing tool. Proofpoint researchers have also observed this actor distributing Maze ransomware, employing similar social engineering techniques to those it uses for Cobalt Strike, while also targeting organizations in Italy and impersonating the Agenzia Delle Entrate, the Italian Revenue Agency. We have also recently observed the actor targeting organizations in the United States using the IcedID banking Trojan while impersonating the United States Postal Service (USPS).

identification.summary: Storm-0247 is Microsoft's name for a China-origin threat actor that Microsoft maps to ToddyCat and Websiic [S1]. Kaspersky named ToddyCat in June 2022 and described an APT that compromised Microsoft Exchange servers to hit mainly government and military organizations in Europe and Asia, using two previously unknown tools, the Samurai backdoor and the Ninja Trojan [S2][S3]. Later Kaspersky reporting (2023-2025) describes an expanding toolkit focused on large-scale data collection and exfiltration, email theft and defense evasion [S5][S6][S7][S8].
identification.firstObserved: Kaspersky: first detected in December 2020, attacking Exchange servers [S2][S3].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Storm-0247 (origin China; other names ToddyCat, Websiic) [S1]. ToddyCat is Kaspersky's name [S2]. Websiic is the name ESET gave in March 2021 to a newly detected actor exploiting the Exchange ProxyLogon vulnerabilities [S4]. Most detailed reporting uses the ToddyCat name, and technical details here come from Kaspersky reporting as covered by trade press. MITRE ATT&CK tracks the group as ToddyCat (G1022).

attribution.sponsor: Microsoft lists the actor's origin as China [S1]. Trade-press coverage describes ToddyCat as China-linked or Chinese [S3][S7]. No cited source names a specific PRC government sponsor.
attribution.confidence: Microsoft's China origin label is a vendor assessment in its naming table and does not name a sponsoring agency [S1]. Coverage of Kaspersky's 2022 report does not clearly attribute ToddyCat to a Chinese state actor. Kaspersky's comment about a 'Chinese-speaking' group in the same period referred to a different group [S3]. No government attribution or indictment was found.
attribution.basis: Microsoft's public threat-actor naming map [S1]. Kaspersky technical reporting from 2022 to 2025, carried in vendor press releases and trade press [S2][S3][S5][S6][S7][S8]. ESET's 2021 ProxyLogon reporting for the Websiic cluster [S4].

actors.objectives: Cyber espionage. The actor collects and exfiltrates sensitive data, at what Kaspersky calls 'industrial scale', from government and defense-related organizations [S2][S6]. From 2024-2025 it also stole email data and Microsoft 365 access tokens to keep reaching victim mailboxes [S8].

regions: Asia, including Taiwan and Vietnam in early intrusions [S2]
Kaspersky also reports related activity against entities in Afghanistan, India, Indonesia, Iran, Kyrgyzstan, Malaysia, Pakistan, Russia, Slovakia, Thailand, the UK and Uzbekistan [S2]
targeting.notes: Kaspersky reports that the group first hit Exchange servers in 2020-2021 and from September 2021 shifted to desktop machines of government and diplomatic entities in Asia [S2]. The 2024 reporting emphasizes government organizations in the Asia-Pacific region, some of them defense-related [S6].

capabilities.summary: Initial access: exploitation of Exchange servers, first through an unknown exploit that deployed the China Chopper web shell and then through ProxyLogon from February-March 2021 [S2][S3]. Custom implants: Samurai, a modular C# passive backdoor working on ports 80/443 and built mainly to run arbitrary C# code, and Ninja, a post-exploitation toolkit that lets several operators work on one host at once [S2][S3]. Exfiltration (2023): LoFiSe finds target files and Pcexter uploads archives to OneDrive. Kaspersky also reported a Dropbox uploader and a passive UDP backdoor, plus staging with 7z [S5]. Persistence and collection (2024): several redundant tunnels (reverse SSH, SoftEther VPN, Ngrok, FRP), some binaries renamed to look legitimate, and WAExp and TomBerBil for WhatsApp Web data and browser credentials [S6]. Defense evasion (2024-2025): abuse of CVE-2024-11859, a DLL search-order hijack in ESET's command-line scanner that requires admin rights, to load TCESB. TCESB uses BYOVD with a vulnerable Dell driver (CVE-2021-36276) and runs AES-decrypted payloads in memory [S7]. Email access (2025): TCSectorCopy reads disk sectors to copy Outlook OST files that Outlook has locked; the actor also used a PowerShell TomBerBil variant run from domain controllers over SMB, and SharpTokenFinder or ProcDump on Outlook.exe to recover Microsoft 365 tokens [S8].
